## Right to rent follow-up check reminders for letting agents in England
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/right-to-rent-follow-up-check-reminders/

A right to rent follow-up check is needed in England when a tenant's first check showed a time-limited right to rent. The Home Office code of practice (1 October 2026) says it must be done before the time-limited statutory excuse ends: the latest of 12 months after the last check, the end of the tenant's permission to be in the UK, or the expiry of the document that proves it. Missing it can leave the landlord, or an agent who took on the duty in writing, open to a civil penalty.

Right to rent follow-up check reminders are easy to forget because the date can be a year or more away from move-in, long after the file has been put away, unlike the [gas safety and EICR dates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/letting-agent-compliance-certificate-reminders/) that come round on a fixed cycle. The initial check gets done because nobody can move in without it. The follow-up only happens if someone remembers. This page sets out when the follow-up is due, how to work out the date from the check you already did, a reminder timeline that starts early enough to deal with problems, and a message you can send the tenant. It is about never missing the date, not legal advice: read the Home Office guidance on gov.uk for the full rules.

### This applies in England only
The Right to Rent Scheme comes from the Immigration Act 2014 and covers residential tenancies in England. The Home Office landlord's guide (1 October 2026) says it applies to tenancy agreements first entered into on or after 1 February 2016 in England, or on or after 1 December 2014 in Birmingham, Wolverhampton, Dudley, Sandwell and Walsall. There is no right to rent check in Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland, so leave properties there out of this workflow. Gov.uk also reminds landlords to check every adult tenant, not only people they think are not British, and not to discriminate.

### When a follow-up check is due
The Home Office code of practice and landlord's guide (both 1 October 2026) set the timing by the evidence used in the first check. You need a follow-up check only when that check gave a time-limited statutory excuse. A List A document, or an online check showing a continuous right to rent, needs no follow-up.
First check was based on | The time-limited excuse ends
--- | ---
A List B document (time-limited permission) | The latest of: 12 months after the check, the end of the person's permission, or the expiry of their immigration document
A Home Office online check showing a time-limited right to rent | On the follow-up date the online service gives you (keep the PDF or HTML copy that shows it)
An eligible visitor (EEA, Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea or USA national) | 12 months after the date of the check
A positive right to rent notice from the Landlord Checking Service | 12 months after the date in the notice

### How to work out the follow-up date
1. Find the evidence of the first check in the tenancy file: the document copies or the online check result, and the date the check was made.
2. If it was an online check, use the follow-up date the Home Office service gave. Record it exactly as shown.
3. If it was a List B document, write down three dates: 12 months after the check, the end of the tenant's permission, and the document's expiry date. The excuse lasts until the latest of the three.
4. Do this for every adult in the property. Each person can have a different date, and a child who turns 18 during the tenancy is included when the next follow-up check is due.
5. Put each date in your tracker against the tenant and the property, and set the reminders from that date (see the timeline below).
6. Have a second person check the date. One typed digit is all it takes to miss a deadline.

### What happens if the tenant can't show a continued right to rent
The guide says to ask the tenant for evidence: a share code for the Home Office online service, or documents from List A or List B. If they can't produce evidence but say they have an application in progress, you contact the Landlord Checking Service. If the check shows they no longer have the right to rent, or they won't cooperate, you must report it to the Home Office as soon as reasonably practicable and before your current excuse expires. Keep the reference number the report gives you. The code adds that a check done after the expiry date may mean you have to explain why it was late. Penalties in the 2026 code are £10,000 per occupier and £5,000 per lodger for a first breach, and £20,000 and £10,000 for a repeat breach within 3 years. Where an agent has accepted responsibility in writing, the penalty falls on the agent, not the landlord. Keep copies of every check for the tenancy and for at least one year after it ends.

### A reminder timeline
Start early. A tenant waiting on a Home Office decision needs time, and the Landlord Checking Service can take up to two working days to reply. The workflow sends the reminders. A person does the actual check.
When | What happens | Who
--- | --- | ---
90 days before | The tenant is added to the month's follow-up list. Landlord told a check is coming, if you manage it for them | Workflow
60 days before | First message to the tenant asking for a right to rent share code or documents | Workflow
45 days before | Reminder to the tenant if nothing has arrived | Workflow
30 days before | Phone call to the tenant. If they mention an application in progress, the Landlord Checking Service route is considered | A person in the office
When evidence arrives | The online check or document check is done, the result is saved, and the next follow-up date is set | A person in the office
14 days before | Anything still open goes to the manager with the full history | Workflow, then a person decides
Before the date | If the tenant has no right to rent or won't cooperate, the report to the Home Office is made and the reference number saved | A person in the office

### Tenant message template
Send the same message to every tenant who needs a follow-up check, with the same wording and timing, whatever their nationality.
Email or text to the tenant:
```
Subject: Your right to rent check at [property address]

Hi [tenant name],

When you moved in, we checked your right to rent in England, as the law requires for every adult tenant. Your check needs to be repeated by [date].

The quickest way is a right to rent share code. You can get one on GOV.UK by searching "prove your right to rent in England". Right to rent share codes start with the letter R. Please send it to us with your date of birth.

If you don't have an eVisa or a share code, reply and we'll arrange a time to see your documents.

If you've applied to extend your permission and are waiting for a decision, please tell us. There's a separate process for that, and we can help.

Please reply by [date, 2 weeks from now].

Thanks,
[your name], [agency name]
```

### What the workflow does, and what stays with you
- Keeps one list of every adult tenant with a time-limited right to rent, their follow-up date and where the evidence is stored
- Sends the tenant messages on your timeline and logs each one
- Collects the share code or document photos in one place and tells the office they've arrived
- Gives the manager a weekly list of follow-ups due in the next 90 days and anything overdue
- Stays with you: running the online check or checking the documents, deciding when to contact the Landlord Checking Service, and making any report to the Home Office

### Do we need a follow-up check when the tenant's visa ends?
Not always on that day. The Home Office guide says not to assume a follow-up is due when permission expires if a longer statutory excuse applies, for example the 12 months after the check. You can still check earlier if you want to.

### Does this apply in Wales or Scotland?
No. Right to rent checks apply to residential tenancies in England only.

The landlord, unless the agent has accepted responsibility for compliance in writing. Then the penalty falls on the agent. Check what your terms of business say.

## Source of funds documents for conveyancing, and how to stop chasing them
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/conveyancing-source-of-funds-document-chasing/

Source of funds documents for conveyancing are the evidence a firm collects to show where a buyer's money for the purchase comes from, such as payslips and savings statements, a signed gift letter, or a completion statement from a sale. The SRA says a bank statement on its own is not enough. A workflow can send the right list for each way of funding, chase what is missing and show the team which files are complete, while your firm decides what evidence it accepts.

Source of funds documents for conveyancing are the part of [client onboarding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-client-intake/) that holds files up most. The buyer sends a passport and one bank statement, the gifting parent hasn't been asked yet, and the fee earner finds the gap a week later. Each request is slightly different, because it depends on how the purchase is funded. That makes it look like work only a person can do, but the request itself follows your firm's own rules. This page is written for conveyancing teams in England and Wales. It covers what to ask for, how to ask and how to chase, not what your AML policy should say.

### What the SRA expects
Under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, conveyancing is in scope, so you check not just that the client has the money but that it comes from a legitimate source. The SRA's thematic review of source of funds and wealth compliance (published 5 November 2025) looked at 5,873 files across 833 firms. The SRA reported that 11% of the files it reviewed had no source of funds checks, and that in 18% source of funds or wealth had not been scrutinised adequately. The SRA's AML questions and answers say you cannot assume funds are legitimate because they come from a UK bank account, and that it is not enough to gather bank statements and put them on file. Source of wealth checks, meaning how the client built up their overall wealth, are required where funds come from a politically exposed person or a client in a high-risk third country, and should follow when the source of funds raises questions. The SRA also publishes an optional source of funds form for clients. Licensed conveyancers regulated by the CLC should check the CLC's own guidance.

### Documents by funding type
This table follows the examples in the SRA's AML questions and answers. It is a starting point for your request list, not a rule. How much you ask for depends on your firm's risk assessment of the client and the matter, and your MLRO or compliance person has the final say.
How the purchase is funded | Documents to request | What the evidence should show
--- | --- | ---
Savings from salary | Recent payslips and savings account statements covering the period the money built up (longer for long-term saving) | Regular deposits that make sense for the client's job, age and income
Gift from family | A signed gift letter or gift deed from each giftor, the giftor's ID, and evidence of the giftor's own source of funds | The gift is genuine, not a loan, and the giftor's money is legitimate
Sale of another property | The completion statement from the sale, or a letter from the selling solicitor, and the statement showing the proceeds received | The proceeds match the amount going into the purchase
Mortgage | The mortgage offer | The lender is a regulated bank or building society
Inheritance | The will and grant of probate, or a letter from the solicitor handling the estate, and the statement showing receipt | The client is a beneficiary and the amount matches
Divorce settlement or court award | The court order or a letter from a regulated solicitor, and the statement showing receipt | The award is real and the amount matches
Loan (not a mortgage) | The loan agreement | The loan is genuine and on commercial terms; more questions if the lender is not regulated
Money from a company | The company's accounts and how the client controls it | The business and its funds make sense

### A request you can copy
Source of funds request to a buyer:
```
Subject: Your purchase of [property address]: where the money is coming from

Dear [client name],

The law requires us to check where the money for your purchase comes from. We ask every buyer for this, and it isn't a sign that anything is wrong. The Solicitors Regulation Authority explains why here: [link to the SRA's page on anti-money laundering checks].

You told us your purchase will be funded by: [funding sources].

For that, please send us:
[document list for each source]

If a family member is giving you money, we will write to them separately with what they need to send.

Please upload everything here: [secure upload link]. Please don't send screenshots, and please send full statements rather than single pages.

If you're not sure what something means, reply to this email and [fee earner name] will help.

Kind regards,
[firm name]
```

### The chase sequence
1. At instruction, the client completes a short form saying how the purchase is funded and naming any giftors.
2. The workflow sends the request above with the document list for each funding source the client ticked, and a separate request to each giftor.
3. As documents arrive, each is marked against the list, so the client is only ever asked for what is still missing.
4. After 3 working days, a reminder [lists the missing items by name](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/).
5. After 7 working days, a second reminder, and the file appears on the fee earner's list for a phone call.
6. When everything on the list is in, the file goes to the fee earner or compliance person to review the evidence and record their decision.
7. If the reviewer asks for more, the workflow sends that follow-up request and the cycle starts again.

### What stays with you
Everything that needs judgement. Your AML policy sets what you accept, and a person decides whether the evidence is enough, whether source of wealth checks are needed and whether anything should be reported. The workflow sends, tracks and reminds. It never tells a client their checks are complete. Records stay in your own systems: the Regulations require due diligence records to be kept for five years after the business relationship ends (regulation 40), so keep the documents in your case management system or document store, not in an inbox.

No. It collects documents against the list your firm sets and tells you when the list is complete. A person reviews the evidence and records the decision.

### Can it handle gifted deposits?
Yes. Each giftor gets their own request for a gift letter, ID and evidence of their own funds, and their documents are tracked separately on the same file.

No. If your app collects source of funds, the workflow sends the client its link and chases until it's done. It only fills the gaps your current tools leave.

## Mortgage broker document collection: checklist, requests and chasers
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/mortgage-broker-document-collection/

Mortgage broker document collection is gathering each client's payslips, bank statements, ID and other evidence a lender needs before an application can be submitted. A workflow can send each client the checklist for their situation (employed, self-employed or contractor), mark off what arrives, chase only what is missing and show the broker whose pack is ready for the lender. The broker still checks every document and decides what goes to which lender.

Mortgage broker document collection is where cases stall. The advice meeting goes well, the client promises to send everything by Friday, and two weeks later you have three payslips, a photo of a passport and no bank statements. Meanwhile the property is under offer and the agent is asking for an update. Asking for documents, keeping track of them and [reminding people](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) is the same job on every case, so it can run on its own while you spend your time on advice and lenders. This page is written for small UK brokerages. Insurance brokers have a similar job at renewal time: see [renewal reminders for insurance brokers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-renewal-reminders/).

### Why lenders need the paperwork
The FCA's responsible lending rules put the duty on the lender. MCOB 11.6.8 R says a lender must obtain evidence of the income the customer declares, must not accept self-certification of income, and the evidence must come from a source independent of the customer. The guidance in MCOB 11.6.9 G says the evidence needed varies with the customer's employment status, naming employed, self-employed, contractor and retired as examples, and that payslips, bank statements or tax returns count as independent even when the customer supplies them. It also says a lender may use information provided by an intermediary but keeps responsibility for compliance. In practice that means each lender sets its own list, and your job is to get a complete, readable pack to the lender first time.

### Document checklist by applicant type
A typical starting list. Every lender has its own criteria for how many months or years of evidence it wants and what it accepts, so check the lender's current requirements before the request goes out and adjust the list per case.
Applicant type | Income evidence | Also ask for
--- | --- | ---
All applicants | Bank statements for the main current account, full pages, as many months as the lender asks | Photo ID, proof of address, evidence of the deposit and where it comes from, details of existing credit commitments
Employed | Recent payslips, and the latest P60 | Details of any overtime, bonus or commission; the FCA's guidance gives overtime as income that may need payslips over a period of time
Self-employed (sole trader or partner) | HMRC tax calculations (SA302) and matching tax year overviews for the years the lender asks, or accounts prepared by an accountant | Business bank statements and the accountant's contact details if the lender wants a reference
Limited company director | Company accounts for the years the lender asks, plus the director's tax calculations and tax year overviews | Business bank statements and details of salary and dividends taken
Contractor | The current contract showing the day rate and term, and evidence of contracting history | Payslips if paid through an umbrella company, and any gaps between contracts explained
Gifted deposit | A signed gift letter from the person giving the money | The giftor's ID and proof of the funds, which the conveyancer will also want

### Getting HMRC documents from self-employed clients
Self-employed clients often don't know where their tax calculations are. Gov.uk says you can get an SA302 tax calculation for the last four years and a tax year overview from your HMRC online account, but not until 72 hours after the tax return was sent. It also says to check that the mortgage provider accepts documents printed yourself. Put those instructions in the request itself, with the link, and many clients can send them the same day. If an accountant files for them, the request can go to the accountant instead.

### A request you can copy
Document request after the fact-find:
```
Subject: Documents for your mortgage application

Hi [client name],

Thanks for your time today. To get your application ready for the lender, please send the documents below. You can upload them here: [secure upload link].

[checklist for the client's situation]

A few things that save time:
- Please send full statements, every page, as PDFs downloaded from your banking app or website, not screenshots.
- Make sure your name, address and account number are visible.
- If something isn't available, reply and tell me, and I'll check what the lender will accept instead.

As soon as everything is in, I'll check it and let you know the next step.

Thanks,
[broker name]
[firm name]
```

### The chase sequence
1. After the fact-find, the client gets the request with the checklist for their applicant type.
2. Each upload is matched to the checklist, so the client sees what is still outstanding.
3. After 2 working days, a short reminder [lists only the missing items](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/).
4. After 5 working days, a second reminder, and the case appears on your list for a call or a WhatsApp message from you.
5. Documents that are about to go out of date for the lender, such as an old payslip, trigger a request for the newer one.
6. When the checklist is complete, the case moves to "ready for review", and you check the pack before anything is submitted.

### Keep the documents secure
- Collect through a [secure upload link or your CRM's client portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/), not as email attachments to a shared inbox
- Store each case's documents in one place with restricted access, not in personal downloads folders
- Never ask for full online banking passwords; ask for downloaded statements instead
- Delete or archive documents according to your firm's retention policy once a case closes

### What stays with you
All advice and every judgement. You decide which lender suits the client, whether the evidence meets that lender's criteria and what to submit. The workflow asks, tracks and reminds. It never tells a client they are approved or that a document is acceptable. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person approves it before it goes out.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you collect documents today and where cases wait. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your CRM, email, upload tool and messaging, where they allow a connection), so you don't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can the checklist change for each lender?
Yes. You keep a base list per applicant type and adjust it on the case before the request goes out, so the client only gets asked for what this lender needs.

### Does it work with our CRM?
It connects where your CRM allows it. On the call we check what your CRM already does on its own, and only automate the gaps.

### Will clients find automatic reminders pushy?
The messages are written in your voice and only list what is still missing. Most clients find a short, specific reminder easier than a vague one.

### Does it check the documents?
It checks that something has arrived for each item. You check that the document is right, readable and acceptable to the lender.

## Timesheet chasing for recruitment agencies: a weekly plan before payroll
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/recruitment-timesheet-chasing/

Timesheet chasing for recruitment agencies is the weekly job of getting hours from every temp or contractor, getting each one approved by the client, and knowing what is still missing before the payroll cut-off. It can run on a fixed timeline: a reminder to the worker when the week ends, a reminder to the client's approver once hours arrive, and a list of gaps for the consultant on payroll morning. A person still checks anything odd before pay is run.

Timesheet chasing for recruitment agencies eats Monday mornings. Hours come in as a photo on WhatsApp, an email attachment, a portal entry or nothing at all. Then the client's approver is on leave, and [payroll closes at noon](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-payroll-inputs-from-clients/). This page gives small UK and US agencies a weekly chase timeline, messages to copy for temps and client approvers, and an honest view of [what to automate](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/).

### Why the chase never ends
- Hours arrive in different formats: photos of paper sheets, emails, texts, portal entries.
- Two people have to act: the worker submits, then someone at the client approves. Either one can stall it.
- Nobody has one list of who has submitted, who has been approved and who is still missing.
- Reminders go out late, by hand, from whoever has time, so the same people are chased every week.
- The cut-off is fixed. If hours miss it, the worker is paid late or the agency pays first and sorts it out after.

### What the rules say about late timesheets
In England, Wales and Scotland, regulation 12 of the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 says an employment business can't withhold a temp's pay because the client hasn't paid, or because the temp hasn't produced a timesheet signed off by the client. The agency can still satisfy itself by other means that the work was done. Gov.uk's guidance for agency workers (checked November 2026) says the agency can delay pay while it gets proof of hours, but only for a reasonable period, and that workers are entitled to the National Minimum Wage for all hours worked even if they weren't recorded on a timesheet. In the US, the Department of Labor's Fact Sheet 21 says employers must keep accurate records of hours worked each day and each workweek for non-exempt workers, may use any timekeeping method that is complete and accurate, and must keep payroll records for at least three years and time cards for two. So a missing timesheet weakens your records and delays payroll, but it isn't a reason to stop paying. Check your own contracts and get advice for your situation; this is not legal advice.

### A weekly timesheet chase timeline
For illustration, this assumes the working week ends on Sunday and payroll closes at 12 noon on Tuesday. Move the times to match your own cut-off.
When | Who gets it | What happens
--- | --- | ---
Friday 3 PM | Every temp on an active booking | Reminder: submit this week's hours by Sunday night, with the link or the reply address.
Monday 9 AM | Temps with nothing received | Second reminder, short, with the cut-off time in it.
Monday, as hours arrive | The client's named approver | Approval request listing each worker and their hours, approve or query in one reply.
Monday 3 PM | Approvers who haven't replied | Reminder with the list of hours still waiting for them.
Monday 4 PM | Temps still missing | Last reminder, plus a note to the consultant to call.
Tuesday 9 AM | The consultant and payroll | Missing list: not submitted, not approved, queried. Each line shows who owns the next step.
Tuesday 12 noon | Payroll | Cut-off. Anything still missing is handled by a person, not by another automatic message.

### Reminder for temps and contractors
Message to the worker (email or text; edit the wording to suit you):
```
Hi [First name], it's [Your name] at [Agency].

Please send your hours for the week ending [date] for your booking at [Client] by [cut-off day and time].

The quickest way: [link], or reply to this message with a photo of your signed sheet.

If you didn't work this week or something has changed, just reply and tell me.

Thanks,
[Your name]
```

### Approval request for the client
Message to the client's approver:
```
Hi [Approver name],

These hours for the week ending [date] are waiting for your approval:

[Worker name]: [hours] hours, [shift details]
[Worker name]: [hours] hours, [shift details]

If they're correct, reply APPROVED or use this link: [link].
If anything looks wrong, reply with the name and the right hours and I'll check it today.

Payroll closes at [cut-off day and time].

Thanks,
[Your name], [Agency]
```

### What to automate and what to keep with a person
1. Keep one list of active bookings: worker, client, approver, pay rate and cut-off. Everything else reads from it.
2. Send the Friday and Monday reminders automatically, and stop them the moment hours arrive.
3. Save every timesheet that comes in, whatever the format, to the right worker and week, with the date it arrived.
4. Send the approval request to the right approver as soon as hours are in, and log the reply and the time.
5. Build the missing list on payroll morning, so the consultant sees gaps in one place instead of searching inboxes.
6. Keep these with a person: queried hours, overtime that looks wrong, a worker who says they worked but has no approval, and any decision to delay pay.

### If you already have a timesheet platform
Many recruitment and payroll systems have timesheet reminders built in. Switch them on first and see what's left. The gap is usually at the edges: workers who send photos, clients who won't log in, and the missing list nobody builds.

### How Mike Automations builds it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how hours reach you today and where the week gets stuck. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every active temp gets the Friday reminder, every approver gets their list on Monday, and payroll gets the missing list at 9 AM on Tuesday". It's built on the tools you already use (your email, Google Sheets or Excel, your recruitment or payroll system where it allows a connection), so your team has nothing new to learn. It goes live in 2-3 days, costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can we hold a temp's pay until the client approves the timesheet?
In England, Wales and Scotland, regulation 12 of the 2003 Conduct Regulations says an employment business can't withhold pay because the worker hasn't produced a timesheet authenticated by the client, though it can check by other means that the work was done. Gov.uk says pay can be delayed only for a reasonable period while you get proof of hours. Take advice on your own contracts.

### Will the reminders annoy our temps?
They stop as soon as hours arrive, so people who submit on time hear from you once a week. You approve the wording, and it comes from your own email or number.

### What if a worker sends a photo of a paper timesheet?
That's fine. The photo is saved to the right worker and week, and the hours are typed in or checked by a person before payroll. If AI reads the photo to prepare the numbers, a person still approves them.

## AI agent for small business: what it can and can't do
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/

An AI agent for a small business is software that uses an AI model to read something (an email, a form, a document), decide which step comes next and use your tools to prepare it, such as a draft reply, a sorted enquiry or a filled-in record. Today it is reliable at reading, sorting and drafting, and unreliable at anything that must be right every time without checking. The safe setup is that the agent prepares the work and a person approves it before anything reaches a customer or moves money.

An AI agent for small business is one of the most talked-about tools right now, and one of the most oversold. This page covers what it is, what it does reliably, where it fits next to [ordinary automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/), and how to keep a person in charge and client data safe.

### What an AI agent is, in plain words
Ordinary automation follows fixed rules: when a form comes in, add a row to the sheet and send email A. An AI agent adds a step that can read and judge: it looks at a messy email, works out what the person wants, picks which of your tools to use and prepares the result. Zapier's help centre, for example, describes Zapier Agents as a way to create AI agents that carry out tasks using Zapier's app connections, and tells you to test an agent before you publish it.

### What it does well today
- Reading and sorting: which enquiries are new jobs, which are complaints, which are spam.
- Pulling details out of messy text: names, addresses, dates and amounts from an email or a form, into the right fields.
- Drafting: [a first reply to an enquiry](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/), a quote summary, a reminder in your usual tone.
- Checking a document against a list: is this the right form, is a page missing, is it signed.
- Answering questions from your own material, such as your prices page or your terms, when it is told to say "I don't know" otherwise.

### What it can't do reliably
- Be right every time. A model can misread a number or state something with confidence that isn't true. Anything that must be exact needs a rule or a person.
- Know what it hasn't been given. If your prices changed last week and nobody updated its material, it will use the old ones.
- Make judgement calls that carry risk: refunds, legal or tax advice, credit decisions, anything about someone's health.
- Replace a process that doesn't exist. If nobody agrees how enquiries should be handled, an agent will just handle them inconsistently, faster.

### Where it fits next to ordinary automation
Most small-business work is rule-based and needs no AI: reminders on a date, a form into a spreadsheet, the next email in a sequence. Rules are cheaper and predictable. A good build uses rules for the whole flow and puts AI only in the one or two steps where the input is messy and a person currently has to read it.

### Agent, automation or do nothing: a decision table
Your situation | Best choice | Why
--- | --- | ---
The task follows the same steps every time (a reminder on a date, a form into a sheet) | Ordinary automation | Rules are cheaper and never guess.
The input is messy free text or documents a person has to read first | AI agent that drafts, a person approves | Reading and sorting is what AI is good at.
The output goes to a customer, moves money or is a legal, tax or health matter | Agent drafts only, never sends on its own | A mistake costs more than the time saved.
It happens a few times a month and takes minutes | Do nothing | Setting it up and checking it costs more than doing it by hand.
Nobody agrees how the task should be done | Do nothing yet: write the process down first | Automating a muddle gives you a faster muddle.

### Tasks: what the agent prepares and what a person approves
Task | The agent prepares | A person approves | Never on its own
--- | --- | --- | ---
New enquiries | Sorts them and drafts a first reply | Reads and sends the reply | Promising a price or a date
Documents from clients | Checks each one against the list and notes what's missing | Confirms the file is complete | Telling a client they're done
Quotes | Drafts the quote from your price list and the job notes | Checks the numbers and sends it | Giving a discount
Payment reminders | Drafts a reminder for overdue invoices | Approves who gets one | Threatening action or changing terms

### Keeping a person in charge
Human approval is built into the tools. n8n's documentation describes a human review step for an AI agent's tools: when the agent wants to use a tool that needs review, the workflow pauses and sends an approval request through a channel you choose, such as Slack, Microsoft Teams, Gmail or n8n's own chat. If the person approves, the action runs. If they deny it, it doesn't run. Whatever tool you use, the rule is the same: the agent prepares, a person approves, and the agent has no permission to send, pay or delete on its own.

### Data protection
1. Know where the data goes. Check which AI service the agent uses and its business terms. OpenAI's API documentation says data sent to its API isn't used to train its models unless you opt in, and Anthropic's commercial terms say it may not train models on customer content. Consumer chat apps can have different settings, so check those separately.
2. Send the minimum. Give the agent only the fields it needs, not the whole client file.
3. Keep significant decisions with a person. In the UK (our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the wider rules), Article 22C of the UK GDPR (in force since 5 February 2026) says that where a significant decision about someone is made solely by automated means, they must be able to get information about it, make representations, obtain human intervention and contest it. In the EU, Article 22 of the GDPR gives people a right not to be subject to such decisions, with exceptions.
4. Say in your privacy notice that you use AI tools, and keep a log of what the agent prepared and who approved it.

### How Mike Automations builds it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about the task you want help with. Often the honest answer is that ordinary automation is enough, and I'll say so. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price that shows which steps use rules, which use AI, and where a person approves. It's built on the tools you already use, goes live in 2-3 days, costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. A person always approves anything the AI prepares.

### Is an AI agent the same as a chatbot?
Not quite. A chatbot answers questions in a chat window. An agent can also use your tools: read your inbox, update a spreadsheet, prepare a document. That's why it needs clear limits and a person approving its work.

### Can an AI agent answer customer enquiries on its own?
It can draft replies well, but sending them without a check is a risk: it can state a wrong price or promise something you can't do. The safer setup is that it drafts, a person approves, and urgent messages go straight to a person.

### Is it safe to use client data with an AI agent?
It can be, if you use business terms that don't allow training on your data, send only the fields needed and keep significant decisions with a person. Take advice if you handle health, legal or financial data.

## Salon cancellation policy template with deposits
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/

A salon cancellation policy with deposits tells clients, before they book, how much deposit is taken, how much notice they must give to cancel or move, and when the deposit is kept. In the UK the CMA says a deposit kept on cancellation should be a genuine reservation with clear, narrow conditions, and normally only a small percentage of the price. Show the policy at booking, in the confirmation and in the reminder.

This salon cancellation policy template with deposits is for UK hair, beauty and nail salons that want fewer empty chairs without arguments at the desk. Below: a policy to copy, which services need a deposit, the UK law points, and the messages that make clients see it. Most booking tools already take deposits. The gaps are the wording, the timing and [what happens after a no-show](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).

### The policy template
Change the bracketed parts. Keep it short: clients read three lines, not a page.
Salon cancellation and deposit policy:
```
Booking and deposits
We take a deposit of [£ amount / % of the service price] for [new clients / colour and treatments over [length] / all bookings]. It comes off your bill on the day.

Changing or cancelling
You can move or cancel for free up to [48] hours before your appointment, using the link in your confirmation or by calling us. Your deposit is refunded or moved to your new time.

Late cancellations and no-shows
If you cancel with less than [48] hours' notice, or don't come, we keep the deposit. That covers the time we held for you. We won't charge anything more.

Running late
If you're more than [15] minutes late, we may need to shorten or move your appointment so the next client isn't kept waiting.

If we cancel
If we need to cancel or move your appointment, you get your deposit back in full, or keep it on account if you'd rather.
```

### Which services need a deposit?
There's no official standard for salons, so decide by what a missed slot costs you. This table is a starting point.
Booking | Deposit? | Reason
--- | --- | ---
Long colour, extensions, treatments | Usually yes | A no-show leaves hours empty that are hard to refill at short notice
New clients booking online | Often yes | No history yet, and a short booking form is easy to forget
Quick trims and regulars | Often no | Low cost if missed, and asking may annoy loyal clients
Peak slots (Saturdays, evenings) | Your call | Those are the slots other clients want

### UK law points to check
- Keep the deposit modest (more in [how to ask for a deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/)). The CMA's unfair contract terms guidance (CMA37, updated 22 July 2026) says a genuine deposit can be kept in full if it works as a binding reservation, you tell the client at the earliest opportunity that it's needed, and the conditions for keeping it are clear and narrow. Such a deposit "will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price".
- Cancellation charges should reflect your real loss. The same guidance says fees should be a genuine pre-estimate of loss, and should take account of your ability to reduce the loss, for example by rebooking the slot.
- If you cancel, refund in full. The CMA says terms that let the trader keep prepayments when the trader cancels are likely to be unfair.
- Online and phone bookings are "distance" contracts under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, which normally give a 14-day right to cancel a service from the day it's booked (regulation 30), with all payments refunded within 14 days (regulation 34). The regulations exclude "services related to leisure activities" booked for a specific date (regulation 28), but they don't say whether a hair or beauty appointment counts. If many of your clients book weeks ahead, get advice from Trading Standards or a solicitor before relying on that exception.
- Bookings made face to face in the salon are not distance contracts, so the 14-day right doesn't apply to them.

### Where clients should see the policy
A policy only works if the client saw it before they missed the appointment. Show it at three points, with the same wording each time.
1. At booking: one line next to the deposit, with a link to the full policy. The client ticks to agree.
2. In the confirmation: the date, time, deposit paid, and "Free to move or cancel until [day, time]".
3. In the reminder, before the free cancellation window closes: a link to move or cancel, sent while changing is still free.
4. After a no-show: a kind message with a rebooking link, sent only after a person has checked what happened.

### Reminder wording
Reminder text before the free cancellation window closes:
```
Hi [name], see you on [day] at [time] for [service] with [stylist]. If you need to move or cancel, it's free until [day, time]: [link]. After that the deposit is kept, as in our policy. Thanks, [salon name]
```

### What you can automate around your booking tool
Most booking tools already handle the deposit itself. Square Appointments' UK help, for example, describes requiring prepayment or holding a card for no-show protection, a cancellation cut-off from one hour to two weeks, and showing the policy in the booking flow and confirmation emails. Check what your own tool does before adding anything. Automation is worth it for the parts around it:
- Filling cancelled slots: when someone cancels, the clients on your waiting list for that service get a message, first to reply gets the slot.
- No-show follow-up: a list of the day's no-shows for you to review, then a rebooking message. A person decides whether to keep the deposit, so a client who was in hospital isn't treated like one who forgot.
- One log of every deposit kept, refunded or waived, so staff apply the policy the same way.

### How Mike Automations would build it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how bookings, deposits and cancellations work in your salon today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the booking tool and messaging you already use, so there's nothing new for staff to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000, one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. You approve every message wording first.

### How much deposit should a salon take?
There's no fixed figure in UK law. The CMA's guidance says a deposit you keep on cancellation should normally be a small percentage of the price and tied to clear, narrow conditions. Many salons only take one for long or high-value services.

### Can I charge the full price for a no-show?
Be careful. The CMA's guidance says cancellation charges should be a genuine pre-estimate of your loss and should allow for rebooking the slot. Charging the full price every time is more likely to be challenged.

### Will clients be charged automatically?
Only if you choose that. The workflow can prepare the list, and a person approves any charge or kept deposit.

## Cleaning business automation: from quote request to paid invoice
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/cleaning-business-automation/

Cleaning business automation means letting software handle the repeat admin around each clean: replying to quote requests, confirming and moving bookings, sending each cleaner the address and access notes, reminding the client, invoicing after the visit and asking for a review. For a small cleaning company the biggest wins are usually recurring clients, because the same five messages go out every week. A person still approves quotes, handles complaints and decides on skipped visits.

Cleaning business automation is for owners of small domestic and office cleaning companies who spend their evenings texting clients, rewriting the rota and checking who has paid. Most of that work is the same every week. Below: what to automate first, one week of a recurring client's flow, and the messages to copy. It works around the booking app, calendar and accounting tool you already have.

### What a small cleaning company should automate first
- Quote requests: [an instant reply](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) that asks for the details you need to price (property size, rooms, how often, pets, start date), so you can quote without three rounds of texts.
- Booking confirmations and rescheduling: a confirmation with a link to move the visit, and a rule for what happens to the cleaner's day when a client moves.
- Cleaner assignment: each cleaner gets tomorrow's jobs in one message, with address, time, access notes and the client's specific requests.
- Client reminders: [a short reminder the day before](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/), so the client leaves the key out or is in to let the cleaner in.
- Recurring invoicing: an invoice sent after each completed visit (or one a month for regulars), with payment reminders that stop once the client pays.
- [Review requests](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/): one message to every client after their first few cleans, not only the ones who seem happy.

### One week of a recurring client's flow
For illustration: a fortnightly domestic clean every other Thursday morning. The same pattern runs for every regular client, so the work grows with the client list without more evenings on your phone.
When | What happens | Automatic or a person?
--- | --- | ---
Monday | Rota for the week is built from the recurring bookings; any clashes or absences are flagged to you | Automatic, a person fixes the flags
Tuesday | Holiday and skip check: clients who said they're away are marked, and their slot is offered to the waiting list | Automatic, a person confirms
Wednesday, 10am | Reminder to the client: day, time window, cleaner's first name, how to get in | Automatic
Wednesday, 6pm | Each cleaner gets Thursday's job sheet: addresses, access notes, alarm instructions, special requests | Automatic
Thursday | Cleaner marks the job done in a form or app, with a note for anything broken or missing | Cleaner
Thursday, after the job | Invoice sent, or added to the monthly invoice for regulars | Automatic
Thursday + 7 days | Payment reminder if unpaid; stops the moment it's paid | Automatic
After the third clean | One review request to every client, with your Google review link | Automatic

### Key and access notes
Key safe codes, alarm codes and "the back door sticks" notes are the most sensitive thing you hold. Keep them in one place, send them only to the cleaner booked for that visit, and only the evening before. Don't put them in group chats or in invoices. If a cleaner leaves, the codes they were sent should be listed so you can ask clients to change them. Our [GDPR checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the wider rules for client data.

### Skipped visits, holidays and rescheduling
1. Ask for holidays in the reminder message, not by memory: "Away on any upcoming dates? Reply with them and we'll skip those cleans."
2. Mark a skipped visit in the booking tool so it doesn't create an invoice or a job sheet.
3. Decide your rule for late cancellations (for example, under 24 hours' notice) and put it in the confirmation, so the reminder can repeat it.
4. When a client moves a clean, re-check the cleaner's day: travel time and a clash go to you, not straight to the cleaner.
5. Offer freed slots to a waiting list of one-off and new clients, first to reply gets it.

### Messages to copy
Reply to a quote request:
```
Hi [name], thanks for asking about a clean at [area]. To give you a fixed price, could you reply with: number of bedrooms and bathrooms, how often you'd like us (weekly, fortnightly, one-off), any pets, and your preferred day and start date. We'll send a price within [one working day]. [Business name]
```

### Day-before reminder
Reminder to the client:
```
Hi [name], a reminder that [cleaner first name] is coming tomorrow, [day], between [time] and [time]. Please leave access as usual ([key safe / spare key / you'll be in]). Away on any upcoming dates? Reply with them and we'll skip those cleans. [Business name]
```

### Cleaner job sheet
Evening message to each cleaner:
```
Tomorrow, [date]:
1. [time] [client first name], [address]. Access: [key safe code / client in]. Alarm: [code or none]. Notes: [e.g. no products on the oak floor, cat stays in].
2. [time] [client first name], [address]. Access: [...]. Notes: [...].
When each job is done, tap: [form link]. Problems or running late: call [number].
```

### Review request
Send the same request to every client. Google's contribution policy says businesses must not selectively ask happy customers for positive reviews, or offer anything in return for a review.
Review request after the third clean:
```
Hi [name], we hope you're happy with your cleans so far. If you have a minute, a short Google review helps other people find a cleaner they can trust: [review link]. If anything could be better, just reply here and I'll sort it. [Owner name]
```

### Reminders, marketing and the rules
In the UK, the ICO treats messages that only confirm or remind someone about an appointment as service messages rather than direct marketing, as long as they contain nothing promotional. Add a discount or a "book a deep clean" offer and the message counts as marketing, with stricter consent rules. Keep reminders plain, and send offers separately to clients who agreed to them. In the US, check texting consent rules with your messaging provider before you start.

### How Mike Automations would build it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how quotes, the rota and invoicing work in your company today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the booking app, calendar, accounting tool and messaging you already use, so your cleaners don't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. You approve every message wording first, and a person stays in charge of quotes, complaints and skipped-visit decisions.

### What should a small cleaning company automate first?
Usually the recurring client flow: the day-before reminder, the cleaner's job sheet and the invoice after each visit. Those happen every week for every regular client, so they save the most time.

### How do I bill recurring cleaning clients?
Either an invoice after each completed visit, or one monthly invoice listing the visits. The workflow only bills cleans marked as done, so skipped and cancelled visits don't appear.

### Is it safe to send key safe codes by message?
Send them only to the cleaner booked for that visit, the evening before, and keep a record of who received which codes. If a cleaner leaves, ask the affected clients to change their codes.

### Do I need new cleaning software?
Not necessarily. The automation is built around the tools you already use, such as your booking app or calendar, your accounting tool and email or text.

## Insurance broker renewal reminders
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-renewal-reminders/

Insurance broker renewal reminders are timed messages that start weeks before each policy's expiry date: first a request for updated client details, then reminders until the client replies, then the renewal terms and a final nudge before cover lapses. Automating them means every renewal date on your policy list triggers the same steps, while your team still checks the details, places the cover and gives the advice. For UK consumer general insurance, the renewal information itself must also meet the FCA's rules in ICOBS 6.5.

Insurance broker renewal reminders are where a small broking team loses the most time for the least thought. Every policy has a renewal date, every client needs to confirm their details before you can quote, and the same few clients go quiet until the week cover runs out. The steps are the same every time, so they can run from your policy list as a workflow, and your team spends its time on the conversations that need a broker.

### Where renewals go wrong in a small brokerage
- Renewal dates live in the broker system, but the chasing happens from personal inboxes
- Clients mention changes (a new driver, an extension, higher turnover) after you've already quoted
- Nobody can see at a glance which renewals are waiting on the client and which are waiting on an insurer
- Reminders depend on one person remembering, so holidays and busy weeks mean late renewals
- The last-minute calls take more time than the renewal itself

### A renewal reminder timeline you can adapt
There's no single right timeline. The days below are an example, not a rule: commercial risks that need to go to market usually start earlier, simple personal lines can start later. Pick the points that suit your book and your insurers, and the workflow runs them for every policy.
Days before renewal | What happens | Who does it
--- | --- | ---
60 | Email asking the client to confirm or update their details, with a short form | Automatic
45 | Reminder if the form isn't back. Policies with changes go to a broker | Automatic, broker reviews changes
30 | Quotes or renewal terms prepared from the confirmed details | Broker
21 (your choice) | Renewal terms sent, with the information the FCA requires for consumers | Broker approves, workflow sends
14 | Reminder if the client hasn't responded to the terms | Automatic
7 | Final reminder, and a call task for the account handler | Automatic, then a person
0 | Renewed, lapsed or moved: status recorded and documents filed | Broker confirms

### Collect updated information before you quote
Most rework at renewal comes from details that changed during the year and nobody mentioned. A short form sent with the first reminder fixes that. Keep it to the questions that change the price or the cover, and use a different version for each policy type. The answers are saved next to the policy, and any "yes, something changed" goes to a broker before quoting starts. A form you can adapt:
1. Has anything changed about the people insured (new drivers, new staff, a change of address)?
2. Has anything changed about what's insured (vehicles, premises, stock, extensions, building work)?
3. Has your business changed (turnover, activities, number of employees)? Commercial policies only.
4. Have you had any claims, losses or incidents since the last renewal?
5. Is there anything else you'd like us to look at this year (extra cover, a different excess)?
6. What's the best phone number and email to reach you about this renewal?

### First reminder email you can copy
Sent at your first reminder point (for example, 60 days before renewal):
```
Subject: Your [policy type] insurance renews on [renewal date]

Hi [first name],

Your [policy type] policy renews on [renewal date]. Before we look at your renewal, please check your details are still right. It takes about 5 minutes: [form link]

If nothing has changed, just tick "no changes" and submit.

If something has changed, for example a new driver, building work or a change in your business, please tell us now so your cover is right from day one.

Any questions, reply to this email or call us on [phone].

[your name]
[brokerage name]
```

### Final reminder you can copy
Sent 7 days before renewal if the client hasn't replied:
```
Subject: 7 days left: your [policy type] insurance renews on [renewal date]

Hi [first name],

Your [policy type] cover ends on [renewal date] and we haven't heard from you yet. Your renewal terms are here: [link or attachment].

[If it renews automatically: If you're happy, you don't need to do anything.]
[If it needs action: To stay covered, please reply to confirm, or call us on [phone].]

If you've already arranged this, thank you, and please ignore this email.

[your name]
[brokerage name]
```

### The FCA renewal points for consumer general insurance
We checked the FCA Handbook on 10 November 2026. ICOBS 6.5.1R applies when a firm proposes to a consumer the renewal of a general insurance contract that lasts 10 months or more and isn't a group policy. In good time before renewal, the consumer must be given: the renewal premium; last year's premium (or the annualised premium after the latest mid-term change), shown so the two are easy to compare; a statement that they should check the cover still meets their needs and can compare prices and cover with other providers; and whether the policy renews automatically or needs them to act. From the fourth renewal onwards, a set statement about shopping around is required, and its exact wording is in ICOBS 6.5.1R(4). All of this must be clear, in writing or another durable medium, and drawn to the consumer's attention as key information. ICOBS 6 Annex 1 gives both the intermediary and the insurer responsibility, "as appropriate", on consumer renewals, so agree with each insurer who sends what. For home and motor, ICOBS 6B.2 adds that the renewal price must not be higher than the equivalent new business price. ICOBS 6.5 covers consumers, not commercial clients. This is a summary, not compliance advice: confirm the current rules with your compliance support.

### What an automated renewal workflow does
1. Reads renewal dates from your broker system or policy spreadsheet every morning.
2. Sends the details form at your first reminder point and reminds the client until it's back, in wording like our [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/).
3. Flags any answer that says something changed, and creates a task for the right broker.
4. Prepares the renewal email from your approved template, with the required figures filled in, for a broker to check and send.
5. Sends the later reminders, stops the moment the client replies or renews, and creates a call task when time is short.
6. Keeps one list showing every renewal, its status and who it's waiting on.

### What stays with your team
The advice, the placing and the compliance sign-off. The workflow never chooses cover, never quotes and never sends renewal terms without a broker approving them. If AI is used to summarise a client's form answers or draft a note, a person reads and approves it first.

### How Mike Automations would build it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how renewals run in your brokerage today and where they slip. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example: every renewal on the list gets its details form on time, and nothing reaches 7 days out without someone knowing. It's built on the tools you already use (your broker system or spreadsheet, email and forms, where they allow a connection), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does this replace our broker software?
No. It reads renewal dates from the system or spreadsheet you already use and does the reminding around it. Where your software can't be connected, a daily export can be enough.

### Can the workflow send the renewal notice on its own?
It can prepare it, but a broker checks and approves the terms before anything goes out. The information the FCA requires is part of the template, and the person approving checks the figures.

### What about clients who renew by phone?
When the account handler marks the renewal as done, the reminders stop. No client should get a reminder about something they've already sorted.

### Do the FCA renewal rules in ICOBS 6.5 apply to commercial clients?
ICOBS 6.5 applies to consumers. You can still send commercial clients a similar summary as good practice. Check your own position with your compliance support.

### How many days before renewal should reminders start?
That's your choice. The FCA rule for consumers says "in good time" rather than a number of days. You might start earlier for commercial risks that need marketing and later for simple personal lines.

## Client reporting automation for marketing agencies
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-reporting-automation/

Client reporting automation for a marketing agency means the monthly numbers are pulled from Google Analytics, Google Ads, Meta and other platforms into one report template on a fixed day, so nobody copies figures by hand. A person on your team still writes the commentary: what happened, why, and what you'll do next month. The workflow then sends the report, tracks who has read it and reminds you about any questions or actions the client raised.

Client reporting automation pays off because monthly reports eat the first week of every month. Someone logs in to each platform for each client, exports the figures, pastes them into slides, fixes the charts and only then starts on the part clients actually read: what it means. The data pull, the layout and the delivery are the same every month, so they can run as a workflow. The thinking stays with your team, as it does in all our [automations for marketing agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agencies/).

### Where monthly reporting eats time
- Logging in to four or five platforms per client to export the same figures every month
- Copying numbers into slides or spreadsheets, then checking nobody pasted last month's
- Reports that differ from client to client because each account manager builds their own
- Commentary written at the last minute because the data took all the time
- Questions from the client getting lost in email threads after the report goes out

### What the platforms can already do on their own
Before building anything, use what's built in. We checked each vendor's help pages on 10 November 2026. Google Analytics 4 lets an administrator schedule a report by email, daily, weekly, monthly or quarterly, as a PDF or CSV attachment, to up to 50 recipients, and Google notes that data can take up to 72 hours to process, so it suggests scheduling monthly reports for the 4th of the month. Google Ads lets you schedule a report from the Report Editor to be emailed to people who have access to the account. Meta Ads Reporting lets someone with administrator, advertiser or analyst access schedule a recurring report by email, but only for single-account reports, not cross-account ones. Looker Studio can email a PDF of a report on a schedule to up to 50 addresses. Each of these sends numbers from one platform. None of them writes the story across platforms, and that's the gap automation fills. For pulling data into your own template, Google offers the Analytics Data API and the Google Ads API, and Meta offers the Insights API in its Marketing API.

### A monthly report template outline
Keep the same structure for every client so the workflow can fill it and the client knows where to look. Change the metrics to match what you sell.
Section | What goes in it | Filled by
--- | --- | ---
Summary | Three to five sentences: the headline result, what drove it, what's next | Account manager
Goals vs actual | The client's agreed goals (leads, sales, cost per lead) against this month and last month | Workflow
Website | Sessions, key events and top landing pages from Google Analytics | Workflow
Paid search | Spend, clicks, conversions and cost per conversion from Google Ads | Workflow
Paid social | Spend, results and cost per result from Meta Ads Reporting | Workflow
Work done | Tasks completed this month, taken from your project tool | Workflow, checked by a person
What we'll do next month | Two or three specific actions and anything you need from the client | Account manager

### How an automated reporting month runs
1. On the day you choose (for example, the 4th, after the platforms have caught up), the workflow pulls last month's figures for each client.
2. It fills each client's report template and calculates the change against last month and against the goals.
3. It flags anything unusual for a person to look at: spend over budget, a tracking gap, a sudden drop.
4. The account manager gets a task with the draft report and writes the summary and next steps.
5. Once a person approves it, the report is sent with a short cover email and saved to the client's folder.
6. A few days later, the workflow checks for replies and creates tasks for any questions or requests.

### Commentary is written by a person
Clients pay for judgement, not for charts. The account manager writes the summary and the next steps, because they know what changed in the client's business, what was agreed on the last call and which number the client actually cares about. If AI is used to draft a first version from the figures, a person rewrites and approves it before it's sent. Nothing goes to a client without someone on your team reading it.

### Cover email you can copy
Sent with the monthly report once it's approved:
```
Subject: [client name]: your [month] report

Hi [first name],

Your report for [month] is attached (and here: [link]).

The short version:
- [one line on the headline result]
- [one line on what drove it]
- [one line on what we'll do in [next month]]

We need one thing from you: [request, or "nothing this month"].

If you'd like to go through it together, reply and we'll find 15 minutes.

[your name]
[agency name]
```

### Do we need a reporting tool, or can we keep our slides?
You can keep your current format if it can be filled automatically, such as a spreadsheet, Google Slides or a Looker Studio report. On the call we look at what you use and whether it's worth changing anything.

### Will clients notice the report is automated?
