### When is Form 1099-NEC due for the 2026 tax year?
Monday, February 1, 2027, for both the IRS copy and the contractor's copy. The usual date is January 31, but in 2027 that is a Sunday, and the IRS moves weekend due dates to the next business day.

### Does the $2,000 threshold apply to 2025 payments?
No. The IRS says the higher threshold applies to tax years beginning after 2025, so it covers payments made from January 1, 2026. Forms for 2025 payments used the $600 threshold.

### Do payments made through PayPal or by card need a 1099-NEC?
No. The IRS instructions say card payments and third-party network payments are reported by the payment company on Form 1099-K, not by the payer on Form 1099-NEC.

### Can clients collect W-9s themselves?
They can, but they usually forget until January. A workflow can do it on their behalf, from your address or theirs, with wording you approve.

## What to automate first in a small service business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/ (2026-11-10)

What to automate first in a small business: the job that happens every week, follows the same steps each time, and costs you money or a client when someone forgets it. Usually that is chasing something: documents, quotes, unpaid invoices or replies to new enquiries. Start with one process, define what "working" means in one sentence, and only then pick the tool.

What to automate first in a small business is a question about your week, not about software. Most small firms don't need "AI transformation". They need one annoying, repetitive job to stop depending on someone remembering it.
Picking the right first process matters more than [picking the right tool](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/). A good first automation pays for itself quickly, is easy to check, and teaches you what to automate next. A bad one takes weeks, breaks often and puts you off the whole idea. Below is a simple test you can run on your own business in half an hour, a scorecard to fill in, and the jobs that usually win.

### Step 1: list the jobs that repeat
Take a sheet of paper or a blank spreadsheet and write down every job you or your team did in the last two weeks that felt like admin. Don't judge them yet. Typical entries: sending the same email to a new client, asking for missing documents, typing enquiry details into a spreadsheet, chasing a customer who hasn't replied to a quote, sending appointment reminders, reminding people to pay.
Look through your sent emails and your phone's message history if you can't remember. The jobs you do without thinking are often the ones that take the most time in total.

### Step 2: score each job on five questions
Give each job 0, 1 or 2 points on each question. The highest total is your first automation. A tie goes to the job that is easiest to describe step by step.
Question | 0 points | 1 point | 2 points
--- | --- | --- | ---
How often does it happen? | A few times a year | Monthly | Every week or every day
Are the steps the same each time? | Every case is different | Mostly, with a few exceptions | Yes, I could write them down now
What happens when it's forgotten? | Nothing much | A delay or an awkward call | A lost job, a late filing or a client who leaves
Does it need your judgement? | Yes, every time | Only at one step | No, it's sending, logging or reminding
Is the information already digital? | Paper only | Partly | Yes: email, forms, a spreadsheet, your job or accounting software

### Step 3: check the winner against the usual first automations
In most small service businesses, the top score lands on one of the jobs below. They repeat, they follow a pattern, and the cost of forgetting them is real. If your winner is on this list, you're on safe ground.
- [Collecting documents from clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeeper-document-collection/), with reminders until everything is in (accountants, bookkeepers, mortgage brokers, solicitors).
- Following up on estimates and quotes that went quiet (trades, cleaners, agencies).
- Appointment confirmations and reminders, with an easy way to reschedule (clinics, salons, home services).
- Logging every new enquiry in one list and sending a quick, honest first reply.
- Asking every customer for a review after the job, the same way each time.
- Sending invoices and polite reminders about unpaid ones.
- Onboarding a new client: engagement letter, ID checks, welcome email and first document request.

### What not to automate first
- Anything that happens a few times a year. The build won't pay back soon, and you'll forget how it works between runs.
- A process nobody can describe step by step yet. [Fix the process on paper first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/), or you'll automate the confusion.
- Decisions that need your judgement: pricing, advice, hiring, complaints. Automate the steps around them instead, such as gathering the information and putting it in front of you.
- Anything where one wrong message would do real damage, unless a person approves each message. If AI drafts something, a person should approve it before it goes out.
- Your whole business at once. One process, live and trusted, beats five half-built ones.

### Step 4: define "working" in one sentence
Before anything is built, write one sentence that says what the automation must do and how you'll know it's doing it. It keeps the build focused and gives you a clear test. Some examples:
- "Every estimate gets two follow-ups, and every Monday I get a list of the ones still open."
- "Every new client gets the document checklist on day one, a reminder every 5 days, and I can see who is still missing what."
- "Every enquiry gets a reply within 5 minutes and lands in one sheet with the date, source and job."

### Step 5: pick the tool last
Only now does the tool matter. Most first automations run on what you already have: your email, a form, a shared spreadsheet or drive, your accounting or job software, plus an automation platform such as Zapier, Make or n8n to connect them. Our comparison of Zapier, Make and n8n explains how each one charges and who each suits. If you're weighing up building it yourself against hiring someone, [the guide to business automation cost](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) breaks down the build, the software and the support.

### For illustration: three jobs, scored
For illustration only, here is how a small plumbing business might score three jobs. Chasing quiet estimates: weekly (2), same steps (2), lost jobs when forgotten (2), no judgement (2), estimates already sent by email (2): total 10. Ordering parts: weekly (2), varies by job (1), delays when forgotten (1), needs judgement (0), partly digital (1): total 5. Yearly service reminders to past customers: monthly batches (1), same steps (2), lost repeat work (2), no judgement (2), customer list in a spreadsheet (2): total 9. The estimate follow-up goes first and the service reminders second. Parts ordering stays manual.

### How we would build your first one
If you'd rather not build it yourself, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) and tell me which job scored highest. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use, so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How do I know if a process is worth automating?
If it happens weekly, follows the same steps, and forgetting it costs you a job, a client or a penalty, it's worth automating. If it happens a few times a year or needs your judgement at every step, leave it manual for now.

### Should my first automation use AI?
Only if a step genuinely needs reading or writing text, such as sorting enquiries or drafting a reply. Most first automations are plain sending, logging and reminding. Where AI drafts something, a person should approve it before it's sent.

### How long does a first automation take to build?
A single process with clear steps usually takes days, not weeks. Ours go live in 2-3 days after the written plan is agreed.

## Zapier vs Make vs n8n: which one suits a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/ (2026-11-10)

Zapier vs Make vs n8n, in short: Zapier is the easiest to start with and connects the most apps, but it charges per task, so busy multi-step workflows cost more. Make handles branching workflows on a visual canvas and charges per credit, roughly one per step. n8n charges per workflow run on its cloud plans and can be self-hosted, which suits firms that want data on their own server and have someone technical to look after it.

Zapier vs Make vs n8n is the question most small businesses hit as soon as they decide to automate something. All three connect your apps and move information between them: a form is filled in, a row is added, an email goes out. The differences are how much they ask of you, how they handle complicated workflows, where they run, and above all how they charge.
This comparison is written for [small service businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) with no developer on staff: accountants, trades, clinics, agencies. Prices below were checked on each vendor's own pricing page on 10 November 2026. Prices change often, so check them again before you buy.

### The comparison table (checked 10 November 2026)
Sources: zapier.com/pricing, make.com/en/pricing and n8n.io/pricing, all read on 10 November 2026. Zapier's pricing page notes that some actions use more than one task, depending on the step type and AI model.
 | Zapier | Make | n8n
--- | --- | --- | ---
What you pay for | Tasks: each action that completes successfully. Triggers, Filters, Paths and Formatter steps don't count. | Credits: most module actions use 1 credit. Routers and error handlers are free; some AI features use more. | Executions: one run of the whole workflow, however many steps it has (cloud plans).
Free option | Free plan: 100 tasks a month, two-step Zaps only, 15-minute checks | Free plan: 1,000 credits a month, 2 active scenarios, 15-minute minimum interval | Community Edition: free to self-host, on your own server
Entry paid plan | Professional from $19.99 a month billed yearly ($29.99 monthly) for 750 tasks | Core $12 a month for 10,000 credits, as shown on monthly billing; yearly payment is cheaper | Starter €20 a month billed yearly for 2,500 executions, hosted by n8n
Apps | Over 10,000 apps listed on zapier.com/apps | 3,500+ apps on the pricing page | 2,000+ integrations, plus an HTTP Request node for other apps with an API
Hosting | Zapier's cloud only | Make's cloud only (AWS, EU or North America) | n8n's cloud, or self-hosted on your own server
Learning curve | Gentlest | Moderate: visual canvas, more settings | Steepest, especially self-hosted
Best fit | Straight-line workflows between popular apps | Workflows with many branches, loops and data shaping | High-volume or data-sensitive workflows, with technical help available

### Zapier: easiest to start, priced per task
- The easiest of the three to learn, and the largest library of ready-made app connections.
- Strongest for straight-line steps between popular apps. It can branch (Paths), filter, loop and run code, but long workflows with many paths get expensive and harder to follow.
- Every action that completes counts as a task, so a five-step Zap that runs 300 times a month uses far more tasks than a two-step one.
- The free plan only allows two-step Zaps, so most real business workflows need a paid plan.

### Make: visual workflows, priced per credit
- A visual canvas that shows the whole workflow, which makes branching, loops and reshaping data easier to see.
- Good for workflows with several paths and conditions, for example "if the client is VAT registered, ask for these documents, otherwise ask for those".
- Make now bills in credits (it used to count "operations"). Most actions use one credit, so the cost tracks the number of steps that run.
- A steeper learning curve than Zapier. Expect to spend time understanding how data moves between modules.

### n8n: priced per run, can live on your own server
- On n8n's cloud plans you pay per execution: one run of the whole workflow, however many steps it has. Long workflows that run often can come out much cheaper than per-step pricing.
- The Community Edition can be self-hosted at no licence fee. n8n's Sustainable Use License allows use for your own internal business purposes, not for reselling n8n as a service.
- Self-hosting means someone has to install it, keep it updated, back it up and keep it secure. If nobody in the business can do that, use n8n's cloud or another tool.
- Comfortable with custom code when a step needs it.

### A worked cost example (for illustration)
For illustration only: an accounting firm wants a workflow that runs each time a client uploads a document. It has one trigger and four actions: save the file to the client folder, update the tracking sheet, check what's still missing, and email the client a thank-you that lists what's left. Say it runs 300 times a month.
 | How usage is counted | Usage per month | Plan that covers it (list price, 10 November 2026)
--- | --- | --- | ---
Zapier | 4 actions x 300 runs | About 1,200 tasks | Professional, 1,500-task tier: $39 a month billed yearly
Make | 5 modules (trigger included) x 300 runs | About 1,500 credits | Core, 10,000 credits: $12 a month
n8n Cloud | 1 execution per run | 300 executions | Starter, 2,500 executions: €20 a month billed yearly

### How to read the example
The numbers are a rough guide, not a quote. Real usage depends on how each step is built: polling triggers, searches inside a step and AI actions can all change the count. Use each vendor's own pricing page with your real volumes before deciding.
At this size, all three cost less than an hour of someone's time each month. The subscription is rarely [the deciding factor](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) for a small business. What decides it is [who builds the workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/), who fixes it when an app changes, and whether your data may leave your own systems.

### How to choose: four questions
1. [Write the process down first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/): what starts it, every step, every app involved and what should happen when something is missing.
2. Is it a straight line between two or three popular apps? Zapier is usually enough and the quickest to set up.
3. Does it have many conditions, loops or data to reshape? Make or n8n will be cleaner and usually cheaper per run.
4. Must the data stay on servers you control, or will it run thousands of times a month? n8n, self-hosted or on its cloud, is the usual answer, as long as someone can maintain it.

### What matters more than the tool
The tool is rarely what makes an automation reliable. What matters is handling the cases that go wrong: a missing field, a duplicate, an email that bounces, an app that changes its login. Whichever you choose, make sure someone is told when a run fails, and that the workflow lives in your own account, not someone else's, so you're never locked in.

### Or skip choosing
If you'd rather not learn any of them, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". The workflow is built on whichever tool fits the process, in your own accounts, and documented. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Is n8n free?
The self-hosted Community Edition has no licence fee for your own internal business use, but you pay for the server and someone's time to run it. n8n's hosted cloud plans start at €20 a month billed yearly (checked 10 November 2026).

### Which is cheapest for a small business?
For a few simple two-app workflows, any of them can cost little or nothing. For long workflows that run often, per-run pricing (n8n) or per-credit pricing (Make) usually works out cheaper than per-task pricing (Zapier). Check each vendor's pricing page with your real volumes.

### Can I switch tools later?
Yes, but workflows don't transfer between them automatically; each one has to be rebuilt. Writing the process down step by step makes a rebuild much quicker.

## Estimate follow-up email templates for contractors (that don't sound pushy)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/estimate-follow-up-email-templates-contractors/ (2026-11-10)

An estimate follow-up email for contractors works best as a short sequence: check the estimate arrived after 2 days, send one useful detail (like your next opening) after about a week, and send a polite close-out after 2 to 3 weeks. Stop the moment the customer replies or books. The templates below cover each step, plus a text version and a reply to a price objection.

These estimate follow-up email templates are for [contractors who send estimates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/contractors/) and then hear nothing. Many estimates don't get a "no". They get silence. The customer got busy, is comparing bids, or lost your email under a pile of others.
A short, well-timed follow-up is often the difference between a lost job and a booked one, and most contractors never send one because there's no time between jobs. Below: a day-by-day schedule, five emails, two texts and an answer to the most common objection. Change the wording so it sounds like you.

### The follow-up schedule
Stop the sequence as soon as the customer replies, books or says no. Nothing annoys a customer more than a "just checking in" after they've already said yes.
When | Channel | Goal | Template
--- | --- | --- | ---
Same day | Email | Send the estimate with a clear next step | Email 0
Day 2 | Text or email | Check it arrived, invite questions | Email 1 or Text 1
Day 7 | Email | One useful detail: your next opening or a lead time | Email 2
Day 10 to 14 | Phone call | A short call for larger jobs only | Your own words
Day 14 to 21 | Email | Polite close-out, easy yes or no | Email 3
Any time | Email | Answer "your price is too high" | Email 4

### Email 0: sending the estimate
Subject: Your estimate for [job] at [address]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for having us out on [day]. Your estimate for [job] is attached. It covers [two or three main items] and is valid until [date].

If it looks good, just reply "yes" and we'll send over a start date. If you'd like to change anything, reply with your questions or call me at [phone].

Thanks,
[your name], [company]
```

### Email 1: did you get it?
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

Just checking the estimate for [job] reached you. Happy to walk you through it or adjust anything. Questions are welcome here or by text at [phone].

Thanks,
[your name], [company]
```

### Email 2: one helpful detail
Only give a lead time or an opening that's true. A real detail is helpful; a made-up deadline is pressure, and customers can tell.
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

A quick update: our next opening is the week of [date], and [material] currently takes about [time] to arrive, so booking soon keeps that date. If you'd like to go ahead, just reply and we'll hold the spot.

[your name]
```

### Email 3: the polite close-out
Subject: Should I close this out?:
```
Hi [first name],

I haven't heard back about [job], so I'll assume the timing isn't right and close this out for now. If you'd still like to go ahead, just reply and we'll pick it up. The estimate is valid until [date].

Thanks for considering us,
[your name]
```

### Email 4: when they say the price is too high
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for telling me, that helps. The estimate includes [what makes it cost what it does: materials, warranty, permit, cleanup]. If the budget is tight, we could [option: phase the work, use a different material, drop an item], which would bring it to about [amount].

Would you like me to send a revised estimate with that option?

[your name]
```

### Two text versions
In the US, business texts sent from a regular 10-digit number have to be registered for A2P 10DLC through your texting provider, and the major carriers block unregistered business texts. Customers should agree to receive texts from you, for example with a checkbox on your estimate request form. Email works from day one.
Text 1 (day 2) and Text 2 (day 7):
```
Text 1: Hi [first name], it's [your name] from [company]. Did the estimate for [job] come through OK? Happy to answer any questions.

Text 2: Hi [first name], [your name] here. We have an opening the week of [date] for your [job]. Want me to hold it? Reply STOP to opt out.
```

### Tips that make follow-ups work
- Reply in the same email thread, so the estimate is one tap away.
- Name the job and the address. Customers who requested three bids need to know which one you are.
- Ask one question per message. "Would you like to go ahead?" gets more replies than a paragraph.
- Keep a list of every open estimate with its date and value, so the big ones get a phone call. When a customer says yes, [ask for the deposit in writing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).
- Selling to UK customers? Say "quote" instead of "estimate" and adjust the spelling. The schedule works the same way.

### Make it automatic
A workflow can send these on schedule for every estimate, stop the moment the customer replies or books, and give you a daily list of open estimates worth a call. It can pull estimates from your job management software, your accounting software or your email. You still decide what to quote and what to say on the phone; it just makes sure no estimate is forgotten. If a change order comes up once the job starts, the same idea applies: see our page on change order approvals.

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you send estimates today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use, so your crew doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How many times should I follow up on an estimate?
Two or three times over two to three weeks is enough for most jobs: a check that it arrived, one useful detail, and a polite close-out. Add a phone call for larger jobs. Stop as soon as the customer replies.

### Is it pushy to follow up on an estimate?
Not if each message is short, useful and easy to answer. Customers often appreciate the reminder. A close-out email that makes "no" easy to say also gets replies that tell you why you lost the job.

### Should I follow up by email or text?
Both work. Texts are read faster; email keeps the estimate attached. In the US, register your number for A2P 10DLC and get the customer's agreement before texting.

## How to reduce no-shows for service appointments
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/ (2026-11-10)

To reduce no-shows for service appointments, do four things: confirm every booking straight away, send a reminder the day before that asks the customer to reply to confirm, make rescheduling a single tap, and phone anyone who hasn't confirmed. Most no-shows are people who forgot or felt awkward cancelling, and all four steps can run automatically except the phone call.

How to reduce no-shows is a question [every business that books time slots](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) asks sooner or later: plumbers, electricians, cleaners, clinics, salons, tutors. A no-show costs you the whole slot: the drive, the preparation, and the job that could have been booked instead.
Most no-shows aren't rude. People forget, or something comes up and cancelling feels awkward, so they say nothing. Both are fixable with a simple reminder routine. Below: the schedule, the messages to copy, how to word your policy, and the rules on texting customers in the UK and US.

### The four things that work
1. Confirm right after booking, with the date, time, address and anything the customer needs to prepare.
2. Remind the day before, and ask for a quick confirmation ("Reply YES to confirm"), so you know who to chase.
3. Make rescheduling one tap. A customer who can move the slot easily won't just disappear.
4. Call the unconfirmed ones. A short list each morning or the evening before is enough.

### A reminder schedule you can copy
When | Message | Channel
--- | --- | ---
Straight after booking | Confirmation with date, time, address, what to prepare, how to reschedule, your policy | Email (and a short text if you have consent)
2 days before (for long jobs or long journeys) | A heads-up with anything the customer must do first, such as clearing access or parking | Email
The day before, early afternoon | Reminder asking them to reply YES, with a reschedule link | Text
The evening before | You get the list of anyone who hasn't confirmed | Your phone or email
2 hours before (early or long appointments only) | "On our way soon" or "see you at 9" | Text
After a no-show | A kind message offering a new slot | Text or email

### Confirmation message
Email or text, sent on booking:
```
Hi [first name], you're booked in with [company] for [job] on [day, date] at [time], at [address]. [What to prepare, e.g. please make sure we can get to the boiler.]

Need to change it? Use this link: [reschedule link]. We ask for [24 hours'] notice to change a booking, so we can offer the slot to someone else.

Thanks, [your name]
```

### Day-before reminder
Text, the day before:
```
Hi [first name], a reminder that [company] is booked for [job] tomorrow, [day] at [time]. Please reply YES to confirm, or move it here: [reschedule link]. Thanks!
```

### After a no-show
Keep it friendly. The aim is to rebook the job, not to win an argument. If you charge a fee for missed appointments, it should already have been stated clearly at booking.
Text or email, same day:
```
Hi [first name], we were booked for [job] today at [time] but couldn't reach you. No problem, things come up. Would you like a new time? You can pick one here: [booking link], or just reply to this message.
```

### How to word your policy
State your policy kindly and once, in the confirmation, not as a threat in every message. Say how much notice you need and why: "so we can offer the slot to someone else" is a reason most people accept. If you [take deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/) or charge for late cancellations, say so plainly before the customer books, and be consistent. Salons and clinics with deposit policies have their own considerations; we cover that on [our page about salon cancellation policies and deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/).

### Email or text? The rules in the UK and US
Texts are read faster, so they work well for the day-before reminder. Email is fine for the confirmation and longer instructions.
In the UK, the ICO treats a message that only confirms or reminds someone about an appointment as a service message, not direct marketing, so the marketing consent rules for texts and emails don't apply to it. That only holds while the message contains nothing promotional: add an offer or a "book your next service" push and it counts as marketing.
In the US, business texts sent from a regular 10-digit number have to be registered for A2P 10DLC through your texting provider, and the customer should agree to receive texts, for example with a checkbox on your booking form. Include a way to opt out, such as "Reply STOP to opt out".

### What to automate
Everything above except the phone call. The workflow sends the confirmation and reminders, reads the YES replies, handles reschedule links, updates your calendar and gives you a list of who hasn't confirmed. If you already use booking or field service software that sends reminders, it fills the gaps rather than replacing it: for example the unconfirmed list, or the rebooking message after a no-show.

### For illustration
For illustration: a customer books a boiler service for Thursday at 9 AM. They get a confirmation at once with a reschedule link. On Wednesday at 2 PM a text asks them to reply YES. At 6 PM you see two unconfirmed appointments and call them: one confirms, one moves to next week, and you fill the Thursday slot from your waiting list.

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you book appointments today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your calendar or booking software, email and texting, where they allow a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### When should I send appointment reminders?
Send a confirmation straight after booking and a reminder the day before that asks for a YES. For early-morning or long-distance jobs, add a short text a couple of hours before.

### Do I need consent to send appointment reminder texts in the UK?
The ICO treats a purely administrative reminder as a service message, not marketing, so the marketing consent rules don't apply. If the message includes anything promotional, it counts as marketing and the consent rules do apply.

### Should I charge for no-shows?
That's a business decision. If you do, state the policy clearly before booking and in the confirmation, and apply it consistently. A kind rebooking message often recovers more value than a fee.

## How to ask every customer for a Google review (and stay within the rules)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/ (2026-11-10)

To ask for Google reviews, send every customer the same short request shortly after the job, with the direct review link from your Google Business Profile, and one reminder a few days later. Don't ask only the happy customers and don't offer anything in return: Google's policy forbids both, and so does consumer law in the UK (the DMCC Act 2024, enforced by the CMA) and the US (the FTC's review rule).

How to ask for Google reviews is mostly a question of habit. Reviews matter for local search, and most happy customers are glad to leave one. They just need to be asked at the right moment, with a link that opens the review form in one tap.
The trick is to ask consistently, and to ask everyone. Below: the rules in plain English for the UK and US, where to find your review link, the timing, copy-ready requests and replies, and what you can safely automate with the same tools that send your [appointment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).

### The rules: ask everyone, offer nothing
Google's contribution policy (the "Fake engagement" rules) says businesses must not discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively ask happy customers for positive ones. It also bans offering incentives, such as payment, discounts or free goods or services, in exchange for a review or for changing or removing a negative one. Asking only satisfied customers is often called "review gating", and it can get reviews removed.
In the UK, the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Schedule 20) bans fake reviews and reviews that hide the fact they were incentivised. The CMA's fake reviews guidance (CMA208, April 2025) says cherry-picking positive reviews can happen "by encouraging just those who are satisfied to leave reviews", and that stopping and starting review invitations to avoid negative ones is a problem too. Since April 2025 the CMA can enforce consumer law directly and, according to its own announcement, fine businesses up to 10% of their global turnover.
In the US, the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule has been in effect since 21 October 2024. It bans fake reviews, offering an incentive conditioned on a review saying something positive or negative, and suppressing negative reviews through threats or intimidation. Courts can impose civil penalties for knowing violations.
The safe approach in both countries is simple: send the same request to every customer, offer nothing for it, and never filter who gets the review link. You can still invite private feedback ("tell us how we did"), as long as the public review link goes to everyone the same way.

### Get your direct review link
Customers need a Google account to leave a review. The direct link saves them searching for your business and picking the wrong listing.
1. On a computer, sign in and open your Business Profile (Google says the QR code can't be generated on a phone).
2. Go to the reviews area and choose "Get more reviews".
3. Copy the link, or right-click the QR code and save the image for receipts, invoices or a card you leave after the job.

### When and how to ask
1. Ask shortly after the job is finished and paid, while it's fresh: the same day or the next morning.
2. Use the direct review link, so the form opens in one tap.
3. Keep it short and personal: name the job, thank them, one line with the link.
4. Send one reminder a few days later if they haven't left a review, then stop.
5. Reply to every review, good or bad, politely and within a few days.

### Review request (email or text)
Sent when the job is marked complete:
```
Hi [first name], thanks for choosing [company] for [job]. If you have a minute, an honest Google review helps other people find us: [review link]

Thank you! [your name]
```

### One reminder
Sent 4 or 5 days later, only once:
```
Hi [first name], just a gentle reminder in case it got buried: if you'd like to share how the [job] went, here's the link: [review link]. No worries if not. Thanks again, [your name]
```

### Replying to reviews
Keep critical replies calm and short, and move the conversation offline. A helpful reply to a critical review often reassures future customers more than another five stars.
Two replies to adapt:
```
Positive: Thanks, [first name]. Glad the [job] went well, and thanks for taking the time to write this. [your name]

Critical: Thanks for the feedback, [first name], and I'm sorry the [issue] wasn't what you expected. I'd like to put it right. Please call me on [phone] or email [email]. [your name]
```

### What to automate (and what not to)
- Automate: sending the request when a job is marked complete or an invoice is paid, the single reminder, and a log of who was asked and when.
- Automate: an alert when a new review arrives, so you can reply quickly.
- Don't automate: any filter that decides who gets the link based on how happy they seem. That's review gating.
- Don't automate: replies posted without you. A draft can be prepared for you to approve, but you should read and send it.

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how jobs are closed and invoiced today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your job or accounting software, email and texting, where they allow a connection). Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can I offer a discount for a review?
No. Google's policy bans incentives for reviews. In the UK, reviews that hide an incentive are banned under the DMCC Act 2024, and in the US the FTC's rule bans incentives conditioned on a positive or negative review. Just ask.

### Can I send the review link only to happy customers?
No. Google forbids selectively asking for positive reviews, and the UK CMA's guidance names encouraging only satisfied customers as a form of cherry-picking. Send the same request to everyone.

### What if a customer was unhappy?
Ask them the same way as everyone else, and fix the problem directly. A calm, helpful reply to a critical review often reassures future customers.

## AI in a small accounting firm: what to automate, and what to keep
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-in-accounting-firms-what-to-automate/ (2026-11-10)

In a small accounting firm, AI is worth using for reading, sorting and drafting: identifying uploaded documents, pulling key fields for a person to check, drafting routine client replies and spotting what's missing from a client's set. It should not give tax advice, decide a treatment or send anything to a client or tax authority without a qualified person approving it. The firm stays responsible for client data, so every AI tool needs checked data terms.

AI in a small accounting firm is useful when it does the dull reading, sorting and drafting, and risky when it's trusted with judgement. It's not a substitute for professional judgement, and in a regulated profession it shouldn't send anything to a client unchecked. Used that way, it removes a lot of dull work without changing who is responsible for the advice.
This post sorts common tasks into three groups (good for AI, [good for plain automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/), keep with a person), explains the data rules on both sides of the Atlantic, and gives you a one-page AI policy you can adapt.

### Where AI helps today
- Reading uploaded documents and suggesting what they are (a P60, a W-2, a bank statement, a receipt) and which client folder they belong in
- Pulling key fields from documents, such as dates, amounts and reference numbers, for a person to check
- Drafting replies to routine client questions, in your tone, for you to approve
- Summarising a long email thread before you call a client
- Spotting what's missing from a client's set of documents against their checklist

### AI, plain automation, or a person?
Many jobs firms want "AI" for don't need it. A reminder that goes out on the 5th of the month is a rule, not intelligence, and rules are cheaper, more predictable and easier to explain. Use AI only where a step involves reading or writing free text.
Task | Best handled by | Why
--- | --- | ---
Sending document requests and reminders | Plain automation | Fixed dates and fixed lists: no judgement needed
Filing emailed attachments into client folders | Automation, with AI to identify unclear files | Most files can be matched by sender; AI helps with the rest
Identifying document types and reading key fields | AI, checked by a person | Free-form documents, but errors matter
Drafting replies to routine questions | AI drafts, a person approves | Saves typing, keeps your name on what's sent
Categorising bank lines | Your accounting software's rules first, AI suggestions second | Rules are predictable; suggestions need review
Tax advice, treatments, fee decisions | A qualified person | Professional judgement and liability
Anything sent to HMRC or the IRS | A qualified person | You sign it, so you check it

### Where AI doesn't belong
- Giving tax advice or deciding a treatment
- Sending anything to a client or tax authority without a person reviewing it
- Anywhere you can't explain what it did and why
- Any step where client data would go to a tool whose data terms you haven't read

### Keep a person in the loop
The safe pattern is simple: AI prepares, a person approves. Drafts wait in a queue. Classifications show how sure they are, so unclear items get a closer look. Nothing leaves the firm without a click from someone qualified, and every approval is logged with who approved it and when.

### Data protection, UK and US
In the UK, UK GDPR makes the controller "responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with" the data protection principles (Article 5(2)). If your firm decides to put client data through an AI service, your firm is accountable for that choice, so keep a record of which tools touch which data and check each provider's terms on data use and storage.
In the US, the IRS's section 7216 regulations govern how tax return preparers may use and disclose tax return information, including when they need the taxpayer's consent. If client return data would go to an outside AI tool, check those rules with your counsel first. Federal law also requires professional tax preparers to have a written information security plan, and the IRS's Publication 5708 is a template for one. Your AI tools belong in it.
Consumer AI chat products and business products are treated differently. OpenAI, for example, says it doesn't train on content from its business workspaces or the API by default, while individual ChatGPT accounts [need the training setting turned off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/). Read the terms of whichever tool you use.

### A one-page AI policy you can adapt
AI use policy (small firm):
```
1. Approved tools: [tool names and plans]. No other AI tools for client work.
2. Client data: never paste client names, addresses, tax references, bank details or figures into a tool that isn't on the approved list.
3. Approval: every AI-drafted message to a client or tax authority is read and approved by [role] before it's sent.
4. Advice: AI is never used to decide a tax treatment or give advice. It may draft general explanations.
5. Records: we keep a list of which tools process which client data, and review it every [6] months.
6. Mistakes: if AI output was wrong and reached a client, tell [name] the same day.
7. US clients only: check section 7216 consent requirements before any return information goes to a third-party tool.

Owner: [name]   Last reviewed: [date]
```

### Start with the boring part
The biggest gains usually come before AI: requests, reminders and filing that run on a schedule. Add AI where it removes a manual sorting or drafting step, with approval built in. Our [free 12-page guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/guide/), "25 AI Automations for Accountants & Small Firms", lists ideas in that order, from document chasing to getting paid.

### For illustration
For illustration: clients upload documents through one link. Each file is read and labelled ("P60, 2025 to 2026, client: J. Smith") and saved in the client's folder. Anything the system isn't sure about goes into a short review list for a bookkeeper. Client questions that arrive by email get a drafted reply waiting for approval. Nothing is sent without a click.

### How Mike Automations would build this
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about which tasks eat your team's week. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, which parts use AI and which use plain rules, and where a person approves. It's built on the tools you already use (Xero or QuickBooks, Gmail or Outlook, your shared drive), with client data kept in your accounts. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can AI replace a bookkeeper in a small firm?
No. It can take over reading, sorting and drafting, but someone qualified still checks the work, makes the judgement calls and signs off what goes to clients and tax authorities.

### Is it safe to use AI with client data?
Only in tools whose data terms you've checked and approved, with a record of which tools process which data. Under UK GDPR your firm stays accountable, and US tax preparers also have [section 7216 rules](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/) on using return information.

### What should a small firm automate first: AI or reminders?
Usually reminders. Scheduled requests and filing give the biggest time savings with the least risk. AI comes next, for reading documents and drafting replies, with a person approving.

## How much does business automation cost for a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/ (2026-11-10)

Business automation cost for a small business comes in three parts: a one-off build, a few software subscriptions, and optional support. With Mike Automations, automating one process end to end costs $2,000 one-off ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), custom systems start at $5,000, and support is optional at $150 a month. The automation platform underneath usually adds somewhere between nothing and a few tens of dollars a month for a small firm.

Business automation cost is hard to compare, because providers quote in different ways: hourly rates, day rates, monthly retainers, per-workflow prices. This guide splits the cost into its three real parts, shows what drives each one, and gives [our own prices in full](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) so you can compare like with like.
Prices for the [automation platforms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) were checked on each vendor's own pricing page on 10 November 2026. They change often, so check them again before you buy.

### The cost table
Cost | What it is | Typical amount | Paid to
--- | --- | --- | ---
Build: one process | Mapping the process, connecting the tools, writing the messages, testing what goes wrong | Mike Automations: $2,000 one-off; $1,500 for the first 3 clients | Whoever builds it
Build: custom system | Clients, jobs, documents and tasks in one place, built around how you work | Mike Automations: from $5,000, one-time, by scope | Whoever builds it
Automation platform | The service that runs the workflow (Zapier, Make, n8n or similar) | Free tiers exist. Entry paid plans checked 10 November 2026: Zapier Professional from $19.99 a month billed yearly; Make Core $12 a month; n8n Starter €20 a month billed yearly | The vendor, from your own account
Software you already have | Email, cloud storage, forms, your accounting or job software | Usually nothing extra; some apps only allow connections on higher plans | The vendor
Texting (if used) | A texting provider; in the US, A2P 10DLC registration for business texts | Varies by provider and volume | The provider
Support | Fixes when an app changes, small changes as your process evolves | Mike Automations: small fixes for 60 days included; then optional $150 a month, cancel with 30 days' notice | Whoever supports it
Your time | A short call, answering questions, testing it with real cases | A few hours spread over the build | n/a

### 1. The build: what drives the price
This is the work of mapping the process, connecting the tools, writing the messages and testing the cases that go wrong. Three things drive it: the number of steps and conditions, how many tools are involved and whether they allow a connection, and whether the data is clean. A single process, such as document collection with reminders or estimate follow-ups, is a very different job from a full internal system.
Ways providers charge for the build:
- Hourly or day rate: flexible, but you carry the risk if it takes longer than expected.
- Fixed price per workflow: you know the cost before anything starts. Ask exactly what is included and what counts as "done".
- Monthly retainer or subscription: the build is spread over months; check what you keep if you stop paying.

### 2. Software subscriptions
Most workflows run on tools you may already pay for, plus an automation platform to connect them. For a small firm, the platform is often the smallest line on the bill. How each one charges matters more than the headline price: Zapier counts tasks (each action that completes), Make counts credits (roughly one per step), and n8n's cloud plans count executions (one per run of the whole workflow). Our comparison of Zapier, Make and n8n has the full table.
Make sure every subscription is in your name and paid from your account. Then the workflow belongs to you, and you're never locked in to whoever built it.

### 3. Keeping it running
Apps change, passwords expire and processes evolve. Either someone in your team learns to look after the workflow, or you pay for support. [Ask any provider](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/) three questions: what happens when something breaks, how quickly they respond, and whether you can leave and keep everything.

### Our pricing, in full
Prices are in US dollars, invoiced in pounds or euros at the equivalent rate. No deposit and no hourly billing. You get the exact scope and a fixed price in a [written plan](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/how-it-works/) within 48 hours of a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/), and a workflow is live in 2-3 days.
- Workflow automation (one process, end to end): $2,000, paid once it's running and you're happy with it. The first 3 businesses pay $1,500.
- Custom system (clients, jobs, documents and tasks in one place): from $5,000, by scope, agreed in writing before any work starts.
- Optional monthly support: $150 a month, cancel with 30 days' notice. Small fixes in the first 60 days are included.

### How to judge whether it's worth it
1. Write down the hours the process takes each month, including the reminders and the chasing.
2. Multiply by what an hour of that person's time is worth to you.
3. Add what it costs when the job is forgotten: a lost job, a late-filing penalty, a client who leaves.
4. Add the platform subscription for a year, and support if you want it.
5. If the yearly savings are larger than the build plus a year of running costs, it's usually worth doing. If not, start with a smaller process.

### For illustration: the sum
For illustration only, with made-up inputs you should replace with your own: a firm spends 5 hours a month chasing documents, and an hour is worth $40 to it. That's $200 a month, or $2,400 a year, before counting any lost clients. Against that: a $2,000 build plus a platform plan of, say, $20 a month ($240 a year). In this example the build pays for itself within the first year, and every year after costs only the subscription.

### Cost traps to watch for
- Per-step pricing on a busy workflow: a long workflow that runs thousands of times a month can push you up several plan tiers.
- Workflows built in the provider's account, not yours: you pay again if you ever leave.
- "Done" never defined: without a written definition of working, the build can drag on and the bill with it.
- Paying before it works: ask whether any money is due before the workflow is running.

With Mike Automations, $2,000 one-off for one process end to end ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), paid once it's running and you're happy with it. Add a platform subscription, which for a small firm is often free to a few tens of dollars a month.

Only for software you choose to use, such as an automation platform, paid directly from your own account. Our support is optional at $150 a month.

### Do you charge in pounds?
Prices are set in US dollars and invoiced in pounds or euros at the equivalent rate.

## How to stop chasing clients for VAT records every quarter
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/vat-quarter-records-chasing/ (2026-11-10)

A UK VAT return and payment are usually due one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period, so a quarter ending 31 December is due by 7 February. To stop chasing clients for VAT records, set your own cut-off about two weeks after the quarter ends, send each client a personal list of what's missing the day after the quarter closes, ask only about items the bank feed doesn't explain, and remind on a fixed rhythm until the list is complete.

Chasing clients for VAT records comes round four times a year for quarterly filers, and each time the same clients send their [invoices and receipts](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/) at the last minute. The work isn't the return. It's getting everything in early enough to check it.
Since 2023 there's also a clearer reason for clients to care: late VAT returns now earn penalty points, and late payments attract penalties that grow with time. Below: the deadline you work back from, the penalties in plain English, a quarterly routine, the messages to send and a timeline you can copy.

### The deadline you're working back from
GOV.UK says the deadline for submitting a VAT return online is usually one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the accounting period, and the payment must reach HMRC by the same date. A quarter ending 31 March is due by 7 May. The deadline doesn't move for weekends or bank holidays, and the payment needs time to clear. Each client's online VAT account shows their exact dates.
All VAT-registered businesses should now be signed up for Making Tax Digital for VAT, so returns go through compatible software unless HMRC has agreed an exemption. Clients on the annual accounting scheme work to different dates, so check each client's set-up.
Your real deadline is earlier: the date by which you need the records to prepare, query and file without a rush. For most practices that's about two weeks after the quarter ends.

### Why clients should care: the penalty rules
For VAT periods starting on or after 1 January 2023, the old default surcharge was replaced. Mentioning these rules, briefly and calmly, gives clients a concrete reason to send records on time.
- Late returns: each late return earns a penalty point. A quarterly filer who reaches 4 points gets a £200 penalty, and another £200 for each further late return while at the threshold. This includes nil and repayment returns.
- Late payment: nothing if paid within 15 days. From day 16, a first penalty of 3% of the VAT owed at day 15. From day 31, another 3% of what's still owed at day 30 is added, and a second penalty builds daily at 10% a year on the balance. Late payment interest runs from the first day.
- Agreeing a Time to Pay arrangement with HMRC can mean lower or no late payment penalties.

### A quarterly records workflow
1. Tag every VAT client with their quarter-end (stagger groups are common), so requests go out on the right dates.
2. About two weeks before each quarter ends, send a short heads-up: what you'll need, and where to send it.
3. The day after the quarter ends, send each client their own list of what's still missing, with one upload link.
4. Where bank feeds already come into the accounting software, ask only about what's unclear, such as uncategorised transactions or missing purchase invoices, instead of asking for everything again.
5. Remind on a fixed rhythm (every 5 to 7 days) until the list is complete, then stop.
6. Keep one daily view for the team: ready to prepare, waiting on client, or close to the deadline.
7. Ten days before the HMRC deadline, phone anyone who still hasn't responded. A person decides whether to file with what you have.

### A timeline for a quarter ending 31 December
For illustration only. Move the dates to suit your own stagger groups and workload.
Date | What happens | Who
--- | --- | ---
17 December | Heads-up: quarter closes soon, keep receipts together | Automatic
1 January | Personal list of what's missing, with the upload link | Automatic
7 to 14 January | Reminders listing only what's still missing | Automatic
15 January | Your cut-off. Anything outstanding goes on the team's call list | Team
16 to 28 January | Prepare, query and approve the return | Team
7 February | HMRC deadline for the return and cleared payment | Team and client

### The message that goes out the day after the quarter ends
Subject: Your VAT quarter to [31 December]: [N] items to send:
```
Hi [first name],

Your VAT quarter ended on [31 December]. To file on time we need a few things by [15 January]:

- [Purchase invoices for the 3 supplier payments listed below]
- [What the £[amount] payment to [payee] on [date] was for]
- [Your cash sales total for the quarter]

You can upload everything here, from your phone or computer: [upload link]

The return and payment are due to HMRC by [7 February]. Late returns now earn penalty points, so getting these to us early keeps you clear.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### What makes clients send records on time
- A personal list, not a generic "please send your VAT records"
- One upload link that works on a phone, with no login
- Reminders that list only what's still missing, and stop when it's done
- Your internal deadline in every message, well before the HMRC one
- Questions about specific bank lines, which are quicker to answer than "send everything"

### For illustration
For illustration: a bookkeeper has 60 clients on quarterly VAT. On 1 April each one gets a list for the March quarter. Clients with uncategorised bank lines get those lines to explain instead of a full request. By 15 April the bookkeeper sees 12 clients still waiting, and calls the 3 who haven't opened anything.
The same routine works for [MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/making-tax-digital-income-tax-practice-workflow/) and for [year-end records](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/limited-company-year-end-records/), so it's worth building once. If you use Xero, our post on [Xero automation ideas for practices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/xero-practice-automation-ideas/) shows where the bank feed can do some of the asking for you.

### When is a quarterly VAT return due?
Usually one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period, for both the return and the payment. A quarter ending 31 March is due by 7 May. Check the client's online VAT account for their exact dates.
