## How to automate engagement letters in a small accounting firm
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/ (2026-11-10)

To automate engagement letters, keep one approved template per service, fill it from the client's intake form, put each draft in a queue for a person to check, then send it for e-signature and remind the client until it's signed. When it's signed, the PDF is filed and onboarding starts on its own. The template, the scope, the fee and the final check stay with you, and the same workflow can re-issue letters when the scope or fee changes.

To automate engagement letters, you only need to automate the parts that are the same every time: the client's details, the services, the fee and your standard terms. Yet in many small firms the letter is still copied from last year's, edited by hand and emailed as an attachment. That's slow, and it's where mistakes creep in.
This post covers how the letter is put together, what can run on its own, the emails that go with it, and how to handle renewals when a client's work changes.

### Start from a template you trust
Automation only copies what you give it, so the template comes first. In the UK, ICAEW's Technical Advisory Service publishes an engagement letters helpsheet (last updated 10 March 2026) with sample wording. It splits a complete letter into parts: the engagement letter itself, schedules for each service (accounts, tax returns, payroll and so on), optional paragraphs, standard terms of business, and a privacy notice.
ICAEW describes the helpsheet as best practice guidance, not a professional standard, and says the wording should be tailored to each engagement with professional judgement. It also says the use of AI to tailor letters should be considered with caution. Other professional bodies, and US firms, will have their own sources. Use whichever applies to you, and check your template with your insurer or professional body if in doubt.
That structure suits automation well: one fixed covering letter, a schedule picked for each service the client takes, and terms that rarely change.

### What can be automated
1. Collect the client's details and the agreed services once, through an intake form or from the notes of your first call.
2. Build the letter from your approved parts: the covering letter, the schedules for the services ticked, your terms and privacy notice.
3. Fill in names, addresses, services, fee, start date and any [records cut-off date](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/records-cut-off-clause-engagement-letter/).
4. Put the draft in a queue for a person to check. Nothing goes out unchecked.
5. Send it for e-signature with one click, with a short covering email.
6. [Remind the client politely](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) every few days until it's signed.
7. When it's signed, file the PDF in the client's folder, update the client record and start the next onboarding step.

### Which details come from where
Letter field | Comes from | Checked by a person?
--- | --- | ---
Client name, address, entity type | Intake form | Yes, against ID documents
Services and schedules | Tick boxes on the intake form or call notes | Yes
Fee and billing terms | Your price list or the quote agreed on the call | Yes, always
Start date and first year covered | Intake form | Yes
Records cut-off date | Your standard dates for each service | Only if it differs from the standard
Terms of business and privacy notice | Your fixed template | When the template changes

### What stays with you
- The template itself, and any professional body requirements for its content
- The scope and the fee
- Anything unusual, such as a client with complex affairs or a service you don't normally offer
- The final check before anything is sent

### The covering email and the reminder
Subject: Your engagement letter from [firm name]: please sign:
```
Hi [first name],

Thank you for choosing us. Your engagement letter is ready to sign here: [e-signature link]

It sets out what we'll do for you ([services]), our fee ([fee]) and what we need from you, including sending your records by [cut-off date] each year.

It takes about two minutes on your phone. If anything doesn't look right, just reply to this email before signing.

[your name]

---

Reminder (sent after 3 days if not signed):

Subject: Quick reminder: your engagement letter

Hi [first name], just a reminder that your engagement letter is waiting here: [e-signature link]. Once it's signed we can get started. Thanks, [your name]
```

### Renewals: when to send a new letter
A letter that was right three years ago often isn't now. Many firms review every client's letter once a year, and re-issue it when something has changed. A workflow can do the noticing for you.
- The client adds or drops a service, such as VAT, payroll or MTD quarterly updates
- Your fee changes, or you move the client to a different billing arrangement
- The client's structure changes, for example from sole trader to limited company
- Your standard terms or privacy notice are updated
- Rules change in a way that alters what you do, such as a client joining MTD for Income Tax

### Why it's worth doing
A letter that goes out the same day the client says yes keeps momentum. A letter that takes a week often means the client starts sending documents before the terms are agreed. Automating the draft and the chase removes the delay without taking the decision away from you.

### For illustration
For illustration: a new client fills in the intake form on Tuesday morning. By lunchtime a draft letter is waiting in the partner's queue. The partner checks the fee, clicks approve, and the client gets it for e-signature. It's signed on Thursday, filed, and the AML document request goes out the same day. The full sequence is in our [client onboarding checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/).

### How we would build it for you
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you send engagement letters today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (your practice software, e-signature service, email and cloud storage, where they allow a connection) and is usually live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can AI write the engagement letter?
It isn't needed for most of it. A template filled from the intake form is more reliable, and ICAEW's helpsheet says AI should be used with caution when tailoring letters. AI can help draft an unusual scope, but a person always reviews the letter before it goes out.

### Which e-signature tools work?
Most common e-signature services can be connected. On the call we check what you already use.

### Do we need a new letter every year?
Not always. Many firms review letters yearly and re-issue them when the services, fee, client structure or their own terms change. Follow your professional body's guidance.

## AML client ID checks: a simple workflow for small UK accounting firms
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/ (2026-11-10)

AML client ID checks are the customer due diligence a UK accountancy firm in scope of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 must carry out: identify and verify the client and any beneficial owners, understand the purpose of the relationship, keep the records for five years after it ends, and keep monitoring. A simple workflow sends one secure request for documents, reminds the client until everything is in, routes the file to a person for the decision and sets the next review date. Your supervisor's rules decide what evidence is enough; the government has decided the FCA will take over AML supervision of accountancy firms, but no start date has been set.

AML client ID checks are part of customer due diligence: checking who the client is, who owns or controls the business, and what the relationship is for. Every [UK accountancy firm](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/accountants/) in scope of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 has to do it, under its supervisor's rules.
The checks themselves need judgement. The admin around them (asking for documents, chasing what's missing, recording what was checked and when, remembering reviews) is where small firms lose time. This article covers what the Regulations ask for, a checklist, a request email you can adapt, and a workflow that keeps it tidy.

### Who supervises you today, and what's changing
Today, firms supervised by a professional body (such as ICAEW, ACCA or AAT) follow that body's requirements and the accountancy sector guidance. GOV.UK says accountancy service providers not supervised by a professional body must register with HMRC, which then supervises them.
That is set to change. On 21 October 2025, HM Treasury announced its decision that the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will take over AML supervision of legal and accountancy firms and trust and company service providers. Its June 2026 response on the FCA's powers says this will be done through primary legislation in a Financial Services Bill, followed by changes to the Money Laundering Regulations. No date has been set for the FCA to take over, and HM Treasury has said the timing depends on parliamentary time.
Until the change takes effect, your current supervisor's rules apply. Whoever supervises you, the core duties below come from the Regulations themselves, so a well-organised process carries straight over.

### What the Regulations ask for, in brief
This is a summary to organise the work, not legal advice. What evidence is enough for each client is your call, under your supervisor's guidance.
- When: customer due diligence is required when you establish a business relationship, when you suspect money laundering, or when you doubt documents you were given earlier (regulation 27).
- What: identify the client and verify their identity, identify and verify beneficial owners, and understand the purpose and intended nature of the relationship (regulation 28). For a company that includes its name, company number, registered office and directors.
- Timing: verification should normally be done before the business relationship starts. It can finish during set-up only where that's needed not to interrupt business and the risk is low (regulation 30).
- Firm-wide risk assessment: a written assessment of the risks your firm faces, which shapes how deep each check goes (regulation 18).
- Records: keep copies of the documents and information obtained for at least five years after the business relationship ends (regulation 40).
- Ongoing monitoring: keep the information up to date and review clients over time, more often for higher-risk ones.

### A CDD checklist for each new client
Adapt the rows to your firm's policy. The 25% figure is the usual beneficial ownership test, but check your supervisor's guidance for the client types you take on.
Item | Individual or sole trader | Company or LLP
--- | --- | ---
Identity evidence | Photo ID and proof of address, or an electronic check | For each director and person giving instructions
Beneficial owners | Not usually applicable | Each person owning or controlling over 25%, verified
Company details | Not applicable | Name, number, registered office, Companies House extract
Purpose of the relationship | Services agreed and expected activity | Services agreed, nature of the business
Risk rating | Low, medium or high, with a short reason | Low, medium or high, with a short reason
Decision | Accepted or declined, by whom, on what date | Accepted or declined, by whom, on what date
Next review | Date set from the risk rating | Date set from the risk rating

### Where the admin goes wrong
- ID documents arrive by email attachment and sit in an inbox
- Nobody tracks which new clients are still missing something, so work starts before the checks are done
- Re-checks for existing clients are forgotten until an inspection
- Records of what was checked, by whom and when are scattered across folders
- The firm-wide risk assessment is written once and never looked at again

### A workflow that keeps it tidy
1. When a new client is accepted in principle, send one secure link for the documents you ask for, never email attachments.
2. If you use a digital identity verification service, send the client its link in the same message.
3. Remind the client every few days until everything is in, listing only what's missing.
4. Hold the engagement: the file is marked "CDD pending" and no work starts until a person clears it.
5. A person reviews the evidence, sets the risk rating and records the decision. The workflow never approves a client.
6. File the record in the client's folder with the date and the reviewer's name, and set the next review date from the risk rating.
7. When a review date comes round, send the client a short request to confirm or update their details, and put the file back in the review queue.

### The request email
Subject: Two quick things before we start: your ID check:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for choosing us. Like every UK accountancy firm, we have to confirm the identity of our clients before we start work. It takes about five minutes.

1. Please upload [a photo of your passport or driving licence] and [a recent bank statement or utility bill showing your address] here: [secure upload link]
2. [Then complete the short online identity check here: [verification link]]

[For your company: please also confirm who owns more than 25% of the shares, and send any shareholder agreement.]

Please don't send ID documents by email. The link above goes straight to secure storage.

Once we have these, we'll confirm and send your first document request.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### For illustration
For illustration: a client signs [the engagement letter](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/). Within minutes they get a secure upload link for their documents and a link to a verification service. Two days later one item is still missing and a reminder goes out. When it's complete, the partner gets a short note to review the file. They set the risk rating to low, approve, and the review date for next year is set automatically.
AML checks sit inside onboarding, between the engagement letter and the first document request. Our [client onboarding checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/) shows the full sequence, and if you also [verify directors for Companies House](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/companies-house-identity-verification-client-tracker/), keep that tracker separate: it's a different legal requirement.

### How we would build it for you
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you onboard and check clients today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (your practice software, email, cloud storage and any ID verification service you have, where they allow a connection) and is usually live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Who will supervise accountancy firms for AML?
Today it's your professional body, or HMRC if you're not supervised by one. HM Treasury has decided the FCA will take over AML supervision of accountancy firms through new legislation, but no start date has been set. Until then, follow your current supervisor's rules.

### How long must we keep CDD records?
The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 (regulation 40) require the documents and information obtained for customer due diligence to be kept for at least five years after the business relationship ends.

### Can the workflow decide whether a client passes?
No. It collects, reminds and records. The decision to accept a client, and any judgement about risk, stays with a person in your firm.

### Is it safe to collect ID documents this way?
Use a secure upload link into storage you control, with access limited to the people who need it. Avoid email attachments for ID documents.

## Client portal vs email: how should clients send you documents?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/ (2026-11-10)

In the client portal vs email debate, the best answer for most small accounting firms is both, joined up: keep the portal as the main route, give clients who never log in a no-login upload link that files into the same place, and automatically file whatever still arrives by email. What decides it is not the software but how many steps the client has to take, because clients send documents the easiest way they know.

Client portal vs email is a question every firm asks once the inbox fills up in January: should we force clients to use a portal? The honest answer depends less on the software and more on whether your clients will [actually use it](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-use-your-client-portal/). Below are the four usual options, how they compare, and a set-up that works with the clients you have rather than the clients you wish you had.

### The four options compared
Option | Effort for the client | Order for you | Main risk
--- | --- | --- | ---
Email attachments | None: they already know how | Low: files scatter across inboxes and threads | Sensitive documents sent unprotected, and nothing tracks what's still missing
Shared folder per client | Medium: they have to find the folder and the right sub-folder | Medium: tidy if they use it properly | Files dropped in the wrong place, or the link lost by February
Client portal | High the first time: an account, a password, sometimes an app | High: one place for documents, messages and signatures | Some clients never log in and email you anyway
No-login upload link | Low: one link that works on a phone | High: files land in the right client folder | Needs to be built and checked so files go to the right client

### What actually decides it
Clients send documents the easiest way they know. If the portal needs a password they've forgotten, they'll photograph the P60 or the W-2 and email it. So the best set-up is the one with the fewest steps for the client, and the most order for you behind the scenes.
Three questions settle most cases. How many of your clients logged in to the portal last season without being reminded? How many documents still arrived by email? And how long did someone spend moving attachments into folders? If the answers are "most", "a few" and "not long", your portal is working and you just need [better reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/). If they're "some", "lots" and "days", you need a second route.

### A combination that works
1. Keep your portal if you have one, and link clients straight to the right place in it from every request.
2. For clients who never log in, offer a plain upload link that files into the same client folder the portal uses.
3. Whatever still arrives by email, save it automatically into the client's folder with a clear file name.
4. Track everything against each client's checklist, wherever it came from, so reminders name only what's still missing.
5. Stop reminders the moment a client is complete, so nobody gets chased for something they've already sent.

### Security: what the rules expect
In the UK, UK GDPR requires personal data to be "processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security" (Article 5(1)(f)), and your firm stays responsible for showing it complies. Passports, bank statements and tax records sent as plain email attachments are hard to square with that, which is why a portal or a secure upload link is the better habit for anything sensitive.
In the US, the IRS and its Security Summit partners point out that federal law requires all professional tax preparers to create and implement [a written data security plan](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/wisp-for-small-tax-practices/) (see IRS Publication 5708). How client documents come in, and where they're stored, belongs in that plan.
None of this bans email. It means you should decide which documents may come by email, steer the sensitive ones to a secure route, and make sure emailed files end up in storage you control rather than in a personal inbox.

### A message telling clients how to send documents
Put this at the top of your first request each season. It gives clients one clear route and a fallback, so they don't invent a third.
How to send us your documents:
```
Subject: How to send us your documents for [tax year]

Hi [first name],

The easiest way to send your documents is through your client portal: [portal link]

If you can't log in, use this upload link instead. No password needed, and it works on your phone: [upload link]

Please don't email ID documents or bank statements. For anything else, email is fine and we'll file it for you.

Here's what we still need from you:
[list of missing items]

We'll remind you about anything that's still missing, and stop as soon as it's all in.

Thanks,
[name]
```

### For illustration
For illustration: most clients upload through the firm's portal, but a handful always reply by email with photos. Those attachments are saved to the right client folder as "Client - Year - Document" and ticked off the checklist. The next reminder lists only what's still missing, so nobody has to sort the inbox by hand and nobody is asked twice.

### How Mike Automations would build this
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how documents reach you today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every document lands in the right client folder, whichever route it came by, and reminders name only what's missing". It's built around the portal, email and storage you already use, so your team and your clients don't learn a new system. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Do we need to replace our portal?
No. A workflow can sit around the portal you already have, give non-users a simpler upload route, and catch what arrives by email.

### Is email safe for client documents?
It's common, but for sensitive documents such as ID and bank statements, a portal or a secure upload link into storage you control is the better habit. UK GDPR expects appropriate security, and US tax preparers need a written data security plan.

### Should we refuse documents sent by email?
Refusing them usually just delays the work. Accept them, file them automatically, and steer the client to the portal or upload link next time.

## How to reply to every new enquiry within minutes (even when you're busy)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/ (2026-11-10)

To reply to new enquiries fast without working faster, make the first reply automatic: every enquiry from your website, email or messages lands in one list, the customer gets an honest acknowledgement within minutes saying when you'll call and how to book, and anything without a personal reply by the next morning goes on your list for that day. You still do the real conversation; the system makes sure nobody waits in silence.

How to reply to new enquiries fast is a problem for [every small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) where the owner is also doing the work: on a roof, with a client, in a meeting. Most small businesses don't lose enquiries because they say no. They lose them because the reply comes the next day, after the customer has already called someone else.
The fix isn't working faster. It's making the first reply automatic and honest, and making sure no enquiry can slip through. Below: the workflow, auto-reply templates for each channel, what to log, and the rules on texting customers.

### Why the first reply matters
Someone who has just filled in your form is thinking about the job right now, and often has two or three other businesses open in other tabs. A quick, friendly reply that says what happens next keeps you in the running. A reply tomorrow often reaches someone who has already booked elsewhere.
The first reply doesn't have to answer everything. It has to do three things: confirm you got the message, say when a person will be in touch, and give an easy next step, such as a booking link.

### The enquiry workflow
1. Every enquiry, from your website form, email or messages, lands in one list: a shared sheet or your job software.
2. Within minutes, the customer gets a short, honest reply: thanks, when you'll call, and a link to book a call or visit.
3. You get a notification with the details, so you can call back when you're between jobs.
4. If nobody has replied personally by the next morning, it goes on your list for that day.
5. Enquiries that go quiet after your reply get [one polite follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/estimate-follow-up-email-templates-contractors/) a few days later, then stop.

### What to log for every enquiry
Field | Why it matters
--- | ---
Date and time received | So you can see how long people wait
Source (form, email, phone, message) | So you know which channels bring work
Name and best contact | So anyone in the team can call back
What they need, and where | So you can prioritise and plan the visit
Status (new, replied, booked, quoted, lost) | So nothing sits at "new" for more than a day
Next action and date | So follow-ups happen without memory

### Auto-reply for website forms
Email, sent within minutes:
```
Hi [first name], thanks for getting in touch about [job]. I'm on a job right now, and I'll call you back by [time or "tomorrow morning"]. If it's easier, you can pick a time here: [booking link].

[your name], [company], [phone]
```

### Out-of-hours reply
Email or message, evenings and weekends:
```
Hi [first name], thanks for your message about [job]. We're closed right now and back at [time] on [day], when I'll get back to you. If you'd like to choose a time for a call or visit now, here's the link: [booking link]. If this is an emergency, [what to do, e.g. call our emergency line on [number]].

[your name], [company]
```

### Follow-up when they go quiet
Keep every automatic message short and honest. It's an acknowledgement, not a sales pitch, and it should never pretend to be a person typing live.
Sent 3 days after your reply, once:
```
Hi [first name], just following up on your enquiry about [job]. Are you still looking for help with it? Happy to answer questions or book a visit: [booking link]. If you've sorted it already, no problem at all.

[your name]
```

### Phone calls you miss
Phone enquiries are the hardest to catch, because a missed call leaves no details. A [text sent automatically after a missed call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/), asking what the job is and offering a booking link, turns a missed call into a written enquiry in the same list. We cover that on our page about missed call text back for contractors.

### Texting rules in the UK and US
In the US, business texts sent from a regular 10-digit number have to be registered for A2P 10DLC through your texting provider, and the major carriers block unregistered business texts. Only text people who have agreed to it, for example with a checkbox on your enquiry form. Email works from day one.
In the UK, the ICO treats messages sent for administrative or customer service purposes as service messages rather than direct marketing, as long as they contain nothing promotional. Keep the auto-reply about the customer's own request; add offers or promotions and it starts to count as marketing.

### For illustration
For illustration: a homeowner fills in the form at 10:40 while you're on a roof. At 10:41 they get a reply with a booking link, and the enquiry appears in your sheet as "new". At lunch you see it and call back. By then they've already picked a slot for a visit, and the status changes to "booked".

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how enquiries reach you today and where they wait. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your website form, email, phone line, calendar and a shared sheet or your job software), so there's nothing new to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Will customers mind an automatic reply?
Not if it's honest and useful: it confirms you got the message and says when you'll be in touch. Pretending to be a live person is what annoys people.

### Can replies go out by text?
Yes, where the customer has agreed to texts. In the US, business texting from a 10-digit number needs A2P 10DLC registration; email works from day one.

### Should AI write the replies?
AI can draft a personal reply from the enquiry details, but a person should approve it before it's sent. The instant acknowledgement works best as a fixed, honest template.

## How to collect payroll inputs from clients on time, every pay run
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-payroll-inputs-from-clients/ (2026-11-10)

To collect payroll inputs from clients on time, send every payroll client the same short form a few days before each cut-off, asking for hours, new starters, leavers, pay changes, or a clear "no changes". Remind only the clients who haven't answered, and on cut-off day work from one list showing who is complete, partial or silent. Keep each answer with its pay period, so you have a record of what the client told you and when.

If you run payroll for clients, you know how to collect payroll inputs from clients in theory: ask, wait, chase. In practice the pay date is fixed and the information only the client has (hours, new starters, leavers, bonuses, changes) [arrives late](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-documents-on-time/), by text, or not at all. When it's late, the pay run is rushed. When it's incomplete, it's wrong, and correcting it takes longer than doing it right the first time.
This post gives you a routine, the fields your inputs form needs, a reminder you can copy, and the official deadlines that make the cut-off matter in the UK and the US. If you place temps, our [timesheet chasing plan for recruitment agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/recruitment-timesheet-chasing/) covers the hours side.

### What usually goes wrong
- The request goes out late, or only to the clients who usually have changes
- Changes arrive in a text, a voicemail or a chat with the client's manager, and never reach the payroll file
- New starter details are missing on the day they're needed
- Nobody knows which clients have confirmed "no changes this period" and which simply haven't replied
- There's no record of what the client said, so a dispute about hours becomes your word against theirs

### Why the cut-off is not just your preference
In the UK, GOV.UK says employers must send the Full Payment Submission (FPS) to HMRC on or before their employees' payday, and must tell HMRC about a new employee on or before their first payday, using the employee's P45 or, if there isn't one, HMRC's starter checklist. A leaver needs a P45. So missing starter or leaver details on cut-off day isn't only an inconvenience: it can mean a late or wrong submission.
In the US, new employees complete Form W-4 so the employer can withhold the right federal income tax, and the federal Administration for Children and Families says federal law requires employers to report new and rehired employees to the state within 20 days of hire (some states set a shorter deadline). New hire paperwork belongs in the same request as the pay run inputs.

### The fields your payroll inputs form needs
Section | What to ask | Notes
--- | --- | ---
Confirmation | Any changes this pay period? Yes / No | A "No" is an answer. It closes the request and stops reminders.
Hours | Hours or timesheet per hourly employee, or an upload | Ask for a file in the same format every time.
One-off pay | Bonuses, commission, overtime, expenses to reimburse | Ask for the amount and the reason, so you can treat it correctly.
Starters | Name, start date, pay rate, role | Triggers a separate request to the new employee for their own details (P45 or starter checklist in the UK, Form W-4 in the US).
Leavers | Name, last working day, any final payments | In the UK you'll need to issue a P45.
Changes | Pay rises, hours changes, address or bank detail changes, absences | Bank details should come from the employee through a secure route, never by plain email.
Sign-off | Name of the person confirming, and the date | Saved with the pay period as your record.

### A pay-run inputs routine
1. Five working days before each cut-off, every payroll client gets the same short form link. Same day, same wording, every period.
2. A new starter on the form triggers a separate request to the employee for their own details, so the client doesn't have to pass them on.
3. Two days before cut-off, clients who haven't answered get a reminder. Clients who have answered get nothing.
4. On the morning of cut-off, you see one list: complete, [partial](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/), or nothing received. You call only the last group.
5. Everything submitted is saved with the pay period, so you have a record of what the client told you and when.

### A reminder you can copy
Payroll inputs reminder:
```
Subject: Payroll for [pay period]: changes needed by [cut-off date]

Hi [first name],

We run [client business name]'s payroll on [processing date] for payday on [payday].

Please tell us about any hours, new starters, leavers, bonuses or pay changes here: [form link]

No changes this time? Just select "No changes" on the form. It takes ten seconds and means we won't chase you.

We need this by [cut-off date and time]. Anything that arrives later goes into the next pay run.

Thanks,
[name]
```

### What stays with you
Running the payroll, checking anything unusual, and making the filings. The workflow collects and organises. A person reviews the inputs and runs the pay, and anything odd (a sudden jump in hours, a leaver with no final pay listed) is flagged for you rather than processed.

### For illustration
For illustration: payroll cut-off is the 20th. On the 13th each client gets the form link. By the 18th, 9 of 12 have answered, including 2 "no changes". The other 3 get one reminder. On the morning of the 20th you call the last client, and the pay run starts on time with a saved record of every answer.

### How Mike Automations would build this
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how payroll inputs reach you today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every payroll client gets the form five working days before cut-off, and you see one status list on cut-off morning". It's built on the tools you already use: your payroll software, Xero or QuickBooks, Gmail or Outlook, and your shared drive. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Do clients need to log in anywhere?
No. A simple form link works on any phone or computer, and the answers come to you in one place.

### Does this replace payroll software?
No. Payroll is still run in your payroll software. The workflow makes sure the inputs arrive on time and complete.

### What if a client sends changes after the cut-off?
Say in your reminder that late changes go into the next pay run, and stick to it unless the change is urgent. The form keeps a dated record, so it's clear what arrived when.

### When must a UK employer report a pay run to HMRC?
GOV.UK says the Full Payment Submission must be sent on or before the employees' payday, even if the employer pays HMRC quarterly.

## Xero automation ideas for small accounting practices
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/xero-practice-automation-ideas/ (2026-11-10)

The best Xero automation ideas for a small accounting practice sit around Xero rather than inside it. Xero already automates bank feeds, bank rules, repeating invoices and invoice reminders. What it doesn't do is the conversation with your clients: asking about unexplained bank lines, chasing missing receipts and tracking who is ready for month end, which is where a workflow saves the most time.

Most Xero automation ideas you'll read about are features Xero already has. They're worth switching on, but in a small practice the hours go somewhere else: asking clients about transactions, [chasing receipts](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/), and keeping track of who is ready for month end or [the VAT quarter](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/vat-quarter-records-chasing/). That's the work this post is about.
What can be connected depends on your Xero plan, your country, the apps you use and what Xero's integrations allow, so treat these as ideas to check, not promises.

### What Xero already automates
Before building anything, make sure each client is using what's in the box. According to Xero's UK product and pricing pages (checked November 2026), Xero includes:
- Bank feeds, with bank rules that treat groups of similar transactions the same way every time
- JAX, Xero's AI assistant, which suggests matches when reconciling based on your rules, existing records and past reconciliations, for a person to review
- Repeating invoices that are created and sent automatically
- Automatic invoice reminders before or after the due date, which only chase invoices still unpaid according to the bank feed
- Hubdoc for capturing bills and receipts, included in its plans when connected to the Xero subscription
- A marketplace of over 1,000 connected apps

### Check the plan before you build
Plan limits change what's worth automating. On Xero's UK pricing page, the entry plan (Ignite) lets a business send quotes and 20 invoices and enter 10 bills, while the higher plans include automated bill entry. A workflow that pushes more invoices or bills into Xero than the plan allows will simply stop working. Plan names and limits differ by country, so check the pricing page for each client's region.

### Xero automation ideas that save a practice the most time
Task | What Xero does | What a workflow adds
--- | --- | ---
Unexplained bank lines | Shows unreconciled transactions and suggests matches | Sends each client one short list of the lines you need explained, with a form to answer each one, and reminds until it's done
Missing receipts | Hubdoc captures receipts the client sends in | Asks for the receipt for a specific transaction, with one upload link, and stops asking once it arrives
Your clients' overdue invoices | Sends automatic reminders on a schedule | Escalates the ones still unpaid after the last reminder to your client, with a suggested call list
Month-end readiness | Reports once the books are up to date | Keeps one status list per client (statements in, queries answered, receipts outstanding), ready each morning
New client set-up | Creates the organisation once you add it | Creates the client folder, sends the first requests and books the kick-off once the engagement letter is signed

### A bank query email you can copy
The most common time sink is the bank query thread. One clear list, sent on the same day each month, gets faster answers than a running email conversation.
Monthly bank query email:
```
Subject: [n] transactions to explain for [month]

Hi [first name],

We've reconciled [client business name]'s bank for [month]. There are [n] transactions we can't match without your help:

[date] - [payee] - [amount]
[date] - [payee] - [amount]

Please tell us what each one was for here: [form link]
If you have a receipt, you can upload it on the same form.

It should take about five minutes. We need this by [date] to finish your [month-end / VAT return].

Thanks,
[name]
```

### How to decide what to automate first
1. Pick the task you repeat for most clients every month.
2. Write down the steps as they happen today, including who asks whom and how.
3. Define "done" in one sentence, for example "every client with unexplained lines gets one clear list on the 3rd".
4. [Automate the requests and reminders first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/). Leave the judgement calls with your team.
5. Run it for one month on a few clients, then roll it out to the rest.

### Where to be careful
- Only give the automation the access it needs, and keep client data in your own accounts
- Never let anything post to the ledger without a person reviewing it
- If AI suggests a category or reads a receipt, show it as a suggestion for a person to approve
- Keep a note of which apps are connected to which client organisation, so access can be removed when a client leaves

### For illustration
For illustration: on the 3rd of each month, every client with unreconciled bank lines gets one email listing them, with a simple form to explain each one. Answers come back into a single sheet for the bookkeeper to review and post. Clients with nothing outstanding get nothing, and on the 8th the bookkeeper sees a short list of who still hasn't replied.

We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about where your team's month goes. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every client with unreconciled lines gets one list on the 3rd and reminders stop when they've answered". It's built on Xero and the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox), so your team doesn't learn a new system. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does this replace Xero bank rules or receipt capture apps?
No. Those handle what happens inside the books. The workflow handles the conversation with the client around them: questions, reminders and status.

### Does it need a paid Xero add-on?
Not always. It depends on what you want to connect and on each client's plan. On a call we check what your current plans and apps already allow.

### Can Xero chase overdue invoices on its own?
Yes. Xero's invoice reminders can go out before or after the due date and only chase invoices still unpaid. A workflow is useful for what happens after the last reminder.

## How to brief an automation project (with a free template)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-brief-an-automation-project/ (2026-11-10)

To brief an automation project, write one page that covers the process as it happens today step by step, who does each step and how often, the tools and accounts it may use, what "done" looks like in a sentence you could test, what must stay manual, and who approves anything sent to clients. The "done means" line matters most, because it is how you and the builder will judge the result.

Knowing how to brief an automation project is the cheapest way to make one succeed. Most automation projects that disappoint weren't built badly. They were briefed vaguely. "Automate our onboarding" can mean ten different things, and the builder will pick one. A one-page brief fixes that, and it takes about twenty minutes.
Below: what a good brief covers, a template to copy, a filled-in example, [the questions to ask whoever builds it](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/), and the warning signs in a proposal.

### Why vague briefs fail
- The builder automates [the tidy version of the process](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/), and the messy cases (the client who emails photos, the job that needs a second quote) break it in week one
- Nobody agreed what "working" means, so nobody can say whether it does
- Something that needed a person's judgement gets automated, and a client receives a message nobody checked
- It runs in the builder's accounts, so when the relationship ends, so does the automation

### What a good brief covers
Section | What to write | Why it matters
--- | --- | ---
The process today | Every step in order, including the messy parts and workarounds | The exceptions are where automations break
Who and how often | Who does each step, and how many times a week or month | Shows where the time goes, and what it's worth
Tools and accounts | Which systems are involved and which accounts it may use | Decides what can connect, and who owns it
Done means | One or two sentences you could test | The only fair way to judge the result
Must stay manual | Advice, pricing, approvals, anything needing judgement | Keeps a person in control of what matters
Messages to clients | Whether any go out, and who approves the wording | Your name is on them
What goes wrong today | The real failures: forgotten reminders, lost files | Tells the builder what to test against

### The automation brief template
Automation brief:
```
Process: [name, e.g. new client onboarding]
How often: [e.g. 5-10 times a month]
Time it takes today: [e.g. about 40 minutes per client, spread over two weeks]

Today, step by step:
1. [who] [does what] [in which tool]
2. ...
3. ...

The messy cases: [e.g. clients who reply by text, clients who send half the documents]

Tools and accounts it may use: [e.g. Outlook, OneDrive, Xero]
Accounts it must NOT touch: [e.g. bank accounts, payroll]

Done means: [e.g. every new client gets a checklist within an hour of signing, and reminders until everything is in]

Must stay manual: [e.g. reviewing ID, setting the fee]

Messages to clients: [yes/no; who approves the wording]

What goes wrong today: [e.g. reminders forgotten in January]

Who to tell when something fails: [name, email]
```

### A filled-in example
For illustration, here is the brief a small bookkeeping practice might write for its month-end receipt chase:
Example brief (for illustration):
```
Process: month-end receipt chase
How often: once a month, about 30 clients
Time it takes today: most of two days for one bookkeeper

Today, step by step:
1. Bookkeeper exports unreconciled lines from Xero for each client
2. Bookkeeper emails each client a list and asks for receipts
3. Clients reply by email, some with photos, some weeks later
4. Bookkeeper saves receipts to the client folder in OneDrive and attaches them in Xero

The messy cases: clients who reply 'see attached' with no attachment; one receipt covering three lines

Tools and accounts it may use: Outlook, OneDrive, Xero (read only)
Accounts it must NOT touch: anything that posts to the ledger

Done means: every client with missing receipts gets one list on the 3rd, reminders on the 7th and 10th, and on the 11th the bookkeeper sees who is still outstanding.

Must stay manual: matching receipts to lines, posting anything in Xero

Messages to clients: yes; the practice owner approves the wording once

What goes wrong today: reminders slip when the team is busy, and receipts get lost in the inbox
```

### Questions to ask whoever builds it
- What happens when something fails, and who gets told?
- Whose accounts does it run in, and what happens if we stop working together?
- How will we test it on real work before paying?
- How do we pause it, and who can change the wording of messages?
- What does it cost to run each month, and does that cost grow with volume?
- What's included if something needs fixing after it goes live?

### Warning signs in a proposal
- No written definition of "working", only a list of features
- Hourly billing with no cap, so you can't know the [final cost](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/)
- Everything runs in the builder's own accounts, with no plan to hand it over
- Messages to clients go out with no approval step
- A promise to automate everything at once, rather than one process first

### How Mike Automations uses your brief
You don't need a polished brief to talk to us. Bring what you have to a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/), and we'll fill in the gaps together. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working" taken from your "done means" line. It's built on the tools you already use and in your accounts. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. If it doesn't do what the plan said, you owe nothing.

### Do I need to know which tool to use?
No. Describe the process and the tools you already use. Choosing the automation platform is the builder's job.

### How long should an automation brief be?
One page is enough. The "done means" line matters most, because it's how you'll judge the result.

### Should I brief several processes at once?
Brief one first, [the one you repeat most often](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/). Once it runs, the second brief is easier because you know what worked.

## ChatGPT prompts for accountants, without risking client data
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/ (2026-11-10)

The most useful ChatGPT prompts for accountants are for drafting: client document requests, chasers, plain-English explanations, checklists and fee or scope emails. Write them with placeholders such as [client name] instead of real client details, and fill those in yourself afterwards. Before using ChatGPT for work, check your firm's policy and your account's data settings, because individual accounts may be used for model training unless you turn that off.

These ChatGPT prompts for accountants are for the writing that surrounds the real work: emails, checklists and explanations. Used carefully, [AI chat tools](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-in-accounting-firms-what-to-automate/) save time there. The rule that matters most is simple: the prompt shouldn't contain anything you couldn't put on a postcard.
Below you'll find the rules to follow first, the data settings to check, eight prompts you can copy, and the point where copying prompts stops being worth it.

### Rules before any prompt
- No client names, addresses, tax references, Social Security numbers, bank details or figures in a general AI chat
- Use placeholders like [client name] and fill them in yourself afterwards, outside the chat
- Check your firm's policy and the AI tool's data settings before using it for work
- Read every draft. You're responsible for anything sent in your name
- Never ask it for advice on a specific client's tax position

### Check your ChatGPT data settings first
OpenAI's help pages (checked November 2026) explain how this works:
- On individual ChatGPT accounts, OpenAI may use your content to train its models unless you opt out. The setting is called "Improve the model for everyone", in ChatGPT's data controls. Turning it off keeps your chat history.
- A Temporary Chat stays out of your history and isn't used to train models while it stays temporary, but OpenAI may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes.
- OpenAI says it doesn't use content from its business workspaces (ChatGPT Business and Enterprise) or from the API to train models by default. Your organisation's own retention and access settings still apply.

### The rules behind the settings
In the UK, UK GDPR keeps your firm accountable for client personal data it decides to process, whichever tool it uses (Article 5(2)). In the US, tax return preparers also have the IRS's section 7216 rules on using and disclosing tax return information, which can require the taxpayer's consent. Placeholders keep both questions out of your prompts entirely, which is why they're rule one.

### Prompt 1: a friendly document request
Prompt:
```
Write a short, friendly email from a small accounting firm to a client asking for their documents for the [tax year] return. List these items as bullet points: [item 1], [item 2], [item 3]. Mention that they can upload everything at [upload link] and that we need it by [date]. Plain English, under 120 words, no jargon.
```

### Prompt 2: a firmer second reminder
Prompt:
```
Rewrite this reminder so it's polite but firmer. Say that we still need [missing items], that the deadline is [date], and that if we don't have everything by [cut-off date] we can't guarantee the return will be filed on time. Keep it under 100 words and keep a friendly tone. Here's the first reminder: [paste reminder without client details]
```

### Prompt 3: explain something simply
Check the result against the official source before sending it. AI explanations can be confidently wrong about thresholds and dates.
Prompt:
```
Explain [topic, e.g. what a payment on account is] to a small business owner with no accounting background, in under 150 words. Use one everyday example. Don't give advice specific to any person.
```

### Prompt 4: turn a process into a checklist
The checklist you get back is also a good starting point for automating the process later.
Prompt:
```
Turn these notes about how we onboard a new client into a numbered checklist with an owner for each step: [paste your notes with names removed].
```

### Prompt 5: a client checklist by income type
Treat the result as a first draft. Check it against your own checklist and the tax authority's guidance before giving it to clients.
Prompt:
```
Create a checklist of records a [type of client, e.g. sole trader who also rents out one property] usually needs to send their accountant for their annual tax return in [UK / US]. Group it by topic and write each item in plain English. Mark anything that depends on their circumstances as 'if this applies'.
```

### Prompt 6: a fee or scope change email
Prompt:
```
Write a clear, polite email from a small accounting firm telling a client that work outside our agreed scope, specifically [describe the extra work], will be charged at [fee]. Explain why in one sentence, offer a short call, and ask them to confirm by replying. Under 150 words.
```

### Prompt 7: reply to a common question
Prompt:
```
A client asked: [paste the question with any personal details removed]. Draft a short reply in a friendly, professional tone. If the answer depends on their circumstances, say we'll look at it and come back to them, rather than guessing.
```

### Prompt 8: tidy up your own notes
Prompt:
```
Turn these rough notes from a team meeting into a short list of actions, each with an owner and a due date: [paste notes with client names replaced by initials or codes].
```

### Where prompts stop and automation starts
Copying drafts between a chat window and your email still takes time, and it's easy to slip client details into the chat by mistake. A workflow can use the same kind of drafting inside your own systems, fill in client details itself from your records, and put every draft in a queue for a person to approve before it's sent. If you want ideas for which tasks to start with, [our free 12-page guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/guide/) "25 AI Automations for Accountants & Small Firms" lists them.

### How Mike Automations would build this
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about which emails and checklists take your team the most time. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every reminder is drafted with the client's own missing items and waits for approval". It's built on the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Xero or QuickBooks, your shared drive), with client data kept in your accounts. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Is it safe to paste client documents into ChatGPT?
Not into a general chat. Keep client data in tools your firm has approved for it, with data settings you've checked. On individual ChatGPT accounts, content may be used for training unless you turn that off.

### Does ChatGPT train on what accountants type into it?
OpenAI says it may use content from individual accounts for training unless you turn off "Improve the model for everyone", and that it doesn't train on business workspaces or the API by default.

### Can AI give tax advice to clients?
It shouldn't. Use it for drafting and explaining general ideas. Advice stays with a qualified person.

## Companies House identity verification for clients: a tracker for UK practices
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/companies-house-identity-verification-client-tracker/ (2026-11-10)

Companies House identity verification for clients is not one deadline: each director must give their personal code in the company's next confirmation statement, and each PSC has their own 14-day window. A practice should track every director and PSC by company, with their personal code, due date and the date it was given to Companies House. If your firm is registered as an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP), it can also verify clients itself and must keep records of those checks for 7 years.

Companies House identity verification for clients has been a legal requirement since 18 November 2025, and every director and person with significant control (PSC) on your client list needs a Companies House personal code. For a [small practice](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/accountants/) the hard part isn't the check. It's knowing, for each client company, who is verified, who isn't, and when each person is due.
This post sets out the rules as GOV.UK states them (checked on 10 November 2026), explains why you'll see both 17 and 18 November 2026 quoted, and gives you a tracker layout and a client email you can copy.

### 17 or 18 November 2026? What GOV.UK actually says
Companies House's own page "Verify your identity for Companies House" says that 18 November 2025 is not a deadline: it marks the start of a 12-month transition period for directors and PSCs of existing companies to verify by their own due dates. Counted from 18 November 2025, twelve months takes you to 17 November 2026. That's why some articles quote 17 November and others quote 18 November as the end. The GOV.UK guidance pages we checked on 10 November 2026 don't name a single cut-off day for everyone.
What GOV.UK does set out is a due date per person. Existing directors give their personal code in the company's next confirmation statement filed from 18 November 2025. PSCs have a 14-day period that depends on their situation (see the table below). Companies House's transition plan, updated in October 2026, says that by no earlier than the end of 2026 it expects to complete the transition period and start compliance activity against people who haven't verified.
So for your client list, the useful question isn't "what's the deadline?" but "when is each person due, and have they done it?" Any director or PSC who missed their own date is already late, whatever the end of the transition period turns out to be.

### Who needs to verify, and when each one is due
GOV.UK lists directors (and equivalents, such as LLP members), PSCs and ACSPs as the people who must verify now. Verification for people who file at Companies House, corporate directors and limited partnerships comes later. A person verifies once and uses the same 11-character personal code for every role they hold.
Person | When they must give their personal code | How
--- | --- | ---
Existing director | In the company's next confirmation statement | Code entered in the confirmation statement. The company can't file it unless every director is verified
New director (appointed from 18 Nov 2025) | At appointment or incorporation | In the appointment or incorporation filing
PSC who is also a director of the same company | 14 days starting the day after the company's confirmation statement date | 'Provide identity verification details for a PSC' service, separately from the director filing
PSC who is not a director | The first 14 days of their birth month | Same PSC service
PSC added after 18 Nov 2025 | When added to the register, or within 14 days | Same PSC service

### Rules practices often miss
- A director who is also a PSC gives the code twice: once in the confirmation statement as director, and again through the PSC service. The Companies House blog (16 January 2026) says this applies even if the code was already given as director.
- Filing a confirmation statement early does not move a PSC's 14-day period.
- A PSC can request a 14-day extension through the same service, but only before their deadline has passed.
- The date of birth Companies House holds must match the verified identity. If it's wrong on the register, the code won't connect until it's corrected.
- Clients may share their personal code with an agent who files for them, such as their accountant. Companies House says to keep it as safe as a UTR.
- If a director or PSC isn't verified on time, Companies House says they may be committing an offence, and its published approach includes a default letter, financial penalties, referral to the Insolvency Service and prosecution.
- The separate requirement for people who file on behalf of companies (presenters) has moved to no earlier than November 2027, with at least 6 months' notice, according to the transition plan updated in August 2026.

### If your firm is an ACSP: what you must track
To verify clients' identities for Companies House, a firm must be registered as an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (also called a Companies House authorised agent), and it must be supervised by a UK anti-money laundering body. Right now only agents who want to verify clients need to register. GOV.UK says all agents who file for clients will need to register in the future.
When your firm verifies someone, you tell Companies House through the "Tell Companies House you have verified someone's identity" service. You give the person's name, date of birth, home address and email address (Companies House emails the personal code there), how the documents were checked, which documents you used with their reference numbers, expiry dates and countries of issue, and the date of the check. GOV.UK points out that the Companies House identity verification standard is different from your [AML customer due diligence](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/), so passing one doesn't mean you've met the other.
You must keep records of every check, including copies of the documents, for 7 years from the date of the check. You must also tell Companies House about changes to your firm's details within 14 days.

### A client tracker you can copy
One row per person per company, not per client. A director of three companies appears three times, with the same personal code. Sort by due date and the list tells you who to chase this week.
Column | What goes in it
--- | ---
Company name and number | As shown on the register
Person and role | Director, PSC, or both (both = two rows)
Confirmation statement date | From the register; drives director and director-PSC due dates
Birth month | Only needed for PSCs who aren't directors
Due date | Worked out from the rules above
How verifying | GOV.UK One Login, or by your firm as ACSP
Personal code received | Yes/no and date. Store the code itself somewhere access-controlled, not in a shared spreadsheet
Code given to Companies House | Date and filing (confirmation statement or PSC service)
Date of birth checked | Matches the register: yes/no
Next action and owner | Who in the practice does what, by when

### A client email asking for their personal code
Email to a client director or PSC:
```
Subject: Companies House identity check for [Company name]: action needed by [due date]

Hi [First name],

Companies House now requires every director and person with significant control to verify their identity. Our records show that you still need to do this for [Company name] as [director / PSC / director and PSC].

What you need to do:
1. Verify your identity, either free online at GOV.UK (search "Verify your identity for Companies House") or with us, as we can verify clients for Companies House. If you'd like us to do it, reply and we'll send you a secure link for your documents.
2. Once verified, you'll receive an 11-character Companies House personal code by email.
3. Send us the code by replying to this email, or tell us you've provided it yourself.

Your due date is [date]. [If PSC: As a PSC, the code must be given to Companies House between [start] and [end].]

If you've already verified, just send us your personal code and we'll take it from there. If anything on your Companies House record is wrong, such as your date of birth, tell us now, because the code won't connect until it's fixed.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Practice name]
```

### What to automate, and what stays with a person
The judgement stays with your team: checking documents to the Companies House standard, deciding if the firm takes on a verification, and submitting anything to Companies House. A workflow should never verify anyone or file on its own.
1. Pull the confirmation statement date and officer list for each client company into the tracker, and work out each person's due date.
2. Six weeks before a due date, send the client email above with the person's details filled in.
3. Remind on a fixed schedule until the code arrives, then stop. Every reminder names the date.
4. When a code arrives, file it to the access-controlled store and flag the row for a person to submit it.
5. Every morning, one list for the team: due in the next 30 days, overdue, and date-of-birth problems.

It's built on the tools you already use (your email, a spreadsheet or your practice software, and your secure storage), so the team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. ### Is the Companies House identity verification deadline 17 or 18 November 2026?
GOV.UK describes a 12-month transition period that started on 18 November 2025, which is why both 17 and 18 November 2026 are quoted. In practice each director is due at their company's next confirmation statement, and each PSC within their own 14-day period, so check each person's own date.

### Can my accountant verify my identity for Companies House?
Yes, if the firm is registered as an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP). Otherwise you can verify free online with GOV.UK One Login and then share your personal code with your accountant.

### Does a director who is also a PSC need to verify twice?
No. They verify once and get one personal code. But they must give that code to Companies House twice: in the confirmation statement as director, and through the PSC service as a PSC.

### Can a workflow submit codes to Companies House for us?
We'd build it to collect, remind and prepare. A person in your practice checks and submits each filing.

## Self Assessment records checklist for clients, by client type
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/self-assessment-records-checklist-for-clients/ (2026-11-10)

A Self Assessment records checklist for clients lists what each client must send for their return, based on their sources of income: P60s and P11Ds for employment, sales and expense records for sole traders, rent and mortgage interest statements for landlords, monthly CIS statements for subcontractors, and sale and purchase documents for capital gains. For the 2025 to 2026 tax year, HMRC must receive online returns and payment by 31 January 2027.

A Self Assessment records checklist for clients works best when it isn't one long list. A landlord doesn't need to read about CIS statements, and an employee with a small side business doesn't need a paragraph on mortgage interest. Each client should see only the parts that apply to them.
Below is a checklist split by client type, ready to paste into your request email. Each table has a column for the items clients tend to miss, so you can name them up front instead of [chasing them in January](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/self-assessment-document-chasing/). The facts come from GOV.UK guidance checked in November 2026, for returns covering the 2025 to 2026 tax year (6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026).

### Every client: the basics to confirm first
Start every request with the same short block. It catches changes that alter the rest of the list, such as a new rental property, a new job or a sale of shares.
Record or question | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
Any change this year: new job, new income, property bought or sold, moved abroad, stopped trading | The client | Clients assume you already know
Bank and building society interest | Annual statements or the bank's online account | Small amounts feel too minor to mention
Dividends from UK companies and investment platforms | Dividend vouchers, platform tax packs | Tax packs arrive weeks after the year ends
Personal pension contributions | Pension provider's annual statement | Extra relief above 20% is claimed on the return
Gift Aid donations | Charity receipts or the client's own list | Nobody keeps the receipts
Child Benefit received, and both partners' income | Child Benefit letters, partner's P60 | The charge depends on the partner's income too
Student loan plan type | Student Loans Company account | Clients don't know their plan number

### Employees with other income
GOV.UK tells employees to keep their P60 (given by every employer they work for on 5 April, by 31 May), any P45 if they left a job, and their P11D for benefits such as a company car or health insurance. Employers must give employees a copy of their expenses and benefits information by 6 July. The High Income Child Benefit Charge applies where either partner's adjusted net income is over £60,000, from the 2024 to 2025 tax year onwards, so ask the question even when the client is mainly an employee.
Record | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
P60 for each job held on 5 April | Employer, or HMRC personal tax account | Second jobs and old employers get forgotten
P45 for any job left during the year | Former employer | Filed away months ago
P11D or details of benefits in kind | Employer | Some benefits are payrolled, so there's no P11D
Work expenses not paid back by the employer (tools, travel, uniform) | Client's receipts | Small and scattered
Side income: tips, commission, online selling, freelance work | Platform statements, invoices, bank statements | Clients think it's too small to count
Employee share scheme documents | Scheme administrator | Option exercises and sales happen at odd times

### Sole traders
GOV.UK says sole traders must keep records of all sales and income, all business expenses, VAT records if registered, and PAYE records if they employ people. Proof includes receipts, bank statements, and sales invoices or till rolls. From the 2024 to 2025 tax year, cash basis is the default, so most clients only need to record money when it actually comes in or goes out. A sole trader must send a return if they earned more than £1,000 from self-employment before expenses.
Record | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
All sales and income, including cash and card takings | Invoices, till reports, card machine and platform reports | Cash jobs and platform payouts
Business bank statements for the full year | Bank | Statements stop at a month that isn't 5 April
Expense receipts and bills | Client's records or bookkeeping software | Receipts kept in a van or a coat pocket
Business mileage or vehicle costs | Mileage log, fuel and repair bills | No log kept until year end
Use of home: share of bills, hours worked at home | Household bills | Clients don't know it can be claimed
Money taken out for personal use, money put in | Bank statements | Only needed if not using cash basis
Self-Employment Income Support Scheme grants, if any | HMRC records | Older years only, but still asked

### Landlords
GOV.UK lists what landlords should keep: the dates the property was let, all rent received, income from services to tenants, rent books, receipts, invoices and bank statements, and allowable expenses such as letting agent fees, cleaning or gardening. Mortgage interest isn't deducted from rent for residential lets. Instead it gives a tax reduction at the basic rate (currently 20%), so you need the lender's annual interest figure, not the total repayments. The first £1,000 of property income is tax-free under the property allowance.
Record | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
Rent received for each property, with dates let | Letting agent statements or bank statements | Self-managed lets have no statement
Letting agent annual statement | Letting agent | Covers a different year end
Mortgage interest statement (interest only, not capital) | Lender | Clients send the repayment total
Repairs, insurance, ground rent, service charges, safety certificates | Invoices and bills | Paid personally, not through the agent
Ownership share for jointly owned property | Client, or the deeds | Assumed to be 50/50
Property bought, sold or remortgaged during the year | Completion statements | Treated as a separate matter

### CIS subcontractors
Under the Construction Industry Scheme, the contractor deducts tax from payments (20% if registered and verified, 30% if not). GOV.UK says the contractor must give a payment and deduction statement within 14 days of the end of each tax month. The return records total pay before deductions as income, and the total deductions as CIS deductions. If statements are missing, the client asks the contractor for a replacement.
Record | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
All 12 monthly payment and deduction statements, from every contractor | Each contractor | One contractor's statements go missing
Invoices to contractors | Client's records | Raised by text or not at all
Materials bought directly | Supplier receipts | Lost on site
Tools, van, fuel, phone and other expenses | Receipts and bank statements | Mixed with personal spending
Any non-CIS work for private customers | Invoices, bank statements | Clients only think about the CIS work

### Pensions, savings, capital gains and other income
Pensioners need their pension provider's P60 and their State Pension figure. For gains, GOV.UK says you can deduct the costs of buying, selling and improving a property (agents' and solicitors' fees, an extension) but not normal maintenance. Where there is tax to pay on a UK residential property sale, it must be reported and paid within 60 days of completion, so ask whether the client has already done this and get the reference. Overseas income needs payslips or statements and proof of any foreign tax paid.
Record | Where the client gets it | Why it gets missed
--- | --- | ---
Pension P60s and State Pension amount | Pension provider; the client for the State Pension amount | Not on a private pension P60
Shares or funds sold: dates, proceeds, original cost | Platform capital gains report | Original cost from years ago
Property sold: purchase and sale completion statements, improvement costs | Solicitor, client's records | The 60-day report was filed separately
Overseas income and foreign tax paid | Foreign payslips, statements, tax certificates | Clients think foreign tax settles it
Income from a trust or estate | Trustees | Arrives late in the year

### A request email you can send to clients
Paste only the sections that apply to each client, and keep the questions at the top. A client can answer three yes-or-no questions on a phone in a minute, which tells you what else to ask for. For the reminders that follow, use the sequence in our [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) rather than writing new ones each time.
Subject: Your 2025 to 2026 tax return: what we need from you:
```
Hi [first name],

It's time to prepare your Self Assessment return for 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. HMRC's deadline is 31 January 2027. To give you time to check it and plan the payment, please send everything by [your cut-off date].

First, three quick questions. Just reply yes or no:
1. Did anything change this year (new job, new income, a property or shares bought or sold, a move abroad)?
2. Did you or your partner receive Child Benefit?
3. Did you pay into a personal pension or give to charity with Gift Aid?

Based on last year, this is what we need:
- [P60 from each employer]
- [Letting agent statement for 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026]
- [Mortgage interest statement from your lender: the interest figure only]
- [All 12 CIS statements from each contractor]
- [Business bank statements for the full year]

People often forget [the item this client missed last year], so it's worth finding first.

You can upload everything here, from your phone or computer: [upload link]

If something on the list doesn't apply this year, reply and tell me. That's just as useful as the document.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### Check MTD for Income Tax while the records are in front of you
The 2025 to 2026 return matters for more than this year's bill. GOV.UK says sole traders and landlords whose qualifying income (self-employment and property income combined, before expenses) is over £30,000 for 2025 to 2026 will need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2027. Clients over £50,000 for 2024 to 2025 should already have started from 6 April 2026, and they still send a normal Self Assessment return for 2025 to 2026.
So ask for gross sales and gross rent as clear figures, not just the profit. Then add a column to your client list for MTD status. Our post on the [Making Tax Digital practice workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/making-tax-digital-income-tax-practice-workflow/) covers what to do next.

### How Mike Automations would build this
The checklist is the easy part. The hard part is sending the right version to every client, ticking items off as they arrive, and knowing who still owes what. A workflow can build each client's list from last year's file and your notes, send the request in the wording you approved, file uploads into the right folder, and send reminders that list only what's still missing.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you request records today.
