### What records does my accountant need for my Self Assessment return?
It depends on your income. Employees need P60s, P45s and P11Ds. Sole traders need sales, expense and bank records. Landlords need rent, expense and mortgage interest statements. CIS subcontractors need every monthly payment and deduction statement. Everyone should mention interest, dividends, pension contributions, Gift Aid and Child Benefit.

### How long should clients keep their records?
GOV.UK says at least 22 months after the end of the tax year for most people who file on time, and at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline for the self-employed.

### What if a client has lost a document?
Ask them to request a copy first (from the bank, employer, contractor or lender). GOV.UK allows provisional or estimated figures when records can't be recreated, but the return must say so, and interest and penalties can apply if the figures turn out wrong.

## When to start chasing Self Assessment clients: a dated timeline
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/when-to-start-chasing-self-assessment-clients/ (2026-11-10)

Start chasing Self Assessment clients in the summer: send the first records request in June or July, once employers have issued P60s (due by 31 May) and P11D information (due by 6 July). Set a records cut-off in the autumn, well before Christmas, so you have time to prepare, review and file before HMRC's 31 January online filing and payment deadline. For the 2025 to 2026 tax year, that deadline is 31 January 2027.

When to start [chasing Self Assessment clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/self-assessment-document-chasing/) is really a question about your capacity, not HMRC's calendar. The online deadline is 31 January, but your deadline is the last date you can receive records and still prepare, review, get approval and file without the whole team working through the holidays.
This post gives a month-by-month timeline from the end of the tax year to 31 January, what to send at each point, how to set a records cut-off from your own numbers, and what to do with records that arrive after 1 January. The HMRC dates are from GOV.UK, checked in November 2026, for returns covering 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026.

### The HMRC dates you are working back from
GOV.UK sets these dates for the 2025 to 2026 tax year. Everything else in your plan should sit in front of them, with room to spare.
Date | What HMRC says | What it means for you
--- | --- | ---
6 April 2026 | Returns can be sent any time from 6 April | You can start as soon as records arrive
31 May 2026 | Employers must give a P60 to employees working for them on 5 April | Employed clients have their main document
6 July 2026 | Employers must give employees a copy of their expenses and benefits information | P11D clients have everything from their employer
31 July 2026 | Second payment on account for 2025 to 2026 | A natural moment to ask for records
5 October 2026 | Tell HMRC if you need to file and have not filed before | New clients must be registered
31 October 2026 | Paper returns must reach HMRC | Only relevant for clients who file on paper
30 December 2026 | Online deadline to pay through the tax code, where the client qualifies | An earlier target for clients who want this
31 January 2027 | Online return, balancing payment and first payment on account for 2026 to 2027 | The hard deadline

### Month by month: what to send and when
This is a suggested plan, not an HMRC rule. Move the dates to suit your practice, but keep the order: request early, remind on a rhythm, set a cut-off, and save January for review and filing.
When | What to send | Who it's for
--- | --- | ---
Late April to May | A short heads-up: the tax year has ended, here's what we'll need, here's your upload link | All Self Assessment clients
June to early July | The full records request with each client's own list (once P60s and P11Ds are out) | All clients
Late July | A reminder alongside the payment on account note, listing only what's still missing | Clients who haven't sent everything
September | Reminder with your records cut-off date in the first line | Partial and silent clients
Early October | Registration check for anyone new to Self Assessment (5 October) | New clients and new income sources
Your cut-off (for example 31 October or 30 November) | Final reminder: after this date, a later filing slot and any late-records fee apply | Everyone not yet complete
December | Draft returns out for approval; tax-code payment target (30 December) for clients who qualify | Complete clients
1 to 15 January | Phone calls, not emails, to anyone still missing records | The last stragglers
16 to 31 January | Approvals, filing and payment reminders only | Clients with returns ready

### How to set your records cut-off from your own numbers
A cut-off that isn't based on capacity is just a hope. Work it out backwards from 31 January in four steps.
1. Count your Self Assessment returns, and split them into simple and complex (several income sources, gains, overseas income).
2. Estimate how many returns your team can prepare and review in a normal week, then halve it for the weeks around Christmas.
3. Leave at least two weeks at the end of January for client approval, filing and payment questions.
4. Count back from that point by the number of weeks of preparation you need. The date you land on is the latest your final records can arrive. Set your published cut-off a few weeks earlier, so late clients still land before it.

### For illustration: working out one practice's cut-off
For illustration: a two-person practice has 150 Self Assessment returns. Together they can prepare and review about 25 a week, or about 12 a week over the Christmas fortnight. They keep the last two weeks of January for approvals, so preparation must finish by mid-January.
If every client sent records on the same day, they would need about seven weeks of preparation, which means all records in by late November. In practice records arrive spread out from the summer, so most returns are done before the autumn. They publish a cut-off of 31 October and expect the final batch to arrive by the end of November. Anything later goes into a January slot with the late-records fee in their [engagement letter](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/records-cut-off-clause-engagement-letter/).

### What to do with records that arrive after 1 January
Late records will happen. Decide in advance how you handle them, so nobody makes it up under pressure.
- Triage by size: [a client missing one small figure](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/) goes ahead now; a client missing a whole income source waits for it.
- Say clearly, in writing, what you can and can't promise for 31 January.
- GOV.UK allows provisional figures when a figure genuinely isn't known by the deadline (for example while waiting for a valuation). The return must say so, it must be amended later, and interest runs on any extra tax from the original due date.
- Make sure the client knows the payment is due on 31 January even if the return is late.
- Apply any late-records fee only if your engagement letter sets it out.

### What a missed 31 January costs your client
Put the real cost in your reminders. It does more than "please send soon". For 2025 to 2026 returns, GOV.UK lists these late filing penalties: £100 straight away, then £10 a day after 3 months (up to £900), then 5% of the tax due or £300 (whichever is greater) after 6 months, and the same again after 12 months. Late payment brings penalties of 5% of the tax unpaid at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months, plus interest.
Clients who joined Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2026 have new penalty rules from that tax year onwards, but GOV.UK confirms the current penalties still apply to their 2025 to 2026 return due on 31 January 2027. Those clients also have a quarterly update due by 7 February 2027, a week after the return, so ask for their records early.

### Already November? A catch-up plan
If you're reading this in November and haven't sent requests, you can still get most of the season back. This week, send every client who hasn't sent records their own list, with a cut-off at the end of November and one upload link. Use our [Self Assessment records checklist for clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/self-assessment-records-checklist-for-clients/) to build each list. Then remind every 7 to 10 days with only what's still missing, and move to phone calls from 2 January.

### How Mike Automations would build this
A timeline only works if every message goes out on the right date to the right clients, and stops when they're complete. That's hard to do by hand for 150 people. A workflow can send each request and reminder on your dates, list only what each client still owes, file what arrives, and give you a morning list of who's complete, partial or silent.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about your season. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your email, your shared drive or practice software where it allows a connection, and your client list), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. Every message uses wording you approved.

### When should an accountant start chasing Self Assessment records?
Send the first full request in June or July, once employers have issued P60s (by 31 May) and P11D information (by 6 July). Remind on a steady rhythm through the autumn, and set a records cut-off well before Christmas.

### What's a sensible records cut-off date?
Work it out from your capacity: count returns, divide by what your team can prepare each week, leave two weeks at the end of January for approvals, and count back. Run those numbers before you publish a date.

### Is mid-December too late to start chasing?
For most practices, yes. December has fewer working days, clients are busy, and anything that arrives after Christmas competes with every other late file. Start in the summer, and use December for review and approvals.

## W-9 request email template: first request, reminder and policy line
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/w9-request-email-template/ (2026-11-10)

A good W-9 request email template asks for the form before the first payment, explains in one line why you need it, and gives one secure way to send it back. Follow up after a week, and put a "no W-9, no payment" line in your vendor terms, because under IRS rules a payer may have to withhold 24% from reportable payments to a vendor who hasn't given a taxpayer ID.

This W-9 request email template comes in three parts: the first request, a reminder, and a policy line that makes the W-9 a condition of getting paid. Copy them, change the parts in [brackets], and send them before the first payment, not in January.
If you're a [bookkeeper or CPA](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeepers/), you can send these on your client's behalf, or hand them to the person at the client who sets up vendors. Either way, the goal is the same: a signed W-9 on file for every vendor before [1099 season](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/1099-season-checklist-bookkeepers/) starts.

### When to request a W-9
The best moment is before the first payment, when the vendor still wants something from you. The IRS backup withholding page says that when someone begins to receive payments reportable on Form 1099, they must give the payer their taxpayer identification number (TIN) in writing and certify that it's correct, and that the payer may give them Form W-9 to do it. After the job is paid, a W-9 request is just one more email to ignore.
- New contractors and freelancers: at onboarding, before the first invoice is paid. General contractors can collect it alongside each sub's [certificate of insurance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/subcontractor-coi-tracking/).
- Attorneys and law firms: ask even if they are incorporated. The IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC list attorneys' fees among the payments to corporations that must generally be reported on Form 1099-NEC.
- Landlords and other payees who may get a Form 1099-MISC, for example for rent.
- Corporations you pay for services: ask anyway. Most payments to corporations don't need a 1099-NEC, and a W-9 with the tax classification ticked is your record of why you didn't file one.
- Existing vendors whose name, business type or address has changed: ask for a new W-9 so the 1099 matches.
- Once a year, in November: a sweep of every vendor paid this year who still has no W-9 on file.

### What the IRS says about Form W-9 and backup withholding
This is a summary for practice workflow, not tax advice for a specific vendor. Check the current IRS instructions for anything unusual, such as foreign payees or exempt payee codes.
- The current Form W-9 is the March 2024 revision (Rev. March 2024), per the IRS "About Form W-9" page. The form itself says: "Give form to the requester. Do not send to the IRS." You keep it on file.
- Form W-9 is for U.S. persons (including resident aliens). Foreign vendors use a Form W-8 instead, so don't send them this template.
- Backup withholding is 24%. The IRS Instructions for the Requester of Form W-9 (03/2024) say that if a payee fails to give a TIN, the payer must withhold 24% of reportable payments and deposit it with the IRS until the problem is fixed.
- For payments like nonemployee compensation there is no grace period: the same instructions say backup withholding applies immediately, even if the payee has applied for a TIN and is waiting for it.
- If a payer doesn't withhold when required, the payer may become liable for the uncollected amount.
- The 1099-NEC threshold changed. The IRS Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC (12/2026) say that for tax years beginning after 2025 the minimum reporting threshold for certain payments rose to $2,000, and may be adjusted for inflation from 2027. Box 1a of Form 1099-NEC now asks for nonemployee compensation of $2,000 or more. Before 2026 it was $600.
- Electronic W-9s are allowed. The requester instructions let you set up a system for vendors to submit W-9s electronically, as long as it meets the IRS conditions, including an electronic signature under penalties of perjury as the final entry.

### Email 1: the first W-9 request
Send this when you set up the vendor, or the day their first invoice arrives. Keep it short, say why you need the form, and give one way to return it.
Subject: W-9 needed before we pay [invoice number]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for working with [client business name]. Before we can pay your first invoice, we need a completed and signed Form W-9 for our records. We use it to report payments to the IRS at year end, as the rules require.

It takes about five minutes. You can fill it in and sign it here: [secure link]

Please don't send your Social Security number or EIN by regular email. Use the link above, or call me on [phone] if you'd rather do it another way.

If your business is a corporation, please still send the form and tick the corporation box. It tells us whether a 1099 is needed.

Thanks,
[your name]
[business name]
```

### Email 2: the reminder (5 to 7 days later)
Most vendors aren't refusing, they just didn't get to it. Reply in the same thread so the first message is right there, and mention the payment, because that's what they care about.
Subject: Re: W-9 needed before we pay [invoice number]:
```
Hi [first name],

A quick reminder that we still need your signed W-9 before we can release payment for [invoice number], [amount].

Same secure link as before: [secure link]

If you've already sent it, thank you, and please reply to let me know how you sent it, so I can find it.

[your name]
```

### Email 3: the "no W-9, no payment" policy line
The easiest W-9 to collect is the one that's required before anyone gets paid. Put this line in your vendor onboarding email, your purchase order terms or your contractor agreement, so it's agreed before the work starts. The client (or their attorney) should approve the exact wording, because it's their policy.
Policy line for vendor terms or onboarding emails:
```
Payment terms: We need a completed and signed IRS Form W-9 (or, for foreign vendors, the correct Form W-8) before we make any payment. Invoices received without one will be paid once the form arrives. If we are required to pay without a valid taxpayer identification number, IRS rules may require us to withhold 24% of the payment (backup withholding) and send it to the IRS.
```

### A simple W-9 tracker
Three emails only work if someone knows who's still missing. One row per vendor, per client, is enough. A shared spreadsheet works for a handful of clients; a workflow can fill it in for you as forms arrive. The rows below are for illustration.
Vendor | Type (from W-9) | Requested | Reminder sent | W-9 received | Paid this year | 1099 needed?
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
J. Smith Design | Individual / sole proprietor | Mar 3 | Mar 10 | Mar 12 | $4,800 | Yes, 1099-NEC
Acme Cleaning Inc. | C corporation | Apr 2 | No | Apr 2 | $6,200 | Usually no
Lee and Park LLP | Partnership (law firm) | May 15 | May 22 | Not yet | $3,000 | Yes, attorneys' fees

### Tips that make W-9 requests work
- Never ask for an SSN or EIN in a plain email reply, and avoid photos of filled-in W-9s sent by text. Give one secure upload link or e-signature form and use it every time.
- Ask before the first payment. A vendor who is waiting to be paid answers in a day. A vendor who was paid in June may never answer in January.
- Check the name and TIN before filing. The IRS General Instructions for Certain Information Returns describe TIN Matching, an IRS e-service that lets payers check name and TIN combinations before they file Forms 1099.
- Keep W-9s with the vendor record, not in someone's inbox, so the bookkeeper and the client can both find them.
- Stop reminders the moment the form arrives, and send a one-line thank-you. A reminder after the vendor has already replied makes you look disorganized.
- Run a November sweep for vendors paid this year with no W-9. Our 1099 season checklist covers the rest of the January run-up.

### How Mike Automations would set this up
The W-9 chase is a good first workflow for a bookkeeping practice. When a new vendor is added in QuickBooks or Xero, the vendor gets Email 1 with a secure form link. If nothing comes back in a week, the reminder goes out. The signed W-9 is saved to the vendor's folder in Google Drive or Dropbox, and your tracker updates itself. You approve the wording once, and you still decide who needs a 1099.

It's built on the tools you already use, it's live in 2-3 days, and it costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid once it's running and you're happy with it.

### When should I send a W-9 request?
Before the first payment, ideally when the vendor is set up. The IRS says a person who begins to receive payments reportable on Form 1099 must give the payer their TIN in writing, and a vendor who is waiting to be paid is far more likely to send it.

### Do I send the completed W-9 to the IRS?
No. Form W-9 (Rev. March 2024) says "Give form to the requester. Do not send to the IRS." Keep it on file and use it to prepare any Form 1099.

### What happens if a contractor won't give me a W-9?
The IRS requester instructions say that if a payee fails to give a TIN, the payer must withhold 24% of reportable payments (backup withholding) and deposit it with the IRS. That's why many businesses make a signed W-9 a condition of payment.

### Do corporations need to fill out a W-9?
It's good practice to ask. Most payments to corporations don't need a 1099-NEC, but attorneys' fees do, and the W-9 records the vendor's tax classification so you know which applies.

## Tax season client email schedule: a week-by-week calendar for 2027
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-season-client-email-calendar/ (2026-11-10)

A tax season client email schedule plans every client email from December to the April 15 deadline: a kickoff note, the organizer and document list, reminders tied to IRS dates, a cut-off date, and an extension notice. For the 2027 season (2026 tax year), the IRS dates to build around are January 15 (last 2026 estimated payment), February 1 (W-2s and 1099-NECs), March 15 (partnership and S corporation returns), April 15 (Form 1040) and October 15 (extended 1040s).

A tax season client email schedule decides in December what every client hears from you, and when, until April 15. Write it once, and the season stops being a series of emails you remember to send at 10 PM.
Below is a week-by-week calendar for the 2027 filing season (2026 tax returns), a note on splitting it by client type, and five short templates. The dates come from the IRS. The internal deadlines are suggestions you should set for your own practice.

### The IRS dates this calendar is built on
These dates are from the IRS early-release draft of Publication 509 (2027), Tax Calendars, checked on November 10, 2026. Pub. 509 already adjusts for weekends and legal holidays. It's still a draft, and the IRS says drafts can change before the final release, so check the final version when it's out, along with any disaster-relief postponements for your clients' area. State deadlines are separate and not covered here.
Date (2027) | What's due | Who it affects
--- | --- | ---
Friday, January 15 | Final 2026 estimated tax payment (Form 1040-ES) | Self-employed and other clients who pay estimates
Monday, February 1 | W-2s to employees; 1099-NEC filed and given to recipients; most other 1099s given to recipients (January 31 falls on a Sunday) | Employers, businesses that pay contractors, and every client waiting for forms
Tuesday, February 16 | Forms 1099-B and 1099-S, and certain 1099-MISC boxes, due to recipients | Clients with brokerage accounts or property sales
Monday, March 15 | Partnership (Form 1065) and S corporation (Form 1120-S) returns and K-1s; Form 7004 for a 6-month extension | Business entity clients, and individuals waiting for K-1s
Thursday, April 15 | Form 1040 and payment of tax due; Form 4868 for a 6-month extension; first 2027 estimated payment; calendar-year C corporations (Form 1120) | Almost everyone
Wednesday, September 15 | Extended partnership and S corporation returns | Business clients on extension
Friday, October 15 | Extended Form 1040 | Individual extension clients

### The week-by-week client email calendar
Each row is one email, or one batch of emails, sent on the Monday of that week. Most clients get only the rows that apply to them. The internal cut-off of Friday, March 19 is an example: pick the date that gives your team enough time.
Week of | Email | Send to
--- | --- | ---
Nov 30, 2026 | Season kickoff: how this year will work, key dates, your internal cut-off date | All clients
Dec 7 | W-9 sweep: vendors paid in 2026 with no W-9 on file | Business clients who pay contractors
Dec 14 | Engagement letter and this season's fee, to sign before work starts | All clients
Dec 21 | No email. Holiday week. | Nobody
Jan 4, 2027 | Organizer and personal document list, with the upload link | Individual clients
Jan 11 | Reminder: last 2026 estimated payment is due Friday, January 15 | Clients who pay estimates
Jan 18 | Final 1099 vendor list and totals to confirm; payroll year-end check | Business clients
Jan 25 | "Forms are on their way": what to expect in the mail and online by February 1 | Individual clients
Feb 8 | First reminder: only the items still missing | Clients with gaps
Feb 15 | Business records reminder: March 15 is four weeks away | Partnership and S corporation clients
Feb 22 | Second reminder; ask K-1 clients when they expect their K-1s | Clients with gaps; K-1 recipients
Mar 1 | Extension decision for business returns (Form 7004) if records aren't in | Partnership and S corporation clients still missing records
Mar 8 | Cut-off notice: send everything by Friday, March 19, or we file an extension | Individuals still missing items
Mar 15 | Last call before the cut-off; K-1s issued today should come to us | Individuals still missing items
Mar 22 | Extension notice: we're filing Form 4868; how much to pay by April 15 | Everyone who missed the cut-off
Apr 5 | Payment instructions and the first 2027 estimated payment | Clients with tax due or estimates
Apr 12 | Final reminder: April 15 is Thursday; sign your e-file authorization | Clients with returns ready to sign
Apr 19 | Thank-you and what happens next; extension clients get their new plan | All clients

### After April 15: the extension track
An extension gives more time to file, not more time to pay. The IRS "When to file" page says you should pay any tax owed by the original due date to avoid possible penalties, and its extension page says Form 4868 gives until October 15 to file. Extension clients need their own short schedule, or they go quiet until October.
Week of | Email | Send to
--- | --- | ---
May 3 | Your extension plan: what's still missing, and a new internal date | Individual extension clients
Aug 2 | Business extension reminder: September 15 is six weeks away | Partnership and S corporation clients on extension
Aug 30 | Individual extension reminder: October 15 is six weeks away | Individual extension clients
Sep 27 | Last call: we need everything this week to file by Friday, October 15 | Individual extension clients still missing items

### Split the schedule by client type
One email to everyone is easier to send and easier to ignore. Four groups cover most practices:
- W-2 only individuals: the kickoff, [the organizer](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-organizer-questions-new-vs-returning-clients/), two reminders and the cut-off. They need few emails, and short ones.
- Self-employed clients and landlords: add the January 15 estimated payment reminder, the first 2027 estimate in April, and an earlier request for their bookkeeping or income and expense summary.
- Partnerships and S corporations: their deadline is March 15, so their reminders run about a month ahead of everyone else. Their owners are often your individual clients too, waiting on the same K-1s.
- [Last year's extension clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/extension-clients-still-havent-sent-anything/): start them earlier, not later. If they were late last April, a personal note in December beats a fourth reminder in March.

### Templates for the key emails
Five short emails carry most of the season. For general reminders about missing items, use our [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/). Change the parts in [brackets].

### Template: season kickoff (week of November 30)
Subject: Your 2026 tax return: how this season will work:
```
Hi [first name],

Tax season is coming, so here's how we'll handle your 2026 return.

- Early January: we'll send your organizer and a list of the documents we need from you.
- Most tax forms (W-2s, 1099s) should reach you by February 1.
- Please send everything by [internal cut-off date]. After that, we'll file an extension for you.
- The federal filing deadline is Thursday, April 15, 2027.

Everything goes through one upload link, which we'll send with your list: [upload link]

Questions before then? Just reply.

[your name]
```

### Template: organizer and document list (week of January 4)
Subject: Your 2026 documents list (about 15 minutes):
```
Hi [first name],

Here's what we need for your 2026 return, based on last year's file:

- [document 1]
- [document 2]
- [document 3]

Upload here as each one arrives: [upload link]
Your organizer: [organizer link]

If something on the list doesn't apply this year, or something new happened (a new job, a home sale, a new business), reply and tell us.

Our cut-off date is [internal cut-off date].

[your name]
```

### Template: estimated payment reminder (week of January 11)
Subject: Reminder: 2026 estimated tax payment due Friday, January 15:
```
Hi [first name],

A quick reminder that your last 2026 estimated tax payment is due Friday, January 15.

Based on what we have, the amount is [amount]. You can pay online at IRS.gov/payments.

If your income changed a lot in the last quarter, reply before you pay and we'll check the figure.

[your name]
```

### Template: cut-off notice (week of March 8)
Subject: We need your remaining documents by [cut-off date]:
```
Hi [first name],

To file your return by April 15, we need the items below by [cut-off date]:

- [missing item 1]
- [missing item 2]

Upload link: [upload link]

If we don't have them by then, we'll file an extension (Form 4868) for you. That gives you until October 15 to file, but any tax you owe is still due on April 15, so we'd send you an estimate to pay.

[your name]
```

### Template: extension notice (week of March 22)
Subject: We're filing an extension for your 2026 return:
```
Hi [first name],

We don't have everything we need yet, so we're filing an extension for you. Your new filing deadline is Friday, October 15, 2027.

An extension doesn't move the payment date. Based on what we know, please pay about [estimated amount] by Thursday, April 15. Payment instructions: [link or attached]

Still missing:
- [missing item]

Send it any time here: [upload link]. Once it's in, we'll finish your return without waiting for October.

[your name]
```

### What to watch before you schedule anything
- Pub. 509 (2027) is a draft today. Re-check the dates when the final version is published.
- We couldn't confirm the date the IRS starts accepting 2026 returns when this was written. Check the IRS newsroom in January, and don't promise clients a filing date before it's announced.
- The IRS can postpone deadlines for areas hit by a declared disaster. The "When to file" page mentions this. Check before sending a deadline email to clients in an affected area.
- State returns have their own dates. Add them as separate rows if you file in several states.
- Every reminder should list only what's still missing, and stop the moment a client is complete.

This calendar is a good fit for a workflow: each client is tagged by type, the right emails go out on the right Mondays, every reminder lists only what's still missing, and anyone who sends everything in stops getting reminders. It runs on the tools you already use (your practice software or a spreadsheet, Gmail or Outlook, and Google Drive or Dropbox), and you approve every template before anything is sent.

Setting it up in November or December means it's working before the January rush.

### When should I send the first tax season email to clients?
Late November or early December, before the holidays. A short kickoff that explains the process, the key IRS dates and your internal cut-off date means the January organizer email isn't a surprise.

### What is the 2027 tax filing deadline?
For 2026 Form 1040 returns, the IRS early-release draft of Publication 509 (2027) lists Thursday, April 15, 2027. With an automatic 6-month extension (Form 4868), returns are due Friday, October 15, 2027, but tax owed is still due April 15.

### How many reminder emails should clients get?
For most individual clients, two reminders and a cut-off notice after the document request is enough, as long as each one lists only what's still missing. More emails to everyone mostly train clients to ignore them.

### When are W-2s and 1099-NECs due in 2027?
The draft Pub. 509 (2027) lists Monday, February 1, 2027, because January 31 falls on a Sunday. That's the date for giving W-2s to employees and for filing and furnishing Form 1099-NEC.

## When a client sent some documents but not all: how to get the rest
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/ (2026-11-10)

When a client sent some documents but not all, treat the file as incomplete, not nearly done: reply within a day with a short list of only the items still missing, each named the way the client knows it. Give every client one status (complete, partial or nothing), keep one upload link, and send reminders that shrink as items arrive until the list is empty.

A client sent some documents but not all, and now the file sits in a half-done pile. You can't finish the return, and the client thinks they've done their part. This is the most common state a client file is in during deadline season, and the hardest to manage, because it looks like progress.
This post covers why partial submissions stall your work, how to show each client exactly what's still missing, a "still missing" message you can copy, and a simple status table that tells you who to chase today. For the full reminder sequence, see our [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/).

### Why 9 out of 10 documents is nearly as bad as none
From the client's side, sending most of the pile feels like the job is done. From your side, a return with one missing P60, 1099 or rental statement can't be finished, and often can't even be started properly. You open the file, read through what's there, find the gap, put it down, and later do the same reading again. Each partial file gets handled two or three times.
Partial files also hide in plain sight. A "nothing received" client is easy to spot on a list. A client who sent eight things in three emails looks active, so nobody checks what's still outstanding until the deadline is close.
- The client believes they're finished, so they stop looking for the rest.
- The missing item is often the hard one: the document they have to request from someone else (a lender, a letting agent, a pension provider, a brokerage).
- Documents arrive across email, post and [a portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/), so nobody holds one true list.
- Your reminder says "please send your records", which the client reads as already done.

### Give every client one of three statuses
The fix starts with a rule your whole team uses the same way. Every client file is in exactly one of three states, and only one of them means "ready to work on".
Status | What it means | What happens next | Who acts
--- | --- | --- | ---
Complete | Everything on the client's list has arrived and been checked | Book the work; stop all reminders; send a thank-you | You
Partial | At least one item arrived, at least one is still missing | Reply within one working day with the "still missing" list; remind weekly | Client
Nothing | No documents received yet | Normal request sequence; phone call after the second reminder | Client
Partial, stuck | Same missing item for 3 or more weeks | Phone call; ask if the item exists this year; agree a date or an estimate | You and the client

### Show the client exactly what's still missing
A good "still missing" list is specific to that client and that year. Build it from last year's return and anything new the client told you: if they had a rental property last year, the rental statement is on the list until they say it's sold.
1. Start each client's list from last year's file, not from a generic checklist. Add anything new they mentioned.
2. Name each item the way the client knows it: "the year-end statement from your investment account", not "brokerage 1099-B"; "the letter from your pension provider", not "P60 equivalent".
3. When documents arrive, tick them off the same day and send nothing about the items already in.
4. Reply to every partial upload within one working day with only what's left. A quick reply tells the client you're watching the list.
5. Give each missing item an "if this doesn't apply, tell us" option, so items that don't exist this year can be closed.
6. For items the client must request from someone else, say who to ask and what to ask for. That is usually what's really holding them up.
7. When the list is empty, change the status to complete and stop reminders at once.

### A "still missing" message you can copy
Keep the opening thanks: it tells the client you noticed what they did, which makes the rest feel like a small ask. Keep the list numbered and short. If the list has more than five items, the client is probably "nothing", not "partial", and needs the full request again.
Subject: Thanks, we're nearly there: [N] items still to send:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for sending [items received]. That's most of it.

To finish your [tax year] return we still need:

1. [missing item, in plain words] (you can get this from [who to ask])
2. [missing item]

If either of these doesn't apply to you this year, just reply "not this year" and we'll take it off the list.

Same upload link as before: [upload link]

If you can send them by [internal deadline], we'll have your return ready for you to review by [date].

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### When to start work on a partial file
Sometimes you should start before the last item arrives. The question is whether the missing item changes the work or only finishes it.
Missing item | Start now? | Why
--- | --- | ---
One small figure you can confirm later (a bank interest amount) | Yes | Prepare everything else; add the figure when it comes
A whole income source (rental, self-employment, a brokerage account) | No | The return and any tax due can change a lot
A document the client isn't sure exists | Ask first | A short call often closes it in two minutes
Anything when the deadline is under two weeks away | Talk to the client | Agree whether to file with an estimate and amend, or to file late and accept the penalty (UK), or, in the US, to file an extension (more time to file, not to pay)

### What the deadline means for partial files
In the UK, gov.uk says an online Self Assessment return for 2025 to 2026 must be in by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027, and a return up to three months late gets an initial £100 penalty. In the US, the IRS says individual returns are due April 15 (moved to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday), and the failure-to-file penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%.
Neither penalty cares that the client sent "most" of their records. Put your [internal cut-off date](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-documents-on-time/) a few weeks before the official one, put it in the first request, and repeat it in every "still missing" message. In Ireland, the [Form 11 Pay and File records timeline](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/form-11-pay-and-file-records-timeline-ireland/) applies the same idea to the 31 October deadline.

### Keep one status list for the whole practice
The status table only works if it's in one place, updated the day things arrive. A shared spreadsheet is enough for a small practice: one row per client, a column per expected document, a status column and a "last reminder" date. Sort by status each morning and you have your chase list for the day.
For illustration: a two-person practice with 120 Self Assessment clients sorts the sheet on Monday morning. 70 are complete, 30 partial and 20 nothing. The 30 partial clients each get their own short list. The four marked "partial, stuck" go on the phone list for Tuesday.

### How Mike Automations would build this
The work above is mostly bookkeeping of the chase itself: ticking items off, rebuilding each client's list, sending the right reminder. That part can run on its own. A workflow reads what arrives in your upload folder or inbox, ticks it off the client's list, and sends the "still missing" message with only what's left, in the wording you approved. It stops the moment the list is empty and tells you who is stuck.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how documents come in today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox, your spreadsheet or practice software where it allows a connection), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. You always decide when a file is complete; the workflow only keeps the list.

### Should I wait for all documents before starting a return?
Usually yes, if the missing item is a whole income source, because it can change the result. If it's one small figure you can add later, prepare the rest now so the file isn't read twice.

### How often should I remind a client with a partial submission?
Reply within one working day of each upload, then once a week with only what's left. After three weeks on the same item, phone them: the item may not exist this year, or they may not know who to ask.

### What if the client says they've sent everything?
Send the list of what you've received and the one or two items you expected from last year. Ask them to confirm each is "not this year". That turns a debate into a quick yes or no.

## Professional clearance letter template for UK accountants
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/professional-clearance-letter-template/ (2026-11-10)

A professional clearance letter is the letter a UK accountant sends to a prospective client's existing accountant, with the client's written authority, asking whether there is anything they should know before accepting the work and asking for handover information. ICAEW calls this a professional enquiry and points out that the existing accountant cannot give or refuse permission to act: the decision is yours. If no reply comes after a reasonable period (ICAEW says less than two weeks is unlikely to be reasonable), you write again by recorded delivery saying you will accept unless you hear back by a set date.

This professional clearance letter template covers the whole exchange: the client's authority, your request to the existing accountant, the reply you send [when you are the one being asked](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-disengagement-checklist-accountants/), and a chase sequence for when nothing comes back. It is written for [small UK practices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/accountants/) whose members belong to ICAEW, ACCA or AAT.
The rules below come from the professional bodies' own guidance, checked in November 2026. They are a summary to help you organise the work, not a substitute for your body's Code of Ethics. If a case is unusual, ring your body's ethics helpline.

### What professional clearance is (and what it isn't)
The duty sits in section 320 of the Code of Ethics, which ICAEW and ACCA both base on the international IESBA Code. ACCA adds its own section B15 on professional appointments. When you are asked to replace another accountant, or to do work that adds to theirs, you contact them before you accept so you can find out about anything that should affect your decision: unpaid tax, irregularities, a dispute, or work obtained by improper means.
ICAEW's helpsheet for incoming accountants calls "clearance" a misnomer. The existing accountant has no authority to give or withhold clearance. Their job is to tell you, honestly and with the client's permission, about anything you need to know. Your job is to weigh it up and decide. ICAEW's outgoing-accountant helpsheet makes the same point from the other side and tells the existing accountant not to use "clearance" or "permission" language in the reply.
AAT's guidance (AT magazine, March/April 2024) puts the practical side plainly: get the client's permission in writing, and the outgoing accountant should respond promptly and honestly.

### Before you write: the client's authority
Confidentiality means the existing accountant usually needs the client's consent before saying anything. ICAEW suggests you explain the process to the prospective client, ask them to tell the existing accountant about the change, and get their written authority for the existing accountant to talk to you and release information. Enclose it with your letter so the reply isn't held up.
If the client refuses to let you make the enquiry, ICAEW says to ask why, record the answer, and take it into account when you decide whether to act.
Client authority (the client signs and dates it):
```
To: [Existing accountant's firm]

I/We have appointed [Your firm name] to act as accountants for [client or company name] from [date].

I/We authorise you to discuss my/our affairs with [Your firm name] and to give them any information they reasonably request, including the handover information listed in their letter.

Signed: ................................
Name: ................................
For and on behalf of: [company name, if applicable]
Date: ................................
```

### The professional clearance request letter
ICAEW's template enquiry letter has five parts: who has approached you and for what work, a request for any circumstances you should know before accepting, a request to confirm if there are none, the list of handover information you need, and the client's signed authority. You can combine the enquiry with the records request in one letter, as long as you don't start work until you are satisfied it's proper to act.
Under the anti-money laundering rules you must not ask whether the existing accountant has made a suspicious activity report (ICAEW, paragraph 320.5A2). They couldn't answer anyway. Leave that question out.
Professional clearance request letter (send by email with a read receipt, or by post):
```
Dear [Name],

[Client or company name] ([UTR / company number])

We have been approached by the above to act as their accountants for [the work, for example: annual accounts, Corporation Tax return, Self Assessment and VAT returns] from [date or period]. Their signed authority is enclosed.

Before we accept, please tell us of any circumstances or information we should consider when deciding whether to act. If there are none, please confirm this.

To help with a smooth handover, please also send:
- the last set of accounts approved by the client and a detailed trial balance agreeing to them
- copies of the most recent tax returns and computations you prepared, with any losses or allowances carried forward
- any open HMRC enquiries or correspondence still in progress
- the VAT and payroll position (last period filed, next due)
- any records belonging to the client that you still hold

Please let us know if you are still working on anything for this client, and the date your responsibility ends.

We would be grateful for a reply by [date, at least 14 days from today].

Yours sincerely,
[Name]
[Firm name, professional body, practising certificate or licence number]
[Phone and email]
```

### What the existing accountant has to send you
ACCA's "Transfer information" factsheet (issued 1 July 2025) says reasonable transfer information should be provided promptly to the new accountant, free of charge. ACCA defines it narrowly: a copy of the last set of accounts formally approved by the client, and a detailed trial balance that agrees to them. Many other items belong to the client anyway and have to be handed over for that reason.
ICAEW's guidance is similar. The existing accountant must deal promptly with any reasonable request for the transfer of records, and should give you information the client can't provide if its absence might harm the client. They shouldn't normally charge, unless there is real work involved, such as retrieving archived files, or the request is for information the client already has.
Unpaid fees are not a reason to ignore your letter. ICAEW says the existing accountant must still respond (with client consent) and may mention the fees in the reply. They may hold a lien over some records for unpaid fees, but ICAEW says a lien is to prompt a slow payer, not to force payment in a genuine dispute.

### The reply template, for when you are the outgoing accountant
When the letter lands on your desk, check you have the client's permission first. ICAEW says respond promptly; if nothing needs flagging, say so; if something does, give the facts, because saying "there are matters" without detail is not enough. Don't confirm or deny any suspicious activity report: that could be tipping off.
Reply to a professional enquiry:
```
Dear [Name],

[Client or company name] ([UTR / company number])

Thank you for your letter of [date]. We have the client's authority to reply.

[Either] We are not aware of any professional reason why you should not accept this appointment.
[Or] Before deciding, you should be aware of the following: [plain facts, for example: the 2025 VAT return is under enquiry; our letter to HMRC of 3 October is unanswered].

Our responsibility for this client ends on [date]. The following work is still with us: [list, or "none"].

Enclosed is the transfer information: the accounts for the period ended [date] as approved by the client, and a detailed trial balance agreeing to them. [Client records we hold will be returned to the client / sent to you on [date].]

[If relevant] Fees of £[amount] for work already completed remain outstanding.

Please contact me if you need anything further.

Yours sincerely,
[Name, firm]
```

### The chase sequence when nobody replies
Silence is the most common problem. ICAEW's helpsheet says to chase, try other means such as a phone call, and if there is still no reply after a reasonable period (possibly 14 to 30 days, and less than two weeks is unlikely to count) the Code requires you to write by recorded delivery or another trackable method, stating that you will accept unless you hear back by a set date. After that date you can assume there is no adverse comment, but you still take other reasonable steps, such as asking the client about any open HMRC or legal matters.
When | What you send | How
--- | --- | ---
Day 0 | Request letter plus the client's signed authority | Email with read receipt, or post
Day 7 | Short reminder: "Following up our letter of [date] about [client]. Could you reply by [day 14]?" | Email, then a phone call
Day 14 | Ask the client to remind the existing accountant and to request their own records | Email to the client
Day 14 to 21 | Final letter: "Unless we hear from you by [date, at least 7 days ahead], we will assume there is nothing you need to tell us and accept the appointment." | Recorded delivery, or email with a read receipt
Deadline passed | File note of every attempt and your decision; ask HMRC or Companies House directly for anything still missing | Client file

### How to track open clearance requests
With three or four [new clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/) at once, the risk isn't the letter, it's losing track of which ones are waiting. A simple tracker is enough. One row per new client:
- Client name, reference, and the existing accountant's firm and email
- Date the client's authority was signed
- Date the request went out, and how
- Date of the day 7 reminder and the final recorded-delivery letter
- Reply received: yes or no, date, and "issues raised: yes or no"
- Transfer information received: accounts, trial balance, tax returns, client records
- Decision: accepted or declined, by whom, and the date
- Next action and its due date, so the sheet sorts itself by what's late

### How Mike Automations would build this
Most of this is dates: who signed, what went out when, what's overdue. A workflow can send the client the authority to sign as soon as they say yes, send your request letter the moment it's signed, put the day 7 reminder and the recorded-delivery date on your list, and tick items off as the existing accountant's reply and files arrive. You read every reply and make every decision; the workflow only keeps the chase moving.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you take on new clients today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox, your spreadsheet or practice software where it allows a connection), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Is professional clearance a legal requirement in the UK?
It comes from the professional bodies' Codes of Ethics (section 320, which ICAEW and ACCA both use, plus ACCA's section B15). Members of those bodies have to follow it. A change of statutory auditor also has its own Companies Act procedures.

### How long should I wait for a reply?
ICAEW's guidance suggests a reasonable period may be 14 to 30 days and says less than two weeks is unlikely to be reasonable. Chase first, then write by recorded delivery giving a final date.

### Can the old accountant refuse to reply because fees are unpaid?
No. ICAEW says unpaid fees are not a reason to ignore a professional enquiry. They can mention the fees in the reply and may hold a lien over some records, but they must still respond.

### Can the outgoing accountant charge for handover information?
ACCA says reasonable transfer information (the last approved accounts and a detailed trial balance) is provided free of charge. ICAEW says there should normally be no charge unless there is real work, such as retrieving archives.

## Extension clients missing documents before October 15: triage, emails and when to let go
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/extension-clients-still-havent-sent-anything/ (2026-11-10)

Extension clients missing documents before October 15 should be sorted into three groups by early August: ready, partial and sent nothing. Each group gets a different email sequence with a firm internal cut-off date in September, and clients who still have sent nothing by then get a written notice that you can't file for them by October 15. An extension only moves the filing deadline, not the payment deadline, so say that in every email.

Every firm has them: extension clients missing documents in September, some of whom still haven't sent anything since April. The extension felt like breathing room in spring. By late summer it's a pile of files that will all land in the first two weeks of October, on top of everything else.
This post is a plan for individual (Form 1040) extension clients: when to triage, a triage table, three escalation emails you can copy, and when to stop and disengage. The October 15, 2026 deadline has passed, so use it to [set up the 2027 season](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-season-client-email-calendar/) now, while this year's stragglers are fresh in your mind.

### What the extension does and doesn't do
The IRS says an extension (Form 4868, or one of the other ways it lists) gives an individual until October 15 to file without the failure-to-file penalty. It also says, plainly, that the extension is only for filing: any tax owed is still due by the April due date. For 2026 returns that means April 15, 2027 for payment and October 15, 2027 for filing (both weekdays, so no weekend shift), unless the IRS postpones them.
That last part matters. The IRS regularly postpones deadlines for taxpayers in federally declared disaster areas (its "Tax relief in disaster situations" page lists them), so check each client's county before you send a deadline email.
Miss October 15 and the failure-to-file penalty applies, because the IRS counts the due date "including extensions". It's 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month late, up to 25%. For returns due after December 31, 2025, a return more than 60 days late has a minimum penalty of $525 or 100% of the tax due, whichever is less. The failure-to-pay penalty (0.5% a month, up to 25%) runs separately from April, and in any month when both apply, the filing penalty is reduced by the payment one.
Many clients think the extension gave them until October to pay. Say otherwise in every email, in one sentence.

### Triage extension clients by early August
Don't wait for September. On the first working day of August, give every extension client one status. The aim is to know which files are really moving before the October rush, not during it.
Status | What it looks like | Risk | What you do in August
--- | --- | --- | ---
Ready | Everything is in, waiting for your team | Low: it's your capacity, not the client | Schedule the work now; aim to file before September
Partial | Some documents in; usually waiting on a K-1, a corrected 1099 or one missing statement | Medium | Send a list of only what's missing (Email 1); ask who they're waiting on
Partial, waiting on a third party | Client is waiting on a K-1 or similar they can't control | Medium-high | Ask for an expected date; prepare everything else now
Sent nothing | No documents since the extension was filed | High | Email 1 plus a phone call within a week
Unreachable | No reply to two emails and a call | Highest | Move straight to Email 2; check you have a current address and phone

### The timeline from April to October 15
Pick one internal cut-off date and use it everywhere. Mid-September leaves you about four working weeks for the late arrivals, which is what most small firms can actually absorb.
When | What to send or do
--- | ---
By the April due date | File the extension. Tell the client in writing: tax was due today; your new document date is [internal date].
Mid-May | Short note with the client's own missing list.
First working day of August | Triage every extension client into the table above.
Early August | Email 1 to partial and sent-nothing clients.
Around September 1 | Email 2 (escalation) to anyone still not complete. Phone every sent-nothing client.
Mid-September | Your internal cut-off. Email 3 (final notice) to anyone still not complete.
Late September | Written notice to clients who missed the cut-off with nothing sent: you can't file for them by October 15.
October 15 | Last day to file on extension.

### Email 1: the August status check
Subject: Your [year] return: what we still need before October 15:
```
Hi [first name],

Your [year] return is on extension, which means it must be filed by October 15. The extension gave you more time to file, not to pay: any tax owed was due on [April due date].

To finish your return we still need:

1. [missing item, in plain words]
2. [missing item]

If you're waiting on something from someone else (a K-1, a corrected form), reply and tell us who and when you expect it. We'll prepare everything else in the meantime.

Upload link: [upload link]
Our date for your documents: [internal cut-off]

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### Email 2: the September escalation
Subject: Action needed: [N] weeks to file your [year] return:
```
Hi [first name],

We still don't have [missing items / your documents] for your [year] return, and the extended filing deadline is October 15.

If we don't receive them by [internal cut-off], we may not be able to file on time. The IRS late filing penalty is 5% of any unpaid tax for each month the return is late, up to 25%.

Please upload what you have today: [upload link]. If something is holding you up, call us on [phone] and we'll work out what we can do.

[your name]
```

### Email 3: the final notice
Send Email 3 only if your engagement letter supports it, and keep the tone factual. Its job is to put the deadline and the consequence in writing, not to scare anyone.
Subject: Final notice: your [year] return and October 15:
```
Hi [first name],

This is our last reminder before the October 15 deadline. We have not received [the items listed below / any documents] for your [year] return:

- [missing item]

If we don't have them by [final date], we won't be able to prepare and file your return by October 15. You would then be responsible for filing it yourself or with another preparer, and late filing penalties may apply.

Upload link: [upload link]
Phone: [phone]

[your name]
```

### When to disengage
Some clients won't answer at all. If a client has sent nothing by your cut-off and hasn't replied to three emails and a call, it's usually time to put in writing that you won't be filing for them this year. Check your engagement letter first, and talk to your insurer or professional body if you're unsure what notice to give.
- Send the notice in writing, dated, before October 15, so the client still has time to act.
- Return the client's records on request. Treasury Circular 230, section 10.28, says a practitioner must promptly return records the client needs to meet their federal tax obligations when the client asks, and a fee dispute generally doesn't change that (state law can narrow what must be returned).
- If you hold a Form 2848 power of attorney for the client, the IRS instructions say you withdraw by writing "WITHDRAW" across the top of the first page and sending a copy to the IRS.
- Bill for work already done, as your engagement letter allows.
- Note the outcome in your client list so next year's onboarding asks the right questions.

### Set up next season so fewer clients end up here
1. Write your internal document date into the engagement letter, not just the emails.
2. When you file each extension, record why: waiting on a K-1, client late, your capacity. Only the first two need chasing.
3. Send each extension client [their own missing list](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/) in May, not a generic reminder.
4. Keep one status list for all extension clients, updated the day documents arrive.
5. Put the August triage date in your calendar now.

### How Mike Automations would build this
Most of this is a schedule plus a list: who is ready, who is partial, who has sent nothing, and which email goes to whom on which date. A workflow can keep that list as documents land in your upload folder, send each client their own missing items on your timeline, stop the moment a file is complete, and give you a short daily list of who needs a phone call. You approve the wording once and decide every disengagement yourself.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how your extension season runs today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (QuickBooks, Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox, your tax software's client list where it allows a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does an extension give my client more time to pay?
No. The IRS says an extension of time to file is not an extension of time to pay. Tax owed was due by the April due date, and the failure-to-pay penalty and interest run from then.

### When should I start chasing extension clients?
Send each client their own missing list in May, triage everyone by early August, and set an internal document cut-off around mid-September. Waiting until October leaves no room for late documents.

### What if a client is still waiting on a K-1 in October?
Prepare everything else first so only the K-1 figures are left. Talk to the client about the options before October 15; don't let the file sit untouched until the K-1 arrives.

## Client disengagement checklist for UK accountants (with a disengagement letter template)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-disengagement-checklist-accountants/ (2026-11-10)

A client disengagement checklist for accountants is the list of steps a UK practice works through when a client leaves: send a disengagement letter setting out what you have done, what is left and the date your responsibility ends; reply to the new accountant's professional enquiry; hand over records; remove the client from your HMRC agent accounts; close off Companies House points; and send the final invoice. ICAEW recommends a written disengagement letter as good practice, so there is no argument later about who was doing what.

This client disengagement checklist is for [small UK practices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/accountants/). Clients leave for ordinary reasons (price, a move, a new business partner) and sometimes because you have asked them to go. Either way, the risk is the same: a VAT return or payroll run that each firm thinks the other is doing, an HMRC login you still hold for someone who isn't your client, or a records request that turns into a complaint.
Below: the checklist in order, the HMRC and Companies House steps checked on gov.uk in November 2026, a disengagement letter template you can adapt, and how to stop it all depending on someone's memory. It is practical guidance, not legal advice. Your professional body's helpsheets and helpline come first.

### The checklist, in order
1. Agree the end date and write it down. Decide the cut-off point for your responsibility, and which jobs in progress you will finish.
2. Send the disengagement letter (template below) with a short status report on each service: last return filed, next one due.
3. Reply to the new accountant's [professional enquiry](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/professional-clearance-letter-template/) once the client has given permission. Do it promptly, even if fees are unpaid.
4. Hand over the transfer information and the client's own records.
5. Remove the client from your HMRC agent services account and your HMRC online services for agents account, service by service, after saving copies of what you filed.
6. Close off Companies House points: registered office, authentication code, filings in progress, [identity verification records](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/companies-house-identity-verification-client-tracker/).
7. Send the final invoice for work done and any agreed remaining work.
8. Switch off everything recurring: reminders, portal access, direct debits, bookkeeping software access, newsletters.
9. Write a file note of the agreed terms and what was done, and keep your [anti-money laundering records](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/) for the required period.

### 1. The disengagement letter: what it must say
ICAEW's "Disengagement letters" helpsheet says the letter should cover the matters you dealt with, what remains to be done, the date by which outstanding matters must be completed, any further work your firm will do, and the fees due for past work and any further work. It suggests sending it with a status report, which is what stops a quarter-end slipping through the gap, especially for ongoing work like payroll and VAT.
If the client never signs and returns it, ICAEW notes the letter still supports your position in any later dispute. If you were relying on their signature as permission to talk to the new accountant, get that permission another way, such as an email from the client.
AAT's guidance on client care also expects a disengagement letter that sets out outstanding work and any work you will not do (AT magazine, March/April 2024).

### 2. Replying to the new accountant
When the new firm's professional clearance letter arrives, get the client's permission first, preferably in writing. ICAEW's outgoing-accountant helpsheet (updated October 2025) says reply promptly, say plainly if there is nothing to flag, and give the facts if there is. Don't use the words "clearance" or "permission": the decision to act is theirs. Unpaid fees are not a reason to stay silent, though you can mention them.
Never confirm or deny whether you have made a suspicious activity report. ICAEW warns that could amount to tipping off. Our professional clearance letter template (linked at the end of this article) includes a reply you can adapt.

### 3. Records handover
ACCA's "Transfer information" factsheet (July 2025) says reasonable transfer information goes to the new accountant promptly and free of charge: a copy of the last accounts formally approved by the client and a detailed trial balance agreeing to them. Records that belong to the client go back to the client (or, with their permission, straight to the new firm).
ICAEW says you may hold a lien over some records where fees are unpaid, but it exists to prompt a slow payer, not to force payment in a genuine dispute, and it never lets you ignore the enquiry. Keep a list of what you sent, to whom and when.

### 4. HMRC agent authorisation
HMRC's guidance "Change or remove your authorisations as a tax agent" (last updated July 2025) says you can remove a client you no longer act for online, but you have to do it separately for each online service. You need to remove them from both your agent services account and your HMRC online services for agents account, or they may still be able to see your details.
Two warnings from the same page. Once you remove a client, you lose access to their data, so save copies of everything you filed for them first. And for PAYE and Self Assessment you can also tell HMRC you no longer act for a client by calling the Agent Dedicated Line.
- Before removal: download copies of returns, submissions and HMRC letters for your file
- Agent services account: remove the client from each service (for example MTD for VAT, MTD for Income Tax)
- HMRC online services for agents: remove the client from each service you hold (for example Self Assessment, Corporation Tax, CIS)
- Write the removal date for each service in the file note

### 5. Companies House points
- Registered office: if the company uses your address, it needs a new one. Companies House's AD01 page says to tell it within 14 days of the change, and filing online needs the company authentication code.
- Authentication code: gov.uk advises companies to change their code if it's known by someone no longer authorised to file for them, and names "your previous accountant" as an example. Put this reminder in your letter.
- Filings in progress: say in the letter which accounts or confirmation statement you will file and which the new firm will.
- Identity verification: if you are registered as an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP) and verified directors' identities for Companies House, gov.uk says you must keep records of those identity checks for 7 years. A client leaving doesn't end that.

### 6. Final invoice and your own records
Send the final invoice with or soon after the letter, listing work completed and any agreed work still to do, so the numbers match what the letter says. If fees are disputed, ICAEW expects you to take reasonable steps to resolve it.
Keep your customer due diligence records. Regulation 40 of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 says they must be kept for at least five years from when you know, or have reasonable grounds to believe, that the business relationship has ended. ICAEW's Practice Assurance guidance also recommends a file note of the agreed disengagement terms and actions.

### Disengagement letter template
Adapt it to your engagement letter and your professional body's guidance. Delete the lines that don't apply.
Disengagement letter (send with a status report):
```
Dear [Client name],

[Company name] ([company number / UTR])

Thank you for letting us know that you have appointed [new firm] / As discussed on [date], we will stop acting for you. This letter confirms where things stand.

Our responsibility for your affairs ends on [date].

Work we have completed:
- [for example: accounts and Corporation Tax return for the year ended 31 March 2026, filed on 12 October 2026]

Work we will still complete before that date:
- [for example: VAT return for the quarter to 30 November 2026] (or: none)

Work that is now your or your new accountant's responsibility, with due dates:
- [for example: payroll from the December 2026 pay run]
- [for example: Self Assessment return for 2025 to 2026, due 31 January 2027]

Records: we will return your records to you / send them to [new firm] with your permission by [date]. We will remove our authorisation to act for you with HMRC once this work is done.

Companies House: [if we provide your registered office] please change your registered office address by [date]. We also recommend you change your company authentication code, since we have known it.

Fees: our final invoice of £[amount] for the work above is enclosed / will follow, payable by [date].

Please sign and return a copy to confirm you agree, or tell us by [date] if anything here is wrong.

Yours sincerely,
[Name, firm]

Signed for the client: ...................... Date: ..........
```

### How Mike Automations would build this
Disengagement goes wrong when it lives in someone's head. A workflow can start the moment you mark a client as leaving: draft the letter with the status of each service filled in from your records, put the HMRC removal and Companies House reminders on the right person's list with dates, raise the final invoice for checking, and stop the recurring reminders. Nothing goes to the client until a person has read and approved it.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how clients leave your practice today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox, Xero or QuickBooks, your spreadsheet or practice software where it allows a connection), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Do I have to send a disengagement letter?
ICAEW describes a written disengagement letter as best practice, and AAT's client care guidance expects one. It records the date your responsibility ends, what's left and who does it, which protects you if there is a dispute later.

### Do I need to remove the client from HMRC myself?
Yes, for your own accounts. HMRC says to remove a client you no longer act for from both your agent services account and your HMRC online services for agents account, separately for each service. Save copies of what you filed first, because access ends when you remove them.

### Can I keep a client's records until they pay?
ICAEW says you may have a lien over some records for unpaid fees, but it should not be used to force payment in a genuine dispute, and it doesn't excuse you from replying to the new accountant. ACCA says reasonable transfer information is provided free of charge.

### How long do I keep the client's AML records after they leave?
At least five years from when you know the business relationship has ended (Money Laundering Regulations 2017, regulation 40). Identity checks you did as a Companies House authorised agent have a 7 year record-keeping rule.

## How to get clients to use your client portal
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-use-your-client-portal/ (2026-11-10)

To get clients to use your client portal, make the first upload take under two minutes, send every request as a link that opens the exact place to upload, and reply to emailed documents by pointing back to the portal. Roll it out to a small group first, chase non-users with short personal reminders, and only switch off email once most clients have uploaded at least once.

How to get clients to use your client portal is a question most small firms ask about six months after they paid for one. The portal works. The team likes it. But half the clients still email [photos of receipts](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/) at 11 at night, and someone has to save them by hand.
This guide covers why clients ignore portals, a rollout plan you can run in a month, three reminder templates, and a clear rule for when to stop accepting email. It's about the portal you already have, whatever software it's part of. If you're still deciding between a portal and email, read [our comparison of the two](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/) first.

### Why clients ignore your portal
Clients don't refuse portals on principle. They take the easiest route they know, and for most people that's email. Look at it from their side and the reasons are usually practical:
- They can't remember the login. They log in once or twice a year, so the password is long gone by the next request.
- The invite went to spam, or to an old address, so they never set the account up.
- On a phone it's awkward: a login page, a menu, then finding the right folder before they can upload anything.
- They don't know what goes where, so they're worried about putting it in the wrong place.
- Email still works. If you file what they email without comment, there's no reason for them to change.
- Nobody told them why. "Please use our portal" sounds like your admin, not their benefit.

### What makes the first upload easy
The first upload decides whether a client keeps using the portal. Before you roll anything out, test it yourself on a phone, logged out, as if you were a client who has never seen it.
- Send links that open the exact request or folder, not the portal's home page.
- Check whether your portal offers a sign-in link by email, a mobile app, or uploads without a full account. If it does, switch it on and use it in your requests.
- Name requests in the client's words: "2025-26 bank statements", not "Doc request #4".
- Put one short line on what to upload and an example of a good photo or file.
- Add a "can't log in?" line with a direct reply address, so a lost password doesn't turn into an email full of attachments.

### A five-step rollout plan
Most portal launches fail because every client gets the same invite on the same day, and the team is flooded with login questions in the busiest week of the year. Spread it out instead.
1. Pick a quiet month. Avoid the run-up to 31 January in the UK and the January to April season in the US.
2. Start with 10 to 20 clients who already reply quickly. They'll find the problems before everyone else does.
3. Send the invite with one real request in it, so the first login has a purpose: "Please upload your September bank statement here."
4. Fix what the pilot group got stuck on, then invite the rest in batches of 20 to 50 a week.
5. Track who has uploaded at least once. That one column tells you who needs help, more than any login count does.

### Reminders for clients who haven't logged in
Keep reminders short, personal and about the specific thing you need. Three messages over about two weeks is enough. After that, pick up the phone: a two-minute call where you stay on the line while they log in fixes most cases.
Reminder 1: the invite (day 0):
```
Subject: Your secure upload link for [client name]

Hi [first name],

We've set up a secure space for you to send us documents, so nothing gets lost in email.

The first thing we need is: [item, e.g. your September bank statement].

Upload it here: [direct link]

It works on your phone. If the link asks you to set a password and you get stuck, just reply to this email and we'll sort it out.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### The follow-up reminders
