Send the second reminder about five days after the invite and the third about a week after that. Both still name the item and include the direct link. Never send a generic "please log in" email.
Reminders 2 and 3 (day 5 and day 12):
```
Subject: Still need: [item] for [client name]

Hi [first name],

A quick reminder that we're still waiting for [item]. You can upload it here in a minute or two: [direct link]

If you can't get in, reply with a good time and I'll call you and walk you through it.

[Day 12 only:] We need this by [date] to [what it's for, e.g. finish your accounts on time].

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### When a client emails documents anyway
This is where most rollouts quietly fail. If you save emailed files yourself and say nothing, you teach the client that email is fine. During the rollout, file what they send so nothing gets lost, and reply every time with one short line pointing back to the portal.
Reply to a client who emailed documents:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks, we've got these and saved them to your file.

Next time, please upload here instead: [direct link]. It keeps everything in one place and it's more secure than email for things like bank statements and ID.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### When to switch off the email fallback
Turning off email too early annoys good clients. Leaving it on forever means the portal never becomes the habit. Use a simple rule for each client type, and give notice before you change anything.
Situation | What to do
--- | ---
Client has uploaded at least twice | Treat the portal as their default. Reply to emailed files with the portal link every time.
Most of your clients (say 80%) have uploaded at least once | Announce a date, about a month ahead, after which documents go through the portal only.
Client has tried and genuinely can't manage it (age, disability, no smartphone) | Keep email or post for them. Note it on their record so nobody chases them about the portal.
Sensitive items: ID, bank statements, payslips | Ask for these through the portal or a secure upload link only, as early as possible.
Client ignores three reminders and a call | Stop pushing the portal. Ask for the documents the easiest way they'll actually send them.

### When to stop forcing it
The goal is documents in on time, not portal logins. A client who sends everything by email in the first week of the month is a better client than one who logs in at the last minute. If a handful of clients will never use the portal, make their email the exception, not your problem: route their attachments into the same client folder automatically and move on.
For illustration: a small practice invites 15 clients in October. Twelve upload within a week. Two need a phone call. One, an elderly sole trader, posts paper records every quarter, so that client is marked "post" and taken off the portal reminders.

### Where automation helps
None of this needs new software. The work is sending the right link to the right client, keeping track of who has uploaded, and following up on time. That's what a simple workflow can do around the portal you already have: send each request with the direct link, remind only clients who haven't uploaded, save emailed attachments to the right client folder, and give you one list of who still needs a call. A person in your firm still decides who gets an exception.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how documents come in today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your portal or practice software where it allows a connection, Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How do I get clients to use our client portal?
Make the first upload easy (a direct link that works on a phone), roll it out to a small group first, send short reminders that name the exact document, and reply to emailed files with the portal link instead of filing them silently.

### Should we stop accepting documents by email?
Not straight away. Wait until most clients have uploaded at least once, then give about a month's notice. Keep a documented exception for clients who genuinely can't use it.

### What if a client keeps forgetting their portal password?
Use whatever passwordless option your portal has, such as a sign-in link by email or a mobile app, and send links that open the exact request. Put a "can't log in?" line in every request so they reply to you rather than emailing files.

### Do we need to replace our portal to automate reminders?
No. Reminders and tracking can run around the portal you already have, using your email and a simple list of who has uploaded.

## How to get bookkeeping clients to send receipts every month
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/ (2026-11-10)

To get bookkeeping clients to send receipts every month, give each client one place to send them (usually a receipt-capture email address or app), agree a monthly send-by date, and remind them on fixed days with a list of only the transactions that still have no receipt. At month end, send one short "still missing" list and decide each item: chase it, accept a bank or card statement, or mark it as no receipt.

Getting bookkeeping clients to send receipts every month is mostly about removing choices. When receipts can go by email, WhatsApp, a shoebox or a shared folder, they go nowhere in particular, and you find out at [quarter end](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/vat-quarter-records-chasing/).
This guide sets out one place to send, how often to ask each type of client, two reminder templates, and a simple way to handle the receipts that never turn up. It works for UK and US practices, and with [Xero](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/xero-practice-automation-ideas/) or QuickBooks Online.

### Why receipts arrive late
- The client has several ways to send them and isn't sure which one you want.
- Receipts pile up in a wallet or a van glovebox until the client "has a moment".
- Online purchases leave the receipt in an inbox the client never searches.
- Reminders say "please send your receipts", which gives no end point. A list of five specific transactions does.
- Nothing happens if they're late, so late becomes normal.

### Give every client one place to send receipts
Pick one route per client and put it in every reminder. Most receipt-capture tools give each client their own email address, so clients can forward or photograph receipts without logging in to anything. Check the current details in your own account, because menus and addresses change.
- Hubdoc (part of Xero): each organisation has its own intake email address. Hubdoc's help centre says each attachment becomes a separate document, and you can set up email rules to forward bills automatically. It also has a mobile app.
- Dext: each user has an email-in address for submitting receipts and invoices. Dext's help centre lists PDFs, common image formats and Word documents as accepted, and recommends forwarding rules for regular supplier invoices.
- QuickBooks Online: an admin creates a forwarding address ending in @assist.intuit.com. Intuit's help says each file should hold one receipt, and forwarding only works from email addresses registered to users on that company, so add the client as a user first.
- No capture tool: a single upload link or shared folder per client, with one sub-folder per month, is fine. The rule is still one place.

### Set up forwarding once, so receipts send themselves
The receipts that go missing most often are the ones that arrive by email: software subscriptions, fuel cards, online orders. Spend ten minutes with each client setting up an email rule that forwards those senders straight to their capture address. Gmail and Outlook both support automatic forwarding rules. After that, only paper receipts need the client's attention.

### How often to ask, by client type
Not every client needs the same rhythm. Match the frequency to how many transactions they have and when you need the books ready. The table below is a starting point, not a rule.
Client type | How often to ask | Send-by date | Notes
--- | --- | --- | ---
Sole trader, few transactions, not VAT-registered | Monthly reminder, quarterly review | 5th of the next month | In the UK, clients in Making Tax Digital for Income Tax send quarterly updates, so receipts must be in before each quarter's update.
VAT-registered business (UK) | Monthly | 5th of the next month | Leave time to query receipts before the VAT return. Receipts are your evidence for reclaiming VAT.
Trades and field businesses (lots of paper) | Weekly photo habit, monthly check | Every Friday, plus month end | Ask them to photograph receipts the same day. Faded till receipts are the usual problem.
Busy retail or hospitality | Weekly | Every Monday for the past week | High volume means a monthly batch is too big to check properly.
Limited company or corporation with payroll | Monthly | 3rd of the next month | Align with your month-end close and any management accounts you send.
Client who only needs year-end accounts | Quarterly | 10th of the month after quarter end | Monthly asks feel like nagging here. Quarterly keeps the year-end pile small.

### The monthly routine
1. On the 1st, send each client a short reminder with their capture address or upload link and the send-by date.
2. After the bank feed has come in, list the transactions over your threshold that have no receipt matched.
3. Two days before the send-by date, send that list: date, supplier, amount. Nothing else.
4. The day after the send-by date, send one final reminder with [what's still missing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/).
5. At month end, close the month. Anything still missing goes on the missing-receipts list (below) with a decision.

### Reminder templates
Keep reminders short and specific. The client should be able to act from their phone without opening anything else.
Monthly reminder (1st of the month):
```
Subject: [Month] receipts for [business name], please send by [date]

Hi [first name],

Time for [month]'s receipts. Please send them by [date].

The easiest way: forward or photograph them to [capture email address], or upload here: [link].

One receipt per photo or file works best.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### The "still missing" message
This is the reminder that gets results, because it gives the client a short, finishable job.
Specific missing receipts (2 days before the send-by date):
```
Subject: 4 receipts still missing for [month]

Hi [first name],

Thanks for what you've sent. These [month] payments still have no receipt:

- [date], [supplier], [amount]
- [date], [supplier], [amount]
- [date], [supplier], [amount]
- [date], [supplier], [amount]

If you have them, forward or photograph them to [capture email address] by [date].

If a receipt is lost, just reply with what it was for and we'll tell you what we can use instead.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### Handling receipts that never turn up
Some receipts are gone for good. Don't hold the whole month open for them. Keep one missing-receipts list per client with a decision against each line, and agree the rules with the client in advance.
In the UK, HMRC's VAT Notice 700 says that to reclaim VAT you must hold valid evidence that you received a taxable supply, and if the evidence isn't there in time, the VAT is claimed in the period you receive it. So for VAT clients, ask the supplier for a copy invoice before giving up. In the US, the IRS says expense records should show the payee, the amount, proof of payment, the date and what was bought, and that a combination of documents, such as a card statement plus an invoice, may be needed.
How long clients must keep records matters too: GOV.UK says sole traders must keep records for at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline, and limited companies for 6 years from the end of the last financial year they relate to. The IRS's general rule is 3 years, with longer periods in some cases.
Status | What it means | Next step
--- | --- | ---
Chase | Receipt probably exists (online order, supplier invoice) | Ask the supplier or client for a copy. Stays on next month's list.
Statement accepted | Small amount, clear business purpose | Note what it was for. Agree a threshold with the client in advance.
Copy requested | VAT-registered client, supplier can reissue | Reclaim the VAT when the copy invoice arrives.
Not business | Personal spend on a business card | Post to drawings or the director's loan account, as you normally would.
No receipt | Lost, no copy available | Record your decision and who agreed it. Raise it at year end.

### For illustration
For illustration: a bookkeeper with 40 monthly clients sends the 1st-of-month reminder to everyone. On the 3rd, 26 clients have no open items. The other 14 get a list of between one and six transactions each. By the 6th, eight lists are cleared, and the remaining items go on the missing-receipts list for a decision, so the month closes on time.

### Where automation helps
The reminders, the per-client lists and the month-end tracker are repetitive, and they're where time goes. A workflow can send each client their reminder on the right day, pull the unmatched transactions from Xero or QuickBooks where the software allows it, send only the missing items, and keep the missing-receipts list up to date. You still decide what's acceptable evidence; the workflow only keeps the list.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how receipts come in today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (Xero or QuickBooks, Hubdoc or Dext, Gmail or Outlook), so your clients don't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How do I get bookkeeping clients to send receipts every month?
Give each client one place to send them, agree a send-by date, and remind them with a list of the specific transactions that still have no receipt, rather than a general request.

### What's the easiest way for clients to send receipts?
A receipt-capture email address or app, such as Hubdoc, Dext or QuickBooks Online receipt forwarding, so they can forward or photograph receipts without logging in. Set up email forwarding rules for regular online suppliers.

### What if a client has lost a receipt?
Ask the supplier for a copy first, especially for VAT. If there's no copy, decide case by case whether a bank or card statement plus a note is enough, and record that decision.

### Should I ask weekly or monthly?
Monthly suits most clients. Weekly suits high-volume or paper-heavy businesses; quarterly suits clients who only need year-end accounts.

## How to sign up clients for MTD for Income Tax before April 2027
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/mtd-income-tax-client-sign-up-tracker/ (2026-11-10)

To sign up clients for MTD for Income Tax before April 2027, find every sole trader and landlord whose qualifying income (self-employment plus property income before expenses) on their 2025 to 2026 return is over £30,000. Make sure each one's authorisation is in your HMRC agent services account, then sign each client up individually through HMRC's online service with compatible software chosen. Track every client through those steps, because adding authorisations does not sign anyone up.

To sign up clients for MTD for Income Tax before April 2027, you need three things per client: proof they're in scope, a working authorisation in your agent services account, and a completed sign-up. HMRC's guidance (checked on 10 November 2026) treats these as separate steps, and a client can be stuck at any one of them.
The first group joined on 6 April 2026. The second group, with qualifying income over £30,000, joins on 6 April 2027 and is usually bigger. This post gives you the rules, the steps from GOV.UK, a tracker layout and a client letter you can copy. For running quarterly updates once clients are in, see [our separate post on the quarterly workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/making-tax-digital-income-tax-practice-workflow/).

### Which clients join in April 2027
HMRC's page "Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax" sets the thresholds by tax year. Qualifying income is total income from self-employment and property, before expenses, taken from the tax return for the year shown.
Qualifying income | Based on the tax year | Must use MTD from
--- | --- | ---
Over £50,000 | 2024 to 2025 | 6 April 2026
Over £30,000 | 2025 to 2026 | 6 April 2027
Over £20,000 | 2026 to 2027 | 6 April 2028

### Working out qualifying income: the cases that trip people up
The April 2027 group is decided by the 2025 to 2026 return, due online by 31 January 2027. So your list isn't final until those returns are in. Build it now from what you know, and flag anyone close to £30,000 to re-check when you finish their return. HMRC says it reviews each return and writes to people over the threshold, but a client who gets no letter is still responsible for checking.
- Add self-employment and property together. HMRC's own example: £25,000 rent plus £27,000 self-employment is £52,000 of qualifying income.
- Employment (PAYE), partnership profit shares, dividends and pensions don't count.
- For jointly owned property, only the client's share counts.
- A source that ceased still counts if the client has another continuing self-employment or property source.
- If every self-employment and property source stopped, the client must tell HMRC, or HMRC may sign them up based on the information it has.
- For a sole trader in a short first year, HMRC annualises the income (6 months of trading is doubled). Landlords must annualise property income themselves.
- Partnerships are not in yet. HMRC says it will set out their timeline later.

### Agent authorisation: the step that catches practices out
MTD for Income Tax uses your agent services account (ASA), which GOV.UK says is different from your HMRC online services for agents account. Existing Self Assessment authorisations are recognised, but only once they're in the ASA. You copy them across by adding your Self Assessment agent codes in the ASA ("Add existing Self Assessment authorisations to your agent services account"). That adds every client linked to that code at once, and makes you their main agent for MTD.
Two warnings from GOV.UK. First, the ASA shows the agent codes you've added, not a list of individual clients, so you need your own list to know who is covered. Second, adding authorisations does not sign anyone up: each client still goes through the sign-up service one by one.
For clients you don't act for on Self Assessment, you ask them to authorise you from the ASA. They get a link and approve it (HMRC calls this the digital handshake). You can ask to be a main agent or a supporting agent. A client can have only one main agent but any number of supporting agents. A supporting agent, such as a bookkeeper doing quarterly updates, can't submit the tax return or see the full tax calculation.

### Signing up each client: the steps from GOV.UK
Clients can also sign up early and volunteer for the current year. HMRC's sign-up page uses this example: a client who must start from 6 April 2027 can sign up now. If they do, any missed quarterly updates for the year so far must be sent from compatible software, and HMRC will confirm when volunteer penalties apply.
1. Confirm the client is in scope and not exempt (HMRC has a checker tool and an exemptions page, for example for people who are digitally excluded).
2. Check the client is registered for Self Assessment and has sent a return in the last 2 years. Both are conditions for signing up.
3. Make sure your authorisation is in your agent services account, either copied from Self Assessment or by digital handshake.
4. Agree compatible software with the client, and who keeps the digital records. HMRC says to check with the software provider that it meets your needs.
5. Gather what the sign-up service asks for: full name, date of birth and National Insurance number; for sole traders, business name, business address and trade; start dates for any income source started in the last 2 tax years.
6. Sign up in the online service with your ASA user ID. Check every self-employment and property source, add missing ones, and tell HMRC about any that have ceased.
7. Record the sign-up date and the first quarterly deadline (7 August 2027 for standard update periods) in your tracker.

### Why the 2027 group needs to be ready on day one
For the 2026 to 2027 tax year HMRC doesn't give penalty points for late quarterly updates. GOV.UK says that from later tax years, each late quarterly update earns a late submission penalty point. So the April 2027 group gets no free first year for quarterly updates. Standard deadlines are 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May.
HMRC began signing up people in the April 2026 group who hadn't signed up themselves from September 2026, using only the information it already held. GOV.UK hasn't said whether it will do the same for the 2027 group. Signing clients up yourself means their income sources are right from the start.

### A sign-up tracker you can copy
Column | What goes in it
--- | ---
Client and UTR reference | One row per client
Qualifying income 2025-26 | Self-employment plus property, before expenses; mark "estimate" until the return is filed
In scope from | April 2027, April 2028, not in scope, or exempt (with reason)
Authorisation in ASA | Yes via SA agent code / yes via digital handshake / not yet
Agent type | Main or supporting; name of any other agent involved
Software agreed | Product and who keeps the records
Sign-up details collected | NI number, trade, business address, source start dates
Signed up | Date, and by whom (practice, client or HMRC)
Letter sent | Date the client letter below went out
First quarterly deadline | 7 August 2027 (standard periods)

### A client letter you can copy
Letter or email to a client joining MTD for Income Tax in April 2027:
```
Subject: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax: what changes for you from 6 April 2027

Dear [First name],

From 6 April 2027, HMRC requires sole traders and landlords with self-employment and property income over £30,000 (before expenses) to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. Based on [your 2025 to 2026 figures / the figures we have so far], this applies to you.

What changes:
- Your income and expenses will be kept as digital records in software that works with HMRC.
- A summary is sent to HMRC every 3 months. The first one is due by 7 August 2027.
- You still have a tax return to finish after the year ends, and your tax is still due by 31 January.

What we'll do: [check our authorisation with HMRC and] sign you up, set up [software name], and send you a short reminder before each quarter ends.

What we need from you by [date]:
1. Confirm your business name, business address and the nature of your trade.
2. Tell us about any business or rental income you've started or stopped since your last return.
3. [If not authorised: Approve the authorisation link HMRC will send you from us.]

If your income for 2025 to 2026 turns out to be £30,000 or less, we'll tell you when your return is done. Reply to this email with any questions.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Practice name]
```

### What a workflow can take off your desk
The parts that need a professional stay with you: deciding if a client is in scope or exempt, the sign-up itself in HMRC's service, and anything that changes a client's tax position.
- Building the first list from last year's figures, and flagging clients near £30,000 for a re-check when their 2025 to 2026 return is done.
- Sending the letter above to everyone in scope, then reminding until the sign-up details are in.
- Holding the tracker and sending the team one daily list: not authorised, details missing, ready to sign up, signed up.
- Setting the quarterly reminders for each client as soon as they're signed up.

### How Mike Automations would build this for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you track MTD clients today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (your email, your accounting or practice software, a spreadsheet and your shared drive), so the team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. It costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does adding Self Assessment authorisations sign my clients up for MTD for Income Tax?
No. GOV.UK says adding your Self Assessment agent codes to your agent services account copies the authorisations across, but each client must still be signed up individually through the online service.

### Which tax return decides if a client joins MTD in April 2027?
The 2025 to 2026 return. If qualifying income (self-employment plus property income before expenses) on that return is over £30,000, the client must use MTD for Income Tax from 6 April 2027.

### Is there a penalty-free first year for the April 2027 group?
Not for quarterly updates. HMRC only waives penalty points for late quarterly updates in the 2026 to 2027 tax year. From later years, each late quarterly update earns a point.

### Can a bookkeeper and an accountant both act for the same client?
Yes. A client can have one main agent and any number of supporting agents. Only the main agent can submit the tax return and see the full tax calculation.

## Automation consultant, freelancer or DIY: which should you choose?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/ (2026-11-10)

Whether to hire an automation consultant, hire a freelancer or do it yourself depends on three things: how many steps and tools the process involves, how much it costs you when it fails, and who will fix it when an app changes. Do it yourself when the process is simple, low-risk and someone on your team enjoys tools. Hire a freelancer when you can describe exactly what to build, and a consultant when you need help working out what to build and someone to stand behind it afterwards.

Should you hire an automation consultant, a freelancer, or do it yourself? It's a fair question, and the honest answer is that each one is right for some businesses and wrong for others. This guide compares the three on [cost](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/), speed, risk and upkeep, and ends with a short self-test you can answer in five minutes.
One point comes up again and again when owners talk about this in online communities: the build is not the hard part. The hard part is who keeps it running six months later, when an app updates, a password expires or your process changes. Keep that question in mind as you read.

### The three options, in plain words
The lines blur. Some freelancers work like consultants, and some consultants are one person. Judge by what they do, not what they call themselves: do they ask about your process before talking about tools, and do they say who fixes it when it breaks?
- Do it yourself (DIY): you or someone on your team sets up the automation in a tool such as [Zapier, Make, n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) or Power Automate. You pay for the tool and with your own time.
- Freelancer: you hire an individual, often through a marketplace, to build a specific thing you describe. They are usually paid by the hour or by the task, and the job ends when the build is delivered.
- Automation consultant: a person or small firm who looks at how the process works today, decides with you what to automate and what to leave manual, builds it and usually offers support afterwards. They are usually paid a project fee or a day rate.

### Side by side: cost, speed, upkeep and risk
None of these is cheap or expensive by default. A DIY build that sends a wrong reminder to fifty clients can cost more than any invoice. A consultant who sells you a long discovery phase for a two-step job is poor value too.
 | Do it yourself | Freelancer | Automation consultant
--- | --- | --- | ---
How you pay | Tool subscription plus your own hours | Usually hourly or per task | Usually a project fee or day rate, sometimes a monthly support fee
Who works out what to build | You | You, mostly: they build what you specify | Both of you: mapping the process is part of the job
Speed to a first working version | Fast for a simple two-step job, slow if you're learning as you go | Depends on how clear your spec is | Depends on their discovery process: ask for a date in writing
Who maintains it | You | Often nobody, unless you agree it up front | Usually the consultant, if you pay for support
Main risk | It works until it quietly stops, and nobody notices | A build only one person understands, who may move on | Paying for weeks of discovery or a bigger project than you need
Best for | Simple, low-risk tasks and owners who like tools | A clearly defined job you could write on one page | Processes that touch clients, money or deadlines, or several tools

### When DIY is the right answer
Plenty of automations should be built by the owner. The tools are designed for it. Zapier's pricing page (November 2026) lists a free plan with 100 tasks a month for two-step automations: one trigger, one action. Make's pricing page lists a free plan with 1,000 credits a month. n8n's documentation says it runs as a free Community edition when you host it yourself, though hosting it means managing a server or Docker. Limits change, so check the pricing pages before you start.
DIY is usually right when:
- The job is one trigger and one or two actions, for example saving email attachments to a folder or adding a new form entry to a spreadsheet.
- Nothing goes to clients automatically, or a person checks each message before it is sent.
- If it stopped working for a week, you would notice and nothing serious would happen.
- Someone on the team actually enjoys this kind of work and has a few hours to spare.
- You're happy to look after it yourself when an app changes.

### When to get a freelancer
A freelancer is a good fit when you already know exactly what you want and could write it down: the trigger, every step, what happens when data is missing, and what done looks like. If you can't write that page yet, a freelancer will have to guess, and guesses cost hours.
Agree three things before work starts: whose accounts the automation runs in, what written notes you get at the end, and what it costs to call them back when something breaks. Zapier's own advice on hiring an expert also suggests [mapping your process first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/), including the exceptions, and naming one person on your side who makes decisions.

### When to get an automation consultant
A consultant earns their fee when the hard part is deciding what to build. That's common when a process crosses several tools, involves clients or money, has deadlines with penalties, or has grown up over years with workarounds nobody wrote down.
The risk with consultants is scope, so take [these questions to ask before hiring an automation expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/) with you. Ask for a written plan with a fixed price before you commit, a date it will be live, and a clear answer on what happens after launch. If the first step is a paid discovery phase lasting weeks, ask whether a smaller first project would show you what they can do.

### A 6-question self-test
Answer yes or no. Count the yeses.
1. Does the process involve more than two tools, or more than three steps?
2. Do messages, invoices or documents go to clients without a person checking each one?
3. Would a week of it silently failing cost you money, a deadline or a client?
4. Does it handle personal data such as ID documents, bank details or health information?
5. Is there nobody on your team with a few spare hours a month to look after it?
6. Are you unsure what the process should look like once it's automated?

### What your score means
Question 6 matters most. If you're unsure what the process should look like, any build is a guess, whoever does it.
Yeses | Our honest suggestion
--- | ---
0 to 1 | Do it yourself. Start on a free plan and keep a short note of what you built and where.
2 to 3 | Get some help. Build it yourself and pay someone for an hour to review it, or hire a freelancer with a one-page spec.
4 to 6 | Hire someone who will map the process, build it and support it. Ask them the questions in our hiring checklist first.

### The middle route most owners overlook
You don't have to choose one option for everything. A common sensible mix: you build the simple internal automations yourself, and pay for help only on the one process that touches clients or deadlines. Or you build a first version and pay for a short review before switching it on. Either way, keep the accounts in your business's name, so whoever helps you can leave without taking your automations with them.

### Where Mike Automations fits
To be clear about our own position: Mike Automations is one person, Michael, who maps the process, builds it and supports it, so it sits closest to the consultant column. You start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) and get a written plan with a fixed price within 48 hours. A workflow automation costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), it is usually live in 2 to 3 days, and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. It runs in your own accounts, and support is optional at $150 a month. If your score above says DIY, do it yourself: that's the right answer.

### Is it cheaper to learn Zapier or Make myself?
In money, usually yes: both list free plans, and paid plans cost far less than a build. In time, it depends. A two-step automation takes an afternoon to learn. A process with several tools, conditions and client messages can take much longer, and you'll be the one maintaining it.

### Do automations need maintenance?
Yes, some. Connections expire, apps change their forms and fields, and your process changes. Whoever builds it, agree before you start who will notice when it fails and who will fix it.

### What's the difference between a freelancer and a consultant?
A freelancer usually builds what you specify, paid by the hour or task. A consultant usually helps you decide what to build, then builds and supports it, paid by project or day rate. Many people do a bit of both, so ask what is included.

## 20 questions to ask before hiring an automation expert
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/ (2026-11-10)

The most important questions to ask before hiring an automation expert are: whose accounts will it run in, what happens when it breaks, what exactly is included for a fixed price, where will client data go, and what do I get if we stop working together. A good expert answers each one in writing, in plain words, before you pay anything. Vague answers on ownership and maintenance are the clearest warning sign.

These are the questions to ask before hiring an automation expert, whether you call them [a consultant, a freelancer](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/) or a Zapier or Make specialist. They are grouped into five areas: scope, data and GDPR, ownership, maintenance, and price and payment. Under each question is what a good answer sounds like, so you can tell a careful builder from a confident one.
You don't need to ask all 20 on a first call. Pick the ones that matter for your process, and ask for the answers in the written proposal. Anything that isn't written down is easy to remember differently later.

### Scope: what exactly will be built
If the expert talks about tools before asking how your process works today, be careful. Zapier's own advice on hiring an expert says to map your current process first, including the exceptions, and name one decision-maker on your side.
Question | A good answer sounds like
--- | ---
1. What will the automation do, step by step, and what will it not do? | A short written list of steps, plus a list of what stays manual, such as pricing, advice or anything needing judgement.
2. What does done look like, and how will we test it? | One or two sentences you could check yourself, and a test on real or realistic work before you pay.
3. What happens with the awkward cases: missing data, duplicates, a client who replies in the wrong place? | Specific examples from your process, and what the automation does in each one, even if the answer is "it flags it to you".
4. Does anything go to clients without a person approving it? | A clear yes or no for each message, and who approves the wording before launch.

### Data and GDPR: where your clients' information goes
In the UK (see our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/)), Article 28 of the UK GDPR says that when someone processes personal data on your behalf, it must be governed by a contract that is "in writing, including in electronic form". So if your builder will handle client data, ask for those terms. In the US the rules depend on your state and industry, but the same four questions still tell you where your data goes. This is general information, not legal advice.
Question | A good answer sounds like
--- | ---
5. Which personal data will the automation touch, and which tools will it pass through? | A named list: for example, client names and emails in Outlook, documents in OneDrive, nothing stored anywhere else.
6. Will you, or any tool you add, store a copy of our data? | Either "no", or a named tool, what it stores, where, and for how long.
7. What access do you need, and how will we remove it afterwards? | Only the access the build needs, given through your own accounts or a user you can switch off, not your main password.
8. Will you sign a written data processing agreement if we need one? | "Yes", without hesitation, or a clear explanation of why they won't be processing personal data at all.

### Ownership: what you keep if you part ways
Ownership is worth putting in writing. In the UK, the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 makes the author the first owner of copyright unless they are an employee (section 11), and an assignment is not effective unless it is in writing and signed (section 90). In the US, work by an independent contractor is generally only a "work made for hire" in certain categories and with a signed written agreement (17 U.S.C. 101), and transfers of copyright need a signed writing (17 U.S.C. 204). Running in your accounts settles most of this in practice, but a clear sentence in the contract costs nothing.
Question | A good answer sounds like
--- | ---
9. Whose accounts will the automation run in? | Yours, in your business's name, paid for by you. You can see it, pause it and keep it.
10. Who owns what you build? | "You do", and the contract says so in writing.
11. What will you hand over at the end? | A short written note: what runs where, what triggers it, which logins it uses, and how to switch it off.
12. If we stop working together, does it keep running? | "Yes, it keeps running in your accounts." Anything that stops when the expert leaves is a rental, not a build.

### Maintenance: what happens when it breaks
Question | A good answer sounds like
--- | ---
13. How will we know if it stops working? | A named alert, for example an email to you when a step fails, not "you'll notice".
14. Who fixes it, how fast, and what does that cost? | A named person, a response time, and a price: included, a monthly fee or a fixed rate.
15. What usually breaks in builds like this? | Honest specifics: expired connections, a renamed spreadsheet column, a form that changed, a plan limit reached.
16. Can we pause it ourselves? | "Yes, here's how", shown to you before launch.

### Price and payment: what you pay, and when
[Day rates and hourly billing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) aren't wrong, but they move the risk of overruns to you. If you go that way, ask for an estimate in hours and a point at which they must check with you before carrying on.
Question | A good answer sounds like
--- | ---
17. Is the price fixed, and what exactly does it cover? | One number in writing, tied to the scope list from question 1.
18. What costs extra, including tool subscriptions? | A list: which subscriptions you'll pay for directly, and what counts as a change of scope.
19. When do I pay, and is there a deposit? | Clear stages tied to things you can check. Be wary of paying in full before anything works.
20. What happens if it doesn't do what we agreed? | A plain answer: they fix it at no charge, or you don't pay for that part.

### Warning signs in the answers
- "We'll set it up in our account to make things easier."
- No written scope, or a scope that only lists tools, not steps.
- No answer to "how will we know if it stops working?"
- Full payment up front for a build you can't test first.
- Pressure to sign before you have the answers in writing.

### A one-page brief to send before the first call
Sending [a short brief](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-brief-an-automation-project/) first makes every answer above more specific. Copy this, fill in the brackets and send it to each person you're considering. For a longer explanation of each line, see our guide to briefing an automation project.
One-page automation brief:
```
Business: [name, what you do, how many people]
Country: [UK / US / other]

The process: [e.g. chasing clients for documents]
How often it happens: [e.g. 40 times a month]

Today, step by step:
1. [who] [does what] [in which tool]
2. ...

Tools we already use: [e.g. Outlook, OneDrive, Xero, a booking system]
Personal data involved: [e.g. names, emails, ID documents]

Done means: [one sentence you could test]
Must stay manual: [e.g. anything sent to a client needs my approval]

What goes wrong today: [e.g. reminders get forgotten in busy weeks]

We need from you, in writing:
- scope and what's not included
- a fixed price and when we pay
- whose accounts it runs in, and what we get at handover
- who fixes it when it breaks, and the cost
```

### How Mike Automations answers these
If you ask us: Mike Automations is one person, Michael, who maps, builds and supports the automation. After a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) you get a written plan with a fixed price within 48 hours. A workflow automation is [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), usually live in 2 to 3 days, with no deposit and no hourly billing. You pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. It runs in your accounts, you own it, and if we stop working together it keeps running. Support is optional at $150 a month. Ask us all 20 questions; you should expect the same from anyone you hire.

### Is "certified expert" an official qualification?
Some automation tools run their own partner or certification programmes, but there is no general licence for automation builders. Treat a badge as a sign they know the tool, and still ask the questions about scope, data, ownership and maintenance.

### Should I ask for references?
Yes, if they have them, and ask to speak to the client rather than read a quote. A newer builder without references can still be a good choice if they let you test the work before you pay.

### How many people should I talk to?
Two or three is usually enough. Send each the same brief so you can compare the written answers side by side.

## How to ask for a deposit on a quote, with wording you can copy
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/ (2026-11-10)

To ask for a deposit on a quote, put it on the quote itself: the amount, what it covers, when it's due and when it's refundable, then send a payment link the moment the customer says yes. Keep the deposit tied to a real cost, such as materials or a reserved date. In the UK a deposit you keep on cancellation should normally be a small percentage of the price, and some US states cap it by law.

If you want to ask for a deposit on a quote without it feeling awkward, the trick is to make it part of the quote, not a separate conversation. Customers who see the deposit, the reason for it and the refund terms in writing before they accept rarely push back. The ones who do are telling you something useful before you order the materials.
This post covers when a deposit is worth asking for, how much to think about, what UK and US rules say, the exact wording for the quote, the invoice and the reminder, and how a paid deposit can confirm the booking on its own. It's written for trades and [service businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) in the UK and the US. In the US, read "estimate" wherever it says "quote".

### First decide: does this job need a deposit?
A deposit should protect you from a real cost, not just make you feel safer. There's no single rule for every trade, so decide by job type. This table is a starting point, not a legal rule.
Job type | Deposit? | Why
--- | --- | ---
Special-order materials (bespoke kitchen, made-to-measure windows) | Usually yes | You pay suppliers before you start and may not get that money back
A big job that blocks out days or weeks in your diary | Often yes | Turning other work away has a cost if they cancel late
Small, quick jobs from stock materials | Often no | The admin of taking and refunding deposits can cost more than it saves
Emergency call-outs the customer asked for | Usually no | Take payment on completion instead; UK cancellation rules treat these differently (see below)
Repeat customers who always pay | Your call | Many trades waive it for people with a track record

### How much deposit should you ask for?
There is no official "normal" deposit for trades, and figures you see quoted online are opinions. What you can check is what the rules say about fairness and caps.
UK: the Competition and Markets Authority's guidance on unfair contract terms (CMA37, updated 22 July 2026) says a genuine deposit can be kept in full if it works as a binding reservation, you tell the customer at the earliest opportunity that it's required, and the circumstances in which it is non-refundable are clear and narrow. It adds that such a deposit "will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price", and that a larger prepayment may be a disguised penalty. If you need more up front to buy materials, say so as a separate materials payment, and be ready to refund what you haven't spent or can't recover.
US: some states set a legal cap. In California, the Contractors State License Board says a home improvement down payment cannot be more than $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price, whichever is less, with no exception for special-order materials. Other states have their own rules, so check your state's contractor licensing board before you set a figure.

### UK customers: the 14-day cancellation right
Many trades get caught out here. Under the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, a quote that a customer accepts in their own home (an "off-premises" contract) or by email, phone or online (a "distance" contract) usually comes with a 14-day right to cancel. A quote accepted face to face at your premises does not.
- For services, the 14 days run from the day the contract is made (regulation 30).
- If they cancel in time, you must refund all payments, deposit included, within 14 days of being told (regulation 34).
- Off-premises contracts where the customer pays £42 or less are outside these rules (regulation 27).
- Urgent repairs or maintenance where the customer asked you to visit are excluded, but extra work you sell on that visit is not (regulation 28).
- To start work inside the 14 days, you need the customer's express request; for off-premises contracts it must be on a durable medium such as email or paper. If they then cancel, they pay a proportionate amount for work done (regulation 36).
- If you don't give the cancellation information, the period can stretch to 12 months, and the customer may owe nothing for work already done (regulations 31 and 36). For off-premises contracts, not giving it is also a criminal offence (regulation 19).

### US customers: the FTC Cooling-Off Rule
In the US, the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule gives customers until midnight of the third business day to cancel many sales made at their home for $25 or more, with a full refund. The FTC lists exemptions, including sales needed to meet an emergency and repairs or maintenance the customer asked for (anything extra you sell on that visit is still covered). Many states add their own home improvement rules on top, so check yours.

### Wording for the quote
Put the deposit on the quote, near the total, in plain words. Change the bracketed parts to suit your job.
Deposit section for a quote or estimate:
```
Deposit: [£/$ amount], due when you accept this quote.
What it covers: [ordering your materials / reserving [dates] in our diary].
Your booking is confirmed once the deposit is paid. We'll send a payment link as soon as you accept.
If you cancel: [you can cancel within 14 days of accepting and get the deposit back in full. After that, we refund the deposit minus the cost of any materials already ordered for you that we can't return.]
If we cancel or can't do the work: you get the deposit back in full.
Balance: [£/$ amount], due [on completion / in stages listed below].
```

### Wording for the deposit invoice
Deposit invoice email:
```
Subject: Deposit for [job] at [address]

Hi [name],

Thanks for accepting the quote for [job]. Here's the deposit invoice for [£/$ amount], as set out in the quote.

Pay here: [payment link]

As soon as it's paid, your dates are booked: [start date]. You'll get a confirmation straight away.

The deposit goes towards the total of [£/$ amount]. The balance of [£/$ amount] is due [on completion].

Any questions, just reply to this email.

Thanks,
[your name]
[business name]
```

### Wording for the reminder
If the deposit hasn't arrived after a couple of days, [one friendly reminder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) is usually enough. Don't threaten. Tell them what happens to the dates.
Deposit reminder (email or text):
```
Hi [name], just checking you got the deposit link for [job]. I'm holding [start date] for you until [day]. After that I may need to offer the slot to someone else. Here's the link again: [payment link]. If anything's changed, just let me know.
```

### Make the paid deposit confirm the booking
Most of the work around a deposit is admin: sending the link, checking whether it's been paid, confirming dates, chasing. None of it needs you. Your invoicing tool (Xero, QuickBooks, Stripe or similar) already knows when a payment lands, so the rest can follow from that.
1. Customer accepts the quote. A deposit invoice with a payment link goes out the same minute.
2. Payment lands. The job is marked "booked" in your job list or spreadsheet, and the dates go into your calendar.
3. The customer gets a confirmation with the dates, what to expect and the balance still due.
4. No payment after [2] days: one reminder goes out with the link again.
5. Still no payment by your cut-off: you get a short list of unpaid deposits to call. You decide whether to release the slot.
6. If the customer cancels, you get a note with the date they accepted, so you can check whether the 14-day UK refund applies before replying.

### How Mike Automations would build this for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you quote and get paid today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (your invoicing software, calendar and job list), so there's nothing new to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000, one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. You approve every message wording before anything goes to a customer.

### For illustration
For illustration: a kitchen fitter sends a quote with a deposit to cover the worktops, which are cut to size. The customer accepts by email on a Monday. The deposit invoice goes out at once, the customer pays on Tuesday, and the fitting dates appear in the calendar with a confirmation sent. Because the quote was accepted by email, the fitter knows the customer could still cancel within 14 days, so the worktops are ordered once the customer has asked in writing for work to start.

### Is it rude to ask for a deposit?
No. Put it on the quote with the reason and the refund terms, so it's part of the deal from the start rather than a surprise afterwards.

### Can I make a deposit non-refundable?
In the UK, only within limits. The CMA's guidance says a deposit kept on cancellation should work as a genuine reservation, with clear and narrow conditions, and will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price. During the 14-day cancellation period it must be refunded in full. Take legal advice for your own terms.

### When should I send the payment link?
As soon as the customer accepts. The quote already told them the deposit confirms the booking, so the link is the next natural step.

### Do I need a deposit for every job?
No. Many trades only ask for one on special-order materials or long bookings, and take payment on completion for small jobs.

## Tax organizer questions for new and returning clients
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-organizer-questions-new-vs-returning-clients/ (2026-11-10)

Tax organizer questions should differ for new and returning clients. A new client needs the full set: identity, filing status, dependents, every income source, prior-year returns and IRS notices. A returning client should get a short list built from last year's return, asking only what changed and confirming each document you received last year.

Most tax organizer questions go to every client in the same long packet, and most clients skip half of it. A new client needs the full picture, because you know nothing yet. A returning client already gave you most of the answers last year. What you need from them is what changed, and the documents that come every year.
Below are the questions to ask each group, as two tables you can copy into your own organizer, the questions that are new for the 2026 tax year, a short client questionnaire template, and a method for building each returning client's missing list from last year's return.

### Questions for a new client
With a new client, the organizer does two jobs: it gets you the facts for this return, and it tells you whether there is history you need to know about before you sign [the engagement letter](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/).
Topic | What to ask | Why it matters
--- | --- | ---
Identity | Full legal names, dates of birth and contact details for the taxpayer, spouse and every dependent. Collect Social Security numbers or ITINs through your secure portal, not by email. | Names and numbers must match Social Security records or the e-filed return can reject.
Filing status | Marital status on December 31, any change in the year, and who lived in the home. | Filing status drives most of the return.
Prior returns | Copies of the last two or three federal and state returns. | You see carryovers, depreciation, estimated payments and anything unusual.
IRS and state letters | Any notice or letter received in the last two years, and any open payment plan. | You find out about problems before they become yours.
Income sources | Every source: jobs, self-employment, rentals, investments, retirement, Social Security, gig and app income, digital assets. | A new client doesn't know what you need, so list it all.
Business or rental | For each one: what it is, when it started, which books or spreadsheet it uses, and who keeps them. | Tells you how much bookkeeping cleanup comes with the return.
Health coverage | Marketplace coverage in the year, and Form 1095-A if they had it. | A missing 1095-A is a common late-season hold-up.
IP PIN | Do they have an Identity Protection PIN from the IRS? | The IRS says an incorrect or missing IP PIN will reject an e-filed return.
Authorization | Permission to see their IRS records, usually on Form 8821 (information only) or Form 2848 (power of attorney). | Transcripts confirm income the client forgot to mention.
Refunds and payments | Bank details for direct deposit or debit, and estimated tax payments made in the year. | Estimated payments are easy to miss without the dates and amounts.

### Questions for a returning client
For a returning client, swap open questions for yes/no confirmations. You already know they had a W-2 from one employer, a brokerage account and a rental. Ask whether that's still true, and ask for the documents by name.
Topic | What to ask | Why it matters
--- | --- | ---
Life changes | Did you marry, divorce, have or adopt a child, or did someone move in or out? | Changes filing status and dependents.
Address | Did you move, or buy or sell a home? | A move can mean a second state return. A home sale needs the closing papers.
Jobs | Same employer as last year? Any new job, second job or job that ended? | Each one means a W-2 to collect.
Accounts | Last year we had statements from [list]. Are all still open? Any new account? | Closed and new accounts are where 1099s go missing.
Self-employment | Is the business still running? Any new side income? | New 1099-NEC or 1099-K income often isn't mentioned unless you ask.
Rental | Same tenants and property? Any major repair or improvement? | Improvements are depreciated, repairs are not.
Big purchases | Did you buy a new car with a loan, install solar panels, or pay college tuition? | Each can mean a deduction or credit with its own document.
IRS letters | Any letter from the IRS or the state since we filed last year? | Catch notices early.
IP PIN | If you have an IP PIN, send this year's. | The IRS says a new IP PIN is generated each year.

### Questions that are new for the 2026 tax year
The IRS page on the 2025 tax law changes (One, Big, Beautiful Bill provisions for individuals and workers, checked on irs.gov in November 2026) lists four new deductions for tax years 2025 through 2028, available whether or not the client itemizes. Each needs a question in your organizer, because clients won't think to mention them.
Deduction | Question to add | Notes from the IRS page
--- | --- | ---
Tips | Did you receive tips in your job or business? | Up to $25,000 a year. A Social Security number is required.
Overtime | Were you paid overtime this year? | Up to $12,500, or $25,000 on a joint return. Only the extra half of overtime pay counts.
Car loan interest | Did you take out a loan after 2024 to buy a new car for personal use? If so, send the loan statement and the VIN. | Up to $10,000 of interest. The vehicle must have had final assembly in the United States, and the VIN goes on the return. Leases don't qualify.
Age 65 and over | Confirm dates of birth for you and your spouse. | An extra $6,000 per eligible person, or $12,000 for a couple if both qualify. The person must be 65 by the last day of the tax year.

### Two more questions every organizer needs
- Digital assets. Form 1040 asks a yes/no question about digital assets. The IRS says to answer yes if the client received digital assets as payment or a reward, or sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of them. Brokers report gross proceeds on Form 1099-DA for transactions from January 1, 2025, and basis for certain transactions from January 1, 2026, so ask whether the client received one.
- E-file signature. Ask how the client wants to sign Form 8879, the IRS e-file signature authorization: in person, or by e-signature through your software. Clients who can't sign quickly hold up returns that are otherwise finished.

### Build the returning client's list from last year's return
The most useful returning-client organizer is a list of the documents you received last year, with a tick box next to each. The client confirms or crosses out, and adds what's new. That's faster for them, and it gives you a precise missing list in January.
1. Export last year's source documents for the client from your tax software or document folder: every W-2, 1099, 1098, K-1 and statement, with the payer's name.
2. Turn each one into a line: 'W-2 from [employer]', '1099-INT from [bank]', '1098 mortgage interest from [lender]'.
3. Add the change questions from the returning-client table and the four new deduction questions.
4. [Send it in December](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-season-client-email-calendar/), so clients know what to watch for in their January mail.
5. As documents arrive, tick them off. Anything still unticked on the date you set is the client's missing list, and it goes into the next reminder by name.

### A client questionnaire template you can copy
This short version works as an email or a form. Ask for sensitive details (Social Security numbers, bank details) only through your secure portal, never in a plain email reply.
Returning client tax questionnaire:
```
Subject: Your 2026 tax return: 10 quick questions

Hi [first name],

To get your 2026 return started, please answer these by [date]. Reply here or use the form: [secure form link]

1. Did your marital status or household change in 2026? (marriage, divorce, new child, someone moved in or out)
2. Did you move, or buy or sell a home?
3. Last year you had income from: [W-2 employer], [bank], [brokerage]. Are these all the same? Anything new?
4. Did you start, stop or change any business or side income?
5. Did you receive tips or overtime pay in 2026?
6. Did you buy a new car with a loan after 2024? If yes, we'll need the loan statement and the VIN.
7. Did you receive, sell or exchange any cryptocurrency or other digital assets?
8. Did you have health coverage through the Marketplace? If yes, we'll need Form 1095-A.
9. Have you had any letters from the IRS or the state since we filed last year?
10. If you have an IRS Identity Protection PIN, please send this year's number through the portal.

Please upload your documents here: [secure upload link]
Please don't send Social Security numbers or bank details by email.

Thank you,
[name]
[firm name]
```

### What to automate, and what stays with you
The questions need your judgment. Sending them, collecting the answers and chasing what's missing does not. A workflow can build each returning client's checklist from last year's document list, send the questionnaire in December, file uploads into the right folder, tick items off as they arrive, and send reminders that name the exact documents still missing.
You still review the answers, decide what they mean for the return, and talk to the client when something big changed. Collecting client data also means protecting it, which is what [a written information security plan](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/wisp-for-small-tax-practices/) is for: see our guide to a WISP for small tax practices.

### For illustration
For illustration: a returning client's December checklist lists seven documents from last year. In January, five arrive through the portal and are ticked off automatically. On February 1, the client gets a reminder that names the two still missing: a 1099-DIV from one brokerage, and a 1098 from the new mortgage lender they mentioned in question 2.

We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you send organizers and collect documents today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example "every returning client gets a checklist built from last year's documents by December 15, and reminders list only what's still missing".
