### What's the difference between a tax organizer and a client questionnaire?
Many firms use the words for the same thing. Usually the organizer is the full packet of forms and schedules, and the questionnaire is the short list of yes/no questions on top. Returning clients mostly need the questionnaire plus a list of last year's documents.

### Which new questions do I need for the 2026 tax year?
The IRS lists four new deductions for tax years 2025 through 2028: qualified tips, qualified overtime, interest on a loan taken out after 2024 for a new US-assembled car, and an extra deduction for people aged 65 and over. Add a question for each one.

## WISP for tax preparers: what a small practice needs
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/wisp-for-small-tax-practices/ (2026-11-10)

A WISP (Written Information Security Plan) is the written document that says how a tax practice protects client data: who is responsible, what the risks are, and which safeguards are in place. Under the FTC Safeguards Rule, which implements the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, tax preparers count as financial institutions, so every paid preparer must have one, whatever the size of the practice. IRS Publication 5708 gives a free template.

A WISP for [tax preparers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeepers/) is not optional, and it doesn't have to be long. The IRS says a sole practitioner can use a shorter, simpler plan than a 10-partner firm. What it must do is describe, in writing, how you keep client data safe and who is in charge of that.
This guide explains what a WISP is, who must have one and why, what IRS Publication 5708 contains, and what the FTC requires. It ends with a one-page outline you can start from. It is a plain-English summary, not legal advice: read the IRS and FTC pages linked by name below, and talk to a security or legal adviser if your practice has special risks.

### What a WISP is
IRS Publication 5708 (Rev. 8-2024), Creating a Written Information Security Plan for your Tax & Accounting Practice, describes a WISP as a documented, structured approach to keeping client data secure. In practice it's a short document covering three kinds of safeguards: physical (locked cabinets, who can enter the office), technical (passwords, multi-factor authentication, encryption, backups) and administrative (who has access, staff training, what happens after a breach).
Publication 5708 says the plan should be written and accessible, kept in a format others can read, such as PDF or Word, and reviewed and updated at least once a year.

### Who must have one
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to protect customer data, and the FTC's Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) sets out how. The rule lists tax preparation firms among its examples of financial institutions. Publication 5708 says tax and accounting professionals are covered regardless of size, and that the Safeguards Rule requires them to put a WISP in place and keep it up to date.
The IRS repeated this in August 2026 (news release IR-2026-92): tax and accounting professionals must create and maintain a written information security plan. And it's on the PTIN form. Line 11 of Form W-12 (Rev. October 2026), the PTIN application and renewal, asks you to confirm you know that paid preparers are required by law to create and maintain one, and points to Publications 5708 and 4557. Ticking that box doesn't create a plan, so if you've renewed without one, now is the time.

### What the FTC Safeguards Rule requires
The required elements are in section 314.4 of the rule. Section 314.6 exempts firms that hold customer information on fewer than 5,000 consumers from four of them. Most small practices fall under that number, but count your clients (and their spouses and dependents) before you rely on it. The rule text was checked on ecfr.gov in November 2026.
Requirement (16 CFR 314.4) | What it means in a small practice | Under 5,000 consumers?
--- | --- | ---
(a) Qualified Individual | One named person in charge of the security program. In a sole practice, that's you. | Applies
(b) Risk assessment | Identify what could go wrong with client data and whether your safeguards cover it. | Applies, but it doesn't have to be written: (b)(1) is exempt
(c) Safeguards | Access controls, an inventory of data and systems, encryption in storage and in transit, multi-factor authentication, secure disposal of data no later than two years after you last used it to serve the client (with exceptions), change management, and activity logs. | Applies
(d) Monitoring and testing | Check your safeguards work. Without continuous monitoring, the rule asks for yearly penetration testing and vulnerability scans at least every six months. | Monitoring applies; the yearly penetration test and six-monthly scans in (d)(2) are exempt
(e) Training | Security awareness training for everyone with access to client data. | Applies
(f) Service providers | Choose providers that can protect the data, require it in the contract, and check them from time to time. | Applies
(g) Keep it current | Update the program when your business, systems or risks change. | Applies
(h) Incident response plan | A written plan for what you do after a security event. | Exempt (Publication 5708 still includes one)
(i) Annual report | A yearly written report from the Qualified Individual to the owners. | Exempt
(j) FTC notification | Tell the FTC as soon as possible, and within 30 days, if unencrypted information on 500 or more consumers is acquired without permission. | Applies

### What IRS Publication 5708 contains
Publication 5708 was written by the Security Summit, the IRS, state tax agencies and the tax industry working together, for smaller practices in particular. It sets out the legal requirements, gives a short outline, then a sample WISP template you fill in with your firm's details, more detail on each section, sample attachments and a glossary. The outline has seven parts:
1. Define the WISP objectives, purpose and scope.
2. Designate a qualified individual, and list authorized users and their access levels.
3. Assess risks: the kinds of information you handle, where it could be lost, and how you monitor and test.
4. Inventory hardware: each device, where it is, and what client information it stores or processes.
5. Document the safety measures in place: data collection and retention, data disclosure, network protection, user access, electronic data exchange, Wi-Fi, remote access, connected devices, reportable incidents, plus an employee code of conduct.
6. Draft an implementation clause: the date the plan takes effect and who signed it.
7. Attachments. The sample set covers record retention, rules of behavior for client data, breach procedures and notifications, a staff acknowledgment form, a hardware inventory, and a list of people authorized to access client data.

### A one-page WISP outline you can start from
This outline follows Publication 5708 and the rule above. Use it to draft, then fill in the full IRS template. Keep it short and true: a plan that describes what you actually do is worth more than a long one nobody follows.
One-page WISP outline:
```
WRITTEN INFORMATION SECURITY PLAN: [Firm name]
Last reviewed: [date]. Next review: [date, within 12 months]

1. Purpose and scope
This plan protects the personal information of our clients, their spouses and dependents, in paper and electronic form, in the office and remotely.

2. Qualified Individual
[Name], [role]. Responsible for this plan, training, and reporting security events.
Authorized users and access: [name: systems and data they can see]

3. Risks
Data we hold: [tax returns, SSNs, bank details, IDs, W-2s, 1099s]
Where it lives: [tax software, client portal, email, cloud storage, paper files]
Main risks: [phishing, lost laptop, wrong recipient, weak passwords, former staff access]
How we check: [monthly access review, software updates, backup test]

4. Hardware inventory
[Device, location, what client data it holds, encrypted yes/no]

5. Safeguards in place
- Multi-factor authentication on email, tax software, portal and cloud storage
- Client documents received through [portal], not plain email
- Devices encrypted and locked when unattended
- Office Wi-Fi uses strong encryption; guests on a separate network
- Remote access only with MFA
- Records kept for [period], then securely destroyed
- Access removed the same day someone leaves

6. Service providers
[Provider: what data it holds, contract includes safeguards yes/no, last checked]

7. Training
Everyone with access is trained before access is granted and once a year. Each person signs an acknowledgment.

8. If something goes wrong
[Qualified Individual] contacts the IRS Stakeholder Liaison, law enforcement, state authorities and affected clients as required. If 500 or more people are affected, notify the FTC within 30 days of discovery.

Signed: [name]   Date: [date]
```

### Where automation fits, and where it adds work
Automation can make a WISP easier to live by. A workflow can send clients a [secure upload link](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/) instead of asking them to email documents, remove a leaver's access from a checklist the day they go, remind the Qualified Individual about the yearly review, track who has signed the training acknowledgment, and flag files that have passed your retention date.
It also adds to the plan. Every tool that touches client data, such as an automation platform, an e-signature service or an AI assistant, is a service provider under section 314.4(f). It belongs on your provider list, behind multi-factor authentication, with its access limited to the data it needs. Separately, the rules in [section 7216 of the tax code](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/) limit how preparers use and disclose tax return information, so check them before you send client data to a new tool.

### For illustration
For illustration: a two-person practice keeps its WISP as a six-page Word document based on Publication 5708. A shared calendar reminder opens the yearly review each June. When a seasonal preparer finishes in April, a checklist removes their tax software, portal and email access the same day and records the date in the authorized-users attachment.

### How Mike Automations would help
We don't write your WISP or give legal advice. We build the workflows that sit behind it: secure document collection, access checklists, review and training reminders, and retention flags, each documented so you can add it to your plan as a safeguard and list the tools as service providers. We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use and goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Do sole practitioners need a WISP?
Yes. IRS Publication 5708 says tax and accounting professionals are financial institutions under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and the FTC Safeguards Rule regardless of size. The plan can be shorter and simpler than a larger firm's.

### When do I have to tell the FTC about a breach?
Under 16 CFR 314.4(j), if unencrypted information on at least 500 consumers is acquired without authorization, you must notify the FTC as soon as possible and no later than 30 days after discovery, using the form on ftc.gov.

### How often should a WISP be reviewed?
Publication 5708 says at least once a year, and whenever your business changes in a way that affects security, such as new software, new staff or a new office.

## Section 7216 consent before you use AI or automation on client tax data
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/ (2026-11-10)

Section 7216 consent is the written, signed permission a tax return preparer needs before disclosing or using a client's tax return information in any way the regulations don't already allow. Sending return data to your own tax software, a US e-file provider or a colleague in your US firm needs no consent; sending it outside the US or using it for non-tax purposes does, and pasting it into a public AI chatbot is not a safe route at all. For Form 1040 clients the consent must follow Rev. Proc. 2013-14: a separate document, set wording, an affirmative signature and a stated duration (one year if none is given).

Section 7216 consent comes up the moment a firm wants to automate client reminders, summarize documents with AI or move return data between tools. AI tools have made an old rule practical: where exactly does your client's data go when you press the button?
This post covers what counts as tax return information, which disclosures need no consent, where AI sits, what a valid consent must contain, and a simple workflow to collect and track consents. It is general information, not legal advice. The rules have edge cases, and the call on your own tools belongs to you and your counsel.

### What section 7216 covers
Under Treasury Regulation §301.7216-1, "tax return information" is any information furnished for, or in connection with, preparing a client's return. That includes the client's name, address and identifying number, documents third parties send you, and anything you derive from that data while preparing the return. So a client list with names and emails pulled from your tax software counts, not just the return itself.
The penalties are real. The regulation describes section 7216 as a misdemeanor, with up to one year in prison, a fine of up to $1,000, or both, for knowing or reckless disclosure or use. Section 6713 adds a civil penalty of $250 per disclosure or use, capped at $10,000 a year.

### What you can do without consent
Section 301.7216-2 lists disclosures and uses that need no consent. The ones that matter for everyday automation are these:
- Using the data, or sharing it with other officers, employees or members of your own firm in the US, to prepare the client's return
- Disclosing it to another tax return preparer in the US to prepare the return or provide auxiliary services, as long as that preparer isn't making substantive determinations or giving advice that affects the tax reported (the regulation defines a substantive determination as analyzing, interpreting or applying the law)
- Sending it to an Authorized IRS e-file Provider to file the return
- Letting the vendor of tax software you provide to the client update that software

### Where AI and automation tools fit
There is no AI-specific rule in the section 7216 regulations. The closest official word is the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility's Issue 2026-19, "Introductory Guidelines for Responsible AI Use in Federal Tax Practice" (June 24, 2026). It reminds practitioners that the section 7216 and 6713 penalties apply, warns that generative AI platforms may expose taxpayer data, especially when it's uploaded to unsecured or public systems, and says client data should be handled only in secure, enterprise-approved AI. It also expects firms to vet third-party AI tools.
Whether a given AI vendor counts as a preparer providing auxiliary services in the US (no consent) or a third party (consent) depends on facts: where the data is processed, what the vendor may do with it, and whether the tool is doing substantive analysis. Commentators disagree on the grey cases, so the safe default many firms use is simple: if client data leaves your own systems for a tool that isn't your tax software or e-file provider, get consent first, or keep the data out.
What goes into the tool | Consent under §7216? | What to do
--- | --- | ---
No client data: a generic prompt, a blank email template, a checklist | Not engaged | Fine to use. This is where most AI drafting help belongs.
Return data in your tax software or sent to your e-file provider | Not needed (§301.7216-2) | Normal practice. Keep your vendor's security terms on file.
Client names and emails in a US reminder or e-signature service used only to collect documents | Grey area | Read the vendor's data terms. Ask counsel, or cover it in a consent.
Client documents or figures in an enterprise AI tool, processed in the US | Grey area, often treated as needing consent | Get counsel's view. If in doubt, get a signed consent naming the tool.
Anything processed, stored or viewed outside the US | Required before disclosure | Get consent first. For Form 1040 clients, mask the SSN unless both sides meet the data protection rules in Rev. Proc. 2013-14.
Client data pasted into a free, public AI chatbot | Not a safe route | Don't. The OPR guidance warns against unsecured or public systems.
Using return data to market other services, such as loans or insurance | Required (consent to use) | A separate consent naming each product or service.

### What a valid consent must contain
Section 301.7216-3 sets the basics for every consent: the names of the preparer and the client; the purpose of the disclosure and the specific recipient, or the particular use; the tax return information covered; and the client's signature and date. Consent must be knowing and voluntary and given before the disclosure (there's no retroactive consent), and you generally can't make your tax preparation services conditional on it.
For clients filing a Form 1040 series return, Rev. Proc. 2013-14 adds the format rules:
- A separate written document for each disclosure or use. It can be attached to the engagement letter, but it can't be buried in it. Disclosure consents and use consents go on separate documents.
- On paper: at least 8½ by 11 inches, 12-point type, with nothing on the page except the consent. On screen: text at least as large as the site's normal body text, with good contrast, printable, and nothing else on the screen except navigation.
- The mandatory statements, in the order the IRS sets, including the statement about contacting the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA).
- Affirmative consent only. No pre-checked boxes and no opt-out forms.
- A duration. If the client doesn't specify one, the consent lasts one year from the signature date.
- No blanks filled in after signing, and no changes to the form once it's signed.
- If the consent covers the whole return, a statement that the client can ask for a more limited disclosure.
- For electronic signatures, the client must type something: a PIN of at least five characters, their own name (not pre-filled), or five or more characters unique to them, such as the answer to a shared secret.

### Sample consent text (Form 1040, disclosure)
The block below combines the mandatory statements from section 5.04 of Rev. Proc. 2013-14 with the details the regulation requires. Read the revenue procedure itself, and have your counsel check the final version and the current TIGTA contact details before you use it.
Consent to disclose tax return information (example to adapt):
```
Federal law requires this consent form be provided to you. Unless authorized by law, we cannot disclose your tax return information to third parties for purposes other than the preparation and filing of your tax return without your consent. If you consent to the disclosure of your tax return information, Federal law may not protect your tax return information from further use or distribution.

You are not required to complete this form to engage our tax return preparation services. If we obtain your signature on this form by conditioning our tax return preparation services on your consent, your consent will not be valid. If you agree to the disclosure of your tax return information, your consent is valid for the amount of time that you specify. If you do not specify the duration of your consent, your consent is valid for one year from the date of signature.

I, [client name], authorize [firm name] to disclose the following tax return information: [for example: copies of my 2026 Forms W-2 and 1099 and the receipts I upload]
to: [recipient, for example: the named AI document service, processing in the US]
for this purpose: [for example: reading figures for my 2026 Form 1040, which [firm name] then checks]
This consent is valid until: [date]

If you believe your tax return information has been disclosed or used improperly in a manner unauthorized by law or without your permission, you may contact the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) by telephone at 1-800-366-4484, or by email at complaints@tigta.treas.gov.

Signed: [typed name]   Date: [date]
```

### A plain consent workflow
1. List every tool that touches client data: tax software, portal, e-signature, email, reminder service, AI tools. Note where each one stores and processes data, and whether its terms let it use your data for anything else.
2. Sort each tool with the table above. Write down the ones that need consent and the ones you'll keep client data out of.
3. Draft one consent per disclosure (or one multi-disclosure form where the client checks each recipient separately), and have counsel review it.
4. Send it with the engagement letter as its own document for e-signature, with the client typing their name.
5. Store the signed PDF in the client's file and record the recipient, purpose and expiry date in the client record.
6. Make every automation check that record first: no consent on file, no data sent to that tool. The work goes to a person instead.
7. Get a reminder a month before a consent expires, and ask the client again only if you still need it.

### What not to do
- Don't make the consent a condition of preparing the return. Under §301.7216-3 that makes it involuntary.
- Don't ask for consent after the fact. It must be signed before the data moves.
- Don't ask for consent to solicit non-tax business after you've handed the client the finished return, and don't ask again for a similar purpose after a client has said no.

### For illustration
For illustration: a three-person firm wants AI to read scanned 1099s. They keep client names and SSNs out of the AI step where they can, ask counsel about the vendor, and send a consent naming the vendor with each engagement letter. Clients who sign go through the AI step; clients who don't are keyed in by hand. A preparer checks every figure either way.

### How we would build it for you
Mike Automations builds workflows where AI only prepares and a person approves, and where client data goes only to tools you've cleared. A consent-on-file check is a normal part of that build. It starts with a free 15-minute call. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, built on the tools you already use, and it's usually live in 2-3 days. Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. We build the workflow; we don't give legal advice, so your counsel signs off on the consent wording.

### Can the consent sit inside my engagement letter?
For Form 1040 clients, no: Rev. Proc. 2013-14 requires a separate written document, though it can be attached to the engagement letter. For other returns, such as business returns, §301.7216-3 allows any format, including an engagement letter, as long as the content requirements are met.

### How long does a section 7216 consent last?
As long as the client specifies. If no duration is given on a Form 1040 consent, it is valid for one year from the date of signature.

## Records deadline clause in your engagement letter: wording and examples
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/records-cut-off-clause-engagement-letter/ (2026-11-10)

A records deadline clause in an engagement letter sets the date by which the client must send complete records, and says what happens if they arrive later: the work joins the queue in order of arrival, you can't promise to file before HMRC's deadline, and any rush work may cost extra. For Self Assessment, a date such as 31 October or 30 November leaves two to three months before the 31 January online deadline. Put the clause in the tax schedule of your professional body's template, state any late fee in plain words, and refer to it in every reminder.

A records deadline clause in your engagement letter turns "please send your records soon" into a date the client agreed to in writing. It doesn't make every client punctual. It does give you a fair basis for how you handle the ones who aren't: who goes first in January, whether rush work costs more, and who carries the risk of a penalty.
This post covers what the clause should say, where it sits in your letter, the options for late records, three example clauses to adapt, and how reminders tie back to it. It's for UK firms preparing Self Assessment returns, but the same approach works for year-end accounts and VAT.

### Why the date matters
For the 2025-26 tax year, gov.uk gives these deadlines: 31 October 2026 for a paper return, 30 December 2026 for an online return if the client wants any balance collected through their tax code, and 31 January 2027 for an online return and payment. Miss the filing deadline and HMRC charges an initial £100 late filing penalty, with more after three months.
Your cut-off date has to sit well before 31 January, because you need time to prepare the return, query gaps, get the client's approval and file. A date such as 31 October (the paper filing deadline) or 30 November gives you two to three months. Pick a date your team can actually work back from, and use the same date for every client in a group so your reminders stay simple.

### What the professional bodies provide
ICAEW's Technical Advisory Service publishes an engagement letters helpsheet with sample wording, revised with a summary of changes in March 2026. It splits a complete letter into the covering letter (Part 1), schedules for each service (Part 2, with schedule E for personal tax and E-B for clients in MTD for Income Tax), optional paragraphs (Part 3), terms of business (Part 4) and a privacy notice (Part 5). ICAEW says the helpsheet is best practice guidance, not a professional standard, that wording should be tailored with professional judgement, and that AI should be used with caution when tailoring letters. The sample wording downloads are for members.
ACCA offers UK members a free engagement letter pack for tax practitioners: a covering letter, schedules for specific services, standard terms and conditions, a privacy notice and cancellation notices for consumers. ACCA's guidance says the letter should set out the work to be done and the basis on which fees are charged.
So start from your own body's template. The records deadline belongs in the service schedule (what the client must provide and by when) with any fee consequence in your fees section or terms. If your template already has a paragraph on client responsibilities, adapt that rather than adding a separate clause that could contradict it. If you're unsure, check with your professional body or your professional indemnity insurer.

### What a good clause covers
- The date: a fixed calendar date each year, not "in good time".
- What "complete" means: all the records on your checklist, plus answers to your questions, not a first batch.
- How to send them: your portal, a named email address, or post.
- What happens after the date: work is done in order of arrival, and you can't guarantee filing by 31 January.
- Who carries the risk: penalties and interest that result from late records are the client's responsibility.
- Any extra fee: the amount or the basis, written plainly, so it's not a surprise later.
- Your side: that you'll tell the client promptly what's missing once their records arrive.

### Options when records arrive late
There's no single right answer. The table sets out the common approaches. Whatever you choose, state it in the letter before the work starts. With individual clients, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says an unfair term isn't binding on a consumer (section 62) and written terms must be transparent, in plain and intelligible language (section 68).
Approach | How it works | Good for | Watch out for
--- | --- | --- | ---
Queue only | Late records are worked on after on-time clients, no extra fee | Small firms with flexible January capacity | No real incentive to be on time
Fixed late fee | A set amount added if complete records arrive after the date | Firms that want a clear, simple rule | Must be in the letter and applied consistently
Tiered dates | Standard fee by the first date, a higher fee by a second date, best efforts after that | Firms with many January stragglers | More dates for clients to remember
Rush rate | Work after the date charged at a stated rate for the extra time | Complex returns | Harder to explain in advance
No guarantee after a final date | After, say, 10 January, you'll try but won't promise to file on time | Every firm, alongside one of the above | Tell the client in writing when you invoke it

### Three example clauses to adapt
These are examples written for this post, not wording from ICAEW, ACCA or any other body. Fit them into your own template, and check them with your professional body or insurer before you use them.
Example clauses to adapt (not professional body wording):
```
Example A: simple deadline, no fee
To allow us to prepare and file your Self Assessment tax return before the filing deadline, please send us complete records and answers to our questions by [31 October] each year. If we receive them after this date, we will deal with your return in order of the date your records are complete, and we cannot guarantee that it will be filed by 31 January. You remain responsible for any penalties or interest that arise from records reaching us late.

Example B: deadline with a late fee
Please send us complete records by [30 November] each year. "Complete" means everything on the checklist we send you in [April] and replies to any questions we raise. If complete records reach us after [30 November], an additional fee of [£ amount] (plus VAT) will apply to cover the extra work needed to meet the filing deadline. We will tell you promptly if anything is missing once your records arrive.

Example C: tiered dates
Our standard fee assumes complete records by [31 October]. If they arrive between [1 November] and [31 December], our fee will be [£ amount / % higher]. If they arrive after [31 December], we will do our best to file by 31 January but cannot guarantee it, and our fee will be [£ amount / % higher]. We will confirm in writing if your return is likely to be filed late, so that you can consider any payment on account.
```

### Make the reminders point to the clause
A clause works best when the client hears about the date more than once. Each reminder should name the date the client agreed to and what happens after it, in the same words as the letter.
Subject: Your records for your 2025-26 tax return: due [date]:
```
Hi [first name],

A quick reminder that, as set out in your engagement letter, we need your complete records for your 2025-26 tax return by [date].

You can upload them here: [portal link]. Your checklist is here: [checklist link].

If we receive them after [date], [we'll deal with your return in order of arrival / an additional fee of [£ amount] applies], and we can't guarantee filing by 31 January 2027.

If something is holding you up, just reply and tell us what's missing.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### How automation helps
1. Store each client's cut-off date and fee terms in the client record, taken from their signed letter.
2. Send the checklist in spring, then reminders at set points before the date (for example, six weeks, two weeks and three days).
3. Track what has arrived against the checklist, so "complete" is a fact, not a guess.
4. On the day after the cut-off, flag clients with incomplete records and draft the late-records notice for a person to check and send.
5. If a late fee applies, add it to the job so it isn't forgotten at billing time.

### For illustration
For illustration: a firm sets 31 October as its cut-off and a fixed late fee. On 1 November, its tracker shows 40 clients with incomplete records. Each gets an email, checked by a partner, quoting the clause and listing exactly what's missing. Clients who finish by mid-November are worked on next; the rest are told in writing that 31 January filing can't be guaranteed.

### How we would build it for you
Mike Automations builds the reminder and tracking side on the tools you already use: your practice software, email, portal and spreadsheets, where they allow a connection. It starts with a free 15-minute call. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, and it's usually live in 2-3 days. Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. The clause wording itself stays with you and your professional body.

### Can I charge a late records fee?
Yes, if it's agreed in the engagement letter before the work starts and written plainly. With individual clients, terms must be fair and transparent under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, so state the amount or basis clearly and apply it consistently.

### What date should the records cut-off be?
Work back from 31 January. Allow time to prepare, query gaps and get approval. A date such as 31 October or 30 November leaves two to three months before the online deadline.

### Do I need a new engagement letter to add the clause?
Usually you'd issue an updated letter or schedule and ask the client to accept it, as you would for any change of terms. Check your own template's wording on changes and your professional body's guidance.

## Texting clients for documents: when SMS and WhatsApp work, and the rules
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/text-or-whatsapp-clients-for-documents/ (2026-11-10)

Texting clients for documents works best as a short nudge that points to your secure upload link, not as the place where documents are sent. In the UK, a reminder with no promotional content is a service message, not direct marketing under PECR; in the US, the FCC requires the client's consent before you send automated texts to their mobile. Never ask for or accept ID numbers, bank details or tax documents in a text or WhatsApp chat.

Texting clients for documents is tempting because clients read texts and ignore email. A WhatsApp message that says "3 things still missing, upload here" often gets a response the same day, where the fourth email in a thread does not.
But a text thread is [a poor filing system](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/), and the rules on consent differ between the UK and the US. This guide covers when a text or WhatsApp message helps, what the rules say (checked on the regulators' own pages in November 2026), what should never go by text, and message templates you can copy.

### When a text or WhatsApp message helps
Use text as the nudge and your portal or upload link as the destination. The message tells the client [what is missing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/) and where to put it. The documents themselves go somewhere you control.
- The client has gone quiet on email. A text is a different channel, so it gets noticed.
- The ask is short: one or two named items, a link and a date.
- The deadline is close and you need an answer this week, not next month.
- The client is a sole trader or contractor who runs the business from their phone.
- You need a quick yes or no ("Did you sell any shares this year?"), not a document.

### When it doesn't
- The request is long. Ten items in a text get skimmed. Send the list by email or in the portal, and text a pointer to it.
- The client would need to reply with a document or a sensitive number. That belongs in your portal.
- You're explaining a tax position or giving advice. Put advice in writing in the client file, where it can be found later.
- The client has asked you not to text them. Respect it and note it on their record.
- You'd be messaging from a team member's personal phone. The thread then lives outside the firm.

### UK rules: PECR and UK GDPR
In the UK, the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) put consent rules on direct marketing sent by text, email or phone. The ICO's guidance says direct marketing doesn't include service messages: messages sent for purely administrative or customer service purposes with no advertising or promotional material. A reminder that a client's records are due is a service message.
The catch is mixing. The ICO also says that if a service message has elements of direct marketing, the whole message counts as direct marketing. So don't add "we also do payroll now" to the bottom of a document reminder. Keep reminders purely about the job.
[UK GDPR still applies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) to every text, because a mobile number and a client's tax affairs are personal data. Record why you hold the number, keep it accurate, and protect the conversation. If your firm is supervised under the Money Laundering Regulations, regulation 40 of the 2017 Regulations requires you to keep customer due diligence records for five years after the business relationship ends, so ID documents need to be in your file, not in a chat.

### US rules: TCPA consent and A2P 10DLC
In the US, the FCC's consumer guidance under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act says its rules ban texts sent to a mobile phone using an autodialer unless the phone owner gave consent first, or the message is for an emergency. The FCC says informational texts need consent that may be oral, while commercial texts need written consent. It also says people can opt out of any robotext at any time and in any reasonable manner, even if they consented before.
In practice: if your reminders are sent by software, get the client's agreement to text reminders in writing, for example a line in the engagement letter or onboarding form, and honor "STOP" or any other clear request to stop. Ask your counsel about anything beyond simple reminders.
There is also a carrier rule. If you send business texts to US numbers from an ordinary 10-digit US number through a texting service, the number has to be registered for [A2P 10DLC](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/) (application-to-person messaging over 10-digit long codes). Twilio's documentation says it blocks messages to US numbers sent from a +1 10DLC number that isn't linked to an approved campaign, and that both the brand and the campaign registration must be complete first. Other texting providers apply the same carrier rules, so check the steps in your own provider's help pages and allow time for approval.

### WhatsApp's own rules
WhatsApp has a policy on top of the law. The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy says you may only contact people who have given you their number and opted in to receive messages from you, and that you must respect any request to stop, on or off WhatsApp.
If you use the WhatsApp Business Platform (the API, which is what automated tools connect to), you can reply freely within the 24-hour customer service window that opens each time the client messages you. Outside that window you can only send approved message templates. So an automated reminder sequence on WhatsApp has to be built from templates that WhatsApp has approved first.

### What never goes by text
The WhatsApp policy itself says don't share or ask people to share full payment card numbers, financial account numbers, personal ID card numbers or other sensitive identifiers. That's a sensible rule for SMS too. In the US, the FTC's Safeguards Rule names tax preparation firms as covered, and requires a written information security program and encryption of customer information in transit. A text thread on a staff member's phone doesn't fit that plan.
Fine by text or WhatsApp | Never by text or WhatsApp
--- | ---
"3 items still missing for your 2025-26 return" | National Insurance numbers, UTRs or Social Security numbers
A link to your secure upload page | Bank account or card numbers
A due date and a reminder | Photos of passports or driving licences
A quick yes or no question | P60s, W-2s, 1099s or bank statements
"Your return is ready to approve, check the portal" | Login details, passwords or one-time codes
Booking a call | Tax advice or figures the client might rely on later

### Consent and record-keeping, step by step
1. Add a line to your engagement letter or onboarding form: the client agrees to receive reminders about their work by text or WhatsApp, at the number they give, and can stop at any time.
2. Record the number, the date they agreed and the channel (SMS, WhatsApp or both) on the client's record.
3. Send reminders from a firm number or business account, never a personal phone.
4. Keep reminders free of marketing. One message, one job.
5. If a client replies with a document anyway, save it to the client file, ask them to use the upload link next time, and delete it from the phone if your policy says so.
6. Copy any reply that changes the work ("I sold the flat in June") into the client file with the date.
7. When a client says stop, switch them to email the same day and note it.

### Message templates
Keep each message under about 300 characters, name the items, give one link and one date. Sign with the firm name so the client knows it's genuine.
First nudge (SMS or WhatsApp):
```
Hi [first name], it's [your name] at [firm]. We still need 3 things for your [tax year] return: [item 1], [item 2], [item 3]. Please upload them here by [date]: [secure link]. Reply STOP if you'd rather we only email.
```

### Follow-up, last call and consent check
Send the follow-up about a week after the first nudge, and the last call a few days before your own cut-off. Clients who reply with a question get a person, not another automated message.
- Follow-up: "Hi [first name], just [item 1] and [item 2] left now. Upload link: [secure link]. Due [date]. Thanks, [firm]."
- Last call: "Hi [first name], we need [item] by [date] to file on time. If you can't find it, reply and we'll tell you what else works. [firm]"
- Consent check (new client): "Hi [first name], this is [firm]. Is it OK if we text you reminders about documents for your account? Reply YES, or STOP and we'll stick to email."

### For illustration
For illustration: a practice emails its document request on 1 May and sends the first text nudge on 15 May to everyone still missing items. The text names the missing items and links to the portal. Replies with questions go to the client manager. Anything sent back by WhatsApp is saved to the client file the same day, and the client gets a short reply pointing them to the upload link for next time.

### How Mike Automations would build this
The parts worth automating are the list of what's missing per client, the timing of each nudge, the consent record, and stopping messages the moment a client uploads or says stop. A workflow can read your checklist or practice software, send the right text on the right day through a registered number or approved WhatsApp templates, and log every message against the client. A person still answers replies and decides what to chase.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you chase documents today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Do clients answer texts faster than emails?
Often, because a text is short and lands on the phone they carry. But it works best as a nudge to your upload link, not as a way to send documents.

### Do I need consent to text UK clients document reminders?
The ICO says purely administrative messages are service messages, not direct marketing, so PECR's marketing consent rules don't apply to them. Keep them free of promotional content, and handle the number under UK GDPR.

### Do I need consent to text US clients?
The FCC says automated texts to a mobile need prior consent, which may be oral for informational texts and must be written for commercial ones. Get it in writing in your engagement letter and honor any opt-out.

### Can clients send documents to me on WhatsApp?
They will try. Save anything they send to the client file and point them to your secure upload link. Never ask for ID numbers, bank details or ID photos by WhatsApp.

## BAS client records reminder schedule for BAS and tax agents (2026-27)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/bas-records-reminders-for-bas-agents/ (2026-11-10)

A BAS client records reminder schedule works back from the ATO lodgment program dates: for 2026-27, registered agents lodging electronically get until 25 November 2026 for quarter 1, 26 May 2027 for quarter 3 and (to be confirmed) 25 August 2027 for quarter 4, while quarter 2 stays at 28 February 2027 with no extra time. Ask for each quarter's records the day after it ends, set your own cut-off about four weeks before the due date, and send reminders that list only what's still missing.

A BAS client records reminder schedule is the simplest fix for the quarterly scramble: every client gets the same requests on the same dates, worked back from the date you actually have to lodge. Most BAS agents and tax agents know the dates. The hard part is [getting records in early enough](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-documents-on-time/) to reconcile, query and lodge without a last-week rush.
Below: the 2026-27 due dates the ATO publishes for registered agents, the conditions that decide whether a client gets the extra time, a quarter-by-quarter reminder table, and a client email you can copy.

### The 2026-27 due dates you work back from
The ATO's BAS agent lodgment program 2026-27 page sets out these dates for quarterly activity statements. The original due date is the 28th of the month after the quarter (28 February for quarter 2). The agent date applies to lodgment and payment when you lodge eligible statements electronically through Online services for agents or the Practitioner lodgment service (PLS). The registered agent lodgment program shows the same dates for tax agents.
Quarter | Period | Original due date | Registered agent due date (electronic)
--- | --- | --- | ---
Q4 2025-26 | April to June 2026 | 28 July 2026 | 25 August 2026
Q1 2026-27 | July to September 2026 | 28 October 2026 | 25 November 2026
Q2 2026-27 | October to December 2026 | 28 February 2027 | No concession: 28 February 2027
Q3 2026-27 | January to March 2027 | 28 April 2027 | 26 May 2027
Q4 2026-27 | April to June 2027 | 28 July 2027 | 25 August 2027 (the ATO says this is to be confirmed in the 2027-28 program)

### Which clients get the extra time
The concession isn't automatic for every client. Per the ATO's activity statements page, check these before you plan a client's chase around the later date:
- You lodge electronically. A quarterly statement lodged on paper doesn't get the lodgment program dates.
- The client's previous activity statement was lodged electronically. If it's their first statement, or the last one went in on paper, an earlier due date may apply.
- Your registered agent number (RAN) is on the client's activity statement account.
- The statement is eligible. It isn't if it includes a monthly PAYG instalment, if the client has a monthly GST cycle, or if it's a PAYG instalment consolidated head entity statement. Instalment notices (forms R, S and T) don't get the extra time either.
- Monthly activity statements are due on the 21st of the following month, with no agent concession, except the December statement: 21 February for business clients with turnover up to $10 million who report GST monthly and lodge electronically.

### When to ask for each quarter's records
The rule of thumb: request records the day after the quarter ends, and set your own cut-off about four weeks before the date you need to lodge. That leaves time to reconcile the bank feed, query the odd transaction, get PAYG withholding figures checked and have the client approve the BAS before it goes in.
Quarter 2 deserves its own plan. It has no agent concession, and it straddles Christmas and January, when many small businesses (and their bookkeepers) close for a few weeks. Send the heads-up before the break, not after it.
Quarter | Heads-up | Records request | Reminders | Your cut-off | Lodge by
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
Q1 (Jul to Sep 2026) | Mid-September | 1 October | Weekly from 8 October | 28 October | 25 November 2026
Q2 (Oct to Dec 2026) | Early December, before the break | 2 January (or first working day) | Weekly from 12 January | 30 January | 28 February 2027
Q3 (Jan to Mar 2027) | Mid-March | 1 April | Weekly from 8 April | 28 April | 26 May 2027
Q4 (Apr to Jun 2027) | Mid-June | 1 July | Weekly from 8 July | 28 July | 25 August 2027 (to be confirmed)

### A reminder workflow, step by step
1. Tag each client with their cycle (quarterly or monthly GST, PAYG withholding, PAYG instalments) and whether they qualify for the agent dates. This decides which row of the table they follow.
2. Two weeks before quarter end, send a short heads-up: what you'll need and where to upload it.
3. The day after quarter end, send each client their own list: missing supplier invoices, unexplained bank lines, cash sales, wages and super paid, and any new vehicle or asset purchases.
4. Where the bank feed already runs into Xero, MYOB or QuickBooks, ask only about uncoded or unclear transactions instead of asking for everything again.
5. Remind weekly. Each reminder [lists only what's still outstanding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/), and stops the moment the list is complete.
6. Keep one view for the team: ready to prepare, waiting on client, or close to the due date.
7. At your cut-off, a person phones anyone still outstanding and decides what happens next. Nothing is lodged without the client's approval.

### The email that goes out the day after quarter end
Subject: Your BAS for [July to September]: [N] items we need by [28 October]:
```
Hi [first name],

Your BAS quarter ended on [30 September]. To lodge on time we need a few things from you by [28 October]:

- [Supplier invoices for the 3 payments listed below]
- [What the $[amount] payment to [payee] on [date] was for]
- [Your cash sales total for the quarter]
- [Wages and super paid in September, if not already in the payroll software]

You can upload everything here, from your phone or computer: [upload link]

We'll prepare the BAS and send it to you to approve before we lodge. Your due date is [25 November]. Getting these to us by [28 October] gives us time to check everything properly.

Thanks,
[your name]
[practice name]
```

### What makes clients send records on time
- A personal list, not a generic "please send your BAS records".
- One upload link that works on a phone, with no login to remember.
- Your own cut-off date in every message, well before the ATO date.
- Specific questions about specific bank lines, which are quicker to answer than "send everything".
- Reminders that stop when the job is done, so clients don't learn to ignore them.

### For illustration
For illustration: a BAS agent has 50 quarterly clients, 44 of whom qualify for the agent dates. On 1 April each one gets a list for the January to March quarter. Six clients lodged on paper last quarter, so they're tagged for the 28 April date and chased first. By 28 April the agent can see 9 clients still waiting, and phones the 4 who haven't opened anything.
The same routine covers monthly clients and the annual tax return season, so it's worth building once. For New Zealand clients, the [IR3 extension of time records timeline](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ir3-extension-of-time-client-records-timeline-nz/) follows the same pattern. If you work in Xero, our post on [Xero automation ideas for practices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/xero-practice-automation-ideas/) shows where the bank feed can do some of the asking for you.

### How we would build it for you
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how your BAS chase works today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (Xero, MYOB or QuickBooks, your email and cloud storage, where they allow a connection) and is usually live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. You or your team still review and approve every BAS: the automation handles the requests, reminders and the list of who's ready.

### When is the quarter 1 2026-27 BAS due for agents?
The original due date is 28 October 2026. Registered agents lodging an eligible statement electronically get until 25 November 2026 for lodgment and payment, according to the ATO's 2026-27 lodgment program.

### Is there an agent concession for the quarter 2 BAS?
No. The ATO lists quarter 2 (October to December) as due on 28 February 2027 with no lodgment program concession, so it needs the earliest records request of the year.

### Why doesn't a client show the later due date?
Usually because their previous activity statement was lodged on paper, it's their first statement, your RAN isn't on their account, or the statement isn't eligible (for example a monthly GST cycle or a monthly PAYG instalment). Check the client's due dates in Online services for agents.

## IR3 extension of time: a client records timeline for NZ tax agents
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ir3-extension-of-time-client-records-timeline-nz/ (2026-11-10)

An IR3 extension of time (EOT) lets clients of a tax agent file their income tax return by 31 March of the following year instead of 7 July, and pay their end-of-year (terminal) tax by 7 April instead of 7 February, as long as the client is linked to the agent's client list. For the 2026 tax year that means 31 March 2027 for the return and 7 April 2027 for the payment. Inland Revenue expects agents to file progressively through the year, so request records in April and work to the interim filing targets rather than leaving it all to March.

The IR3 extension of time is the reason most New Zealand tax agents can spread their filing over a year. It's also the reason so many end up with a March crunch: when the deadline is 31 March, it's easy for clients to [send their records in February](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-documents-on-time/).
Below: what the EOT gives you and what it doesn't, the dates for the 2026 returns as Inland Revenue publishes them, a month-by-month records timeline, a client list check, and the email to send in April.

### 7 July or 31 March: which date applies
Inland Revenue says income tax returns must be filed by 7 July if no extension of time is granted. Clients of tax agents can be given an EOT to file up to 31 March the following year. The tax year runs from 1 April to 31 March, so for the 2026 tax year (1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026) the dates below apply. They assume a 31 March balance date; other balance dates shift them.
Client | 2026 IR3 due | End-of-year (terminal) tax due
--- | --- | ---
No tax agent, no EOT | 7 July 2026 | 7 February 2027
Client of a tax agent, with a valid EOT | 31 March 2027 | 7 April 2027

### The client must be linked to your agency
In an August 2026 news item, Inland Revenue said it had noticed some tax agents had not linked themselves or their associated entities to their client list, and that to receive an extension of time you must be linked to the tax agency. A client who isn't linked is on the 7 July date, and late filing penalties apply after it.
When you link a new client, Inland Revenue gives you an EOT for them unless they have more than one return outstanding. If a client has 2 or more unfiled returns when you link them, the EOT isn't automatic.

### The filing targets that sit behind 31 March
The EOT isn't a single March deadline. The Tax agents' EOT agreement (IR9XA, April 2026) sets guideline percentages for the filing period 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027:
- 40% of clients' returns filed by the second Friday in September (11 September 2026)
- 60% by the second Friday in November (13 November 2026)
- 80% by the second Friday in February (12 February 2027)
- 100% by 31 March 2027

### What happens if returns run late
- A client whose return isn't filed by 31 March may lose their EOT for the following tax year. Inland Revenue says it will contact the client if it doesn't hear from you.
- An agent that files less than 90% of required returns by the due date for 2 years may have its EOT withdrawn.
- If a client hasn't given you the information you need, you can ask Inland Revenue to send them a reminder (an "L letter") from the Intermediary Centre in myIR, between 1 August and 15 February.
- If a client can't file by 31 March through no fault of their own, you can request deferred status ("D status") between 1 August and 30 March, but only for a client with an existing EOT or an L letter.

### A client records timeline for the year
For illustration, based on the 2026-27 filing period. Move the dates to suit your client mix: many practices put simple returns (wage earners with one rental, sole traders on bank feeds) first and complex group work later.
When | What you do | Why
--- | --- | ---
Early April | Check every client is linked and has an EOT; flag anyone with 2+ returns outstanding | Unlinked clients are on 7 July
Mid-April | Send each client their own records list with one upload link | Records are freshest straight after 31 March
May to June | Weekly reminders listing only what's missing; file simple returns as they're ready | Builds towards the 40% target
Before 7 July | File any client without an EOT | Late filing penalties apply after 7 July
From 1 August | Request L letters for clients who still haven't sent records | The L letter window opens
11 September | 40% filed | IR9XA guideline
13 November | 60% filed | IR9XA guideline
Early December | Final call before the holidays: what's still missing and your January cut-off | Avoids losing January
12 February | 80% filed; last L letters by 15 February | IR9XA guideline
By 30 March | Request D status for any genuine exception | Last day for D status requests
31 March | 100% filed | EOT due date
7 April | End-of-year tax paid by EOT clients | Payment due date with an EOT

### Client list check before you send anything
1. Export the client list report from myIR and compare it with your practice software.
2. Mark anyone not linked to your agency, and link them, or plan to file them by 7 July.
3. Mark clients with 2 or more returns outstanding: their EOT isn't automatic.
4. Tag each remaining client by return type (IR3 with rental, IR3 self-employed, company, trust) so [requests and reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) say the right things.
5. Note who needed an L letter or D status last year. They're the ones to start with.

### The email that goes out in April
Subject: Your 2026 tax return: [N] items we need by [31 May]:
```
Kia ora [first name],

The 2026 tax year ended on 31 March. To prepare your return we need a few things from you by [31 May]:

- [Bank statements for your business account, 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026]
- [Rental income and expenses, including rates, insurance and repairs]
- [What the $[amount] payment to [payee] on [date] was for]

You can upload everything here, from your phone or computer: [upload link]

Because you're a client of ours, your return isn't due until [31 March 2027] and any tax to pay until [7 April 2027]. Sending records now means we can tell you early if you have tax to pay, instead of in March.

Ngā mihi,
[your name]
[practice name]
```

### How we would build it for you
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how your records chase works today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (Xero, MYOB, your email and cloud storage, where they allow a connection) and is usually live in 2-3 days: each client's records list goes out in April, reminders list only what's missing, and your team sees who's ready, who's waiting and who needs an L letter. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. A person on your team still decides on every L letter, D status request and return.

### When is an IR3 due with a tax agent's extension of time?
By 31 March of the following year. For the 2026 tax year that's 31 March 2027, with end-of-year (terminal) tax due by 7 April 2027. Without an EOT the return is due by 7 July 2026.

### Why would a tax agent's client be on the 7 July date?
Most often because they're not linked to the agent's client list in myIR, or because they had 2 or more returns outstanding when the agent linked them, so no automatic EOT was given.

### What is an L letter?
A reminder Inland Revenue sends, at the tax agent's request, to a client who hasn't provided the information needed for their return. Agents can request it in myIR between 1 August and 15 February for clients with a current EOT.

## T1 tax season document collection: what to request from Canadian clients, and when
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/t1-tax-season-document-collection-canada/ (2026-11-10)

T1 tax season document collection in Canada means getting each client's T-slips (T4, T4A, T5, T3 and others) and receipts in before you can file their T1 return. Most slip issuers must send slips by the end of February, T1 returns for the 2026 tax year are due April 30, 2027, and self-employed clients (or their spouses) have until June 15, 2027 to file but must still pay any balance by April 30. A practice should request documents by client type in January and chase what's missing from early March.

T1 tax season document collection is the part of a Canadian practice's year that eats the most time and earns the least. You can't file a T1 return until the slips and receipts are in, and clients don't know which ones they're waiting for.
This post sets out the dates for the 2026 tax year (returns filed in 2027), what to ask each type of client for, and an email you can send in January. The rules come from canada.ca, checked on November 10, 2026. CRA hadn't yet published its dates page for the 2026 tax year, so the 2027 dates below are worked out from the rules it states every year. Check them again in January.

### The key dates for the 2026 tax year
CRA's "Preparing to do your taxes" page says a return is usually due on or before April 30 of the following year, or by June 15 if the person or their spouse or common-law partner was self-employed. Any balance owing is due no later than April 30 for everyone, self-employed or not. That last point is the one clients miss: June 15 is a filing date, not a payment date.
If a due date falls on a weekend or a CRA-recognized public holiday, CRA treats a return as on time if it's received or postmarked on the next business day. For payments, CRA says the first business day after the due date.
Date (2027) | What happens | What it means for your requests
--- | --- | ---
Early January | Your request goes out | Send each client a list built for their situation
March 1 (Monday) | Last day of February falls on Sunday, February 28, so T4, T4A and T5 returns are on time if CRA gets them by the next business day | Most employment, pension and investment slips should be with clients by now
March 1 | End of the first 60 days of 2027: RRSP contribution deadline for the 2026 tax year, by our count (CRA's 2027 date not yet published) | Ask for RRSP receipts after this date, including contributions made in January and February
March 31 | T3 slips for calendar-year trusts: CRA says T3 slips and the T3 Summary are due 90 days after the trust's year end | Mutual fund and trust slips often arrive last. Don't wait for them before asking for everything else
April 30 (Friday) | T1 filing deadline for most people, and the payment deadline for everyone | Self-employed clients still need a balance estimate by now
June 15 (Tuesday) | T1 filing deadline if the client or their spouse or common-law partner was self-employed | Business records for the T2125 are the long pole here

### Why a single generic list doesn't work
A retired couple with a RRIF and a salaried employee with a side business need very different things from you. A generic list of 40 items makes both of them guess, and guessing is how you end up with half a pile in April. It works better to sort clients into a few types once, then send each type only what applies, with last year's slips as a prompt.
Last year's return is your best checklist. If a client had a T5 from a bank last year, ask for it by name this year. If a slip doesn't come back, ask whether the account was closed, rather than assuming it was forgotten.

### Checklist by client type
The slip names below are CRA's. Slips that issuers file with CRA also show up in the client's CRA account, and CRA's list of services for representatives of individuals says authorized representatives at every level can view tax information slips. That makes CRA a useful cross-check, though not a replacement for asking the client.
Client type | Slips to request | Receipts and records to request
--- | --- | ---
Employee | T4 from every employer; T4E if they received EI | RRSP receipts, charitable donations, medical expenses, child care, union or professional dues not on the T4
Student or parent of one | T2202 tuition slip; T4A for scholarships or RESP payments | Moving receipts if they moved for school; who will claim unused tuition
Investor | T5, T3, T5008 from each bank or brokerage | Year-end statements for any account with no slip; capital property sales and purchase costs
Retired | T4A(P) for CPP, T4A(OAS), T4A for pensions, T4RIF or T4RSP | Pension splitting decision with spouse; medical and donation receipts
Self-employed (sole proprietor) | T4A for any fees or commissions paid to them; T5018 for construction subcontracting | Income and expense records for the T2125, vehicle log, home office costs, GST/HST returns filed, instalments paid
Landlord | T5 or T3 if rent is held through an investment | Rent received, mortgage interest, property tax, insurance, repairs, and capital items bought, for form T776
Anyone with a life change | Slips from a new employer or a closed account | Marriage, separation, new child, move, death in the family: one line each, so you know what to ask next

### A January request email you can copy
Email to a returning T1 client:
```
Subject: Your 2026 tax return: what we need from you

Hi [First name],

It's time to start your 2026 tax return. Here's what we need, based on your return last year:

[List of slips by issuer, e.g. T4 from ABC Ltd., T5 from XYZ Bank, RRSP receipt from DEF Investments]
[List of receipts, e.g. medical, donations, child care]

Most slips arrive by early March. Please send each one as soon as you have it, by uploading here: [link]. You don't need to wait until you have everything.

If anything changed in 2026 (a new job, a closed account, a move, a marriage or separation, a new child, starting a business), reply and tell us in a line or two.

Key dates:
- Your return is due April 30, 2027 [or June 15, 2027 if you or your spouse were self-employed].
- Any balance owing is due April 30, 2027 in every case.

We'd like everything by [your internal cut-off date] so we have time to do it properly.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Practice name]
```

### A chasing schedule that matches when slips arrive
1. Early January: send the request email above, built from last year's return, with an upload link.
2. When a document arrives: tick it off and reply with what's still outstanding, by name.
3. First week of March: most T4, T4A and T5 slips should exist by now. Send each client a short "still waiting for" list.
4. First week of April: T3 slips should be out. [Remind once more](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/), and for self-employed clients ask for a figure to estimate the balance due April 30.
5. Mid-April: call the clients who haven't sent anything. Decide with them whether you'll file by April 30 or they'll pay an estimate on time.
6. After April 30: switch the self-employed clients to a June 15 schedule with one reminder in mid-May.

### Rules to build into the process
- Never tell a self-employed client they have until June 15 without also saying payment is due April 30.
- Ask for slips by issuer name, not by slip type. "T5 from XYZ Bank" gets a faster answer than "all T5s".
- Treat a missing slip from last year as a question, not an omission. The account may have closed.
- Get your [representative authorization](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/cra-represent-a-client-authorization-new-clients/) in place before the season, so you can check slips in CRA's system. New clients take the longest, see our post on CRA authorization.
- CRA says to keep supporting documents for 6 years. Tell clients what you keep and what they should keep.

### What to automate, and what stays with a person
Most of this is mechanical: building each client's list from last year, sending it, logging what arrives, and sending the "still waiting for" list on the dates above. A workflow can do that from your existing email, shared drive and a spreadsheet or practice software, and give you one morning list of who's complete, who's [partial](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/) and who's sent nothing.
The judgement stays with you: what a life change means for the return, whether a client is self-employed for the June 15 date, and what goes to CRA. A workflow should never file or decide anything on its own.
