A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you collect T1 documents today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. It costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### When is the T1 deadline for the 2026 tax year?
Based on CRA's standing rules, April 30, 2027 for most people, and June 15, 2027 if the person or their spouse or common-law partner was self-employed. Any balance owing is due April 30, 2027 for everyone. CRA hadn't published its 2026 tax year dates page when we checked on November 10, 2026.

### When do clients get their T4 and T5 slips?
CRA says issuers must generally provide slips before March 1 of the following year. T3 slips from trusts and mutual funds can come later: CRA's due date is 90 days after the trust's year end, which is March 31 for a calendar-year trust.

### Can I see a client's slips in CRA's system?
Yes, once the client has authorized you. CRA's list of Represent a Client services for individuals says representatives at every authorization level can view tax information slips. Slips that issuers file late or never file won't be there, so still ask the client.

## How new clients authorize a representative with the CRA: a step list for bookkeepers and accountants
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/cra-represent-a-client-authorization-new-clients/ (2026-11-10)

To authorize a representative with the CRA, a client either adds the representative's RepID, GroupID or business number in their own CRA account (My Account or My Business Account), or confirms an authorization request the representative submits through Represent a Client, which CRA says may need to happen within 10 business days. Form AUT-01 gives offline access only (phone, mail, fax, in person), not online access. For a new client, the fastest route is usually to send them your RepID with short instructions and track who hasn't done it.

Getting a new client to authorize a representative with the CRA is a small task that stalls a surprising amount of work. Until it's done you can't see [their slips](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/t1-tax-season-document-collection-canada/), their notice of assessment or their business accounts, and the client usually doesn't know what a RepID is.
This post sets out the routes CRA offers, as canada.ca describes them (checked on November 10, 2026), which one to ask for, and a client email and onboarding steps you can copy.

### Your identifier: RepID, GroupID or BN
CRA's help pages for representatives list three identifiers a client can use to authorize you. You get a RepID when you register with Represent a Client. A GroupID authorizes a group of representatives. A business number (BN) registered with Represent a Client authorizes all the employees of that business.
For a small practice, the choice matters later more than now. If the client authorizes your personal RepID, a colleague can't pick up the file without a second authorization. If several people work on files, a GroupID or the practice's BN avoids that. Decide which identifier your practice gives out and use it on every client email.

### The routes CRA offers, and which to ask for
CRA's "Authorize a representative: How to give authorization" page (updated June 30, 2026) lists the routes by account type. The main ones for individuals and businesses are below.
Route | Who does what | Good for | Watch out for
--- | --- | --- | ---
Client adds you in their CRA account | Client signs in to My Account or My Business Account, goes to Profile, selects Add under authorized representatives, and enters your identifier | Clients who already use their CRA account. CRA calls it the fastest route | Client must already be registered. Many aren't
You submit a request in Represent a Client, client confirms | You add the authorization; the client confirms or denies it in their CRA account | Most new clients: you control the details, they just approve | CRA says the client may need to confirm within 10 business days
You submit a request using the client's tax information (individuals only) | You enter details from a notice of assessment for a return processed at least six months ago, and the client signs a signature page | Individuals who can't or won't register for My Account | The signed signature page has to be submitted within 30 business days, according to CRA's brochure
EFILE (businesses) | A registered electronic filer in good standing submits it through CRA-certified software | Practices that already EFILE | Keep the signed page for six years; don't send it unless CRA asks
Form AUT-01 by mail or fax | Client completes and signs the form; it's sent to CRA | Offline access only: phone, mail, fax, in person | Gives no online access. Must reach CRA within six months of being signed. One form per representative

### Levels of access and expiry
CRA's "Level of access you can give" page sets out the levels. Level 1 allows access to information only. Level 2 allows access to information and to make certain account changes. Business accounts also have Level 3, which adds delegated authority: a Level 3 representative may authorize other representatives for the business.
When you submit a request in Represent a Client, you choose the level, an expiry date (or "Does not expire"), and for a business, the program accounts you need, such as income tax, GST/HST or payroll. Ask for what the engagement needs and no more. A bookkeeper doing monthly records may only need Level 1 on some accounts; a practice filing returns and handling reassessments usually needs Level 2.

### Step list: authorizing a new client through Represent a Client
1. Before you send anything, confirm [the engagement is signed](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/) and decide the level, expiry date and (for businesses) the program accounts.
2. Sign in to your CRA account, open your Representative account and select Authorization request.
3. Choose your identifier (RepID, GroupID or BN) and the type of client, then select Add authorization.
4. Enter the client's identifying information. For an individual, choose a confirmation method: the client confirms in My Account, or you provide tax information from a notice of assessment processed at least six months ago.
5. Add the level of authorization and the expiry date, and for a business, the program accounts. Select Confirm.
6. If a signature page is needed, print it, get the client's signature and submit it in Authorization request.
7. Send the client the email below the same day, so they know a request is waiting.
8. Check the pending request after 3 business days and again after 7. If the client hasn't confirmed, call them. CRA may also call the client to confirm the request.
9. Once authorized, note the level, accounts and expiry date in your client record, with a reminder before the expiry date.

### A client instruction email you can copy
Email to a new client: confirm our CRA authorization:
```
Subject: One step so we can work with the CRA for you

Hi [First name],

To look after your [personal taxes / business accounts], we need your permission with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). This lets us see your tax slips and account information and speak to the CRA for you. You can remove it at any time.

We've sent the CRA a request today. Here's what to do:

1. Sign in to your CRA account at canada.ca: [My Account for individuals / My Business Account for businesses].
2. You'll see a pending request from [Practice name]. Check that the details match: [level of access, accounts, expiry date].
3. Select Confirm.

Please do this within the next few days. The CRA may need you to confirm within 10 business days.

If you'd rather add us yourself, go to Profile, then select Add under authorized representatives, and enter our [RepID / GroupID / business number]: [identifier].

If you don't have a CRA account and don't want one, reply and we'll use another option.

The CRA may phone you to confirm this request. That's normal.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Practice name]
```

### Tracking who hasn't confirmed
The request isn't the hard part. Knowing which of your [new clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/) still haven't confirmed is. A simple tracker with one row per client and account solves it.
Column | What goes in it
--- | ---
Client and account | Individual, or business and program account
Route | Client adds us / RAC request with confirmation / tax information / EFILE / AUT-01
Level and expiry | Level 1, 2 or 3, and the date or "does not expire"
Request date | When you submitted it
Confirm by | 10 business days after the request, for requests the client must confirm
Signature page | Needed? Date received and date submitted
Status | Pending, confirmed, denied, expired, cancelled
Next action | Who does what, by when

### Rules practices often miss
- AUT-01 does not give you online access. If you need to see slips and accounts online, it's the wrong form.
- A separate AUT-01 is needed for each representative, and CRA must receive it within six months of the date it was signed.
- For sole proprietors, CRA says confirmation may not be needed if certain conditions are met. Don't assume it; check the request status.
- When a client leaves, they can cancel your authorization online or with Form AUT-01X. Remove your own access when the engagement ends, too.
- Expiry dates come round quietly. Put each one in your calendar with a month's notice.

### What to automate, and what stays with a person
The routine parts are easy to automate: sending the instruction email when an engagement is signed, adding a row to the tracker, reminding the client on day 3 and day 7, flagging anyone past their confirm-by date for a call, and warning you a month before an authorization expires.
Submitting the request in Represent a Client, choosing the level and accounts, and anything the client signs stay with a person in your practice. A workflow should never sign in to CRA or submit anything on its own.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you onboard new clients today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (your email, a spreadsheet or practice software, your calendar), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. It costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does Form AUT-01 give my accountant online access?
No. CRA says AUT-01 gives a representative offline access only, by phone, fax, mail or in person. For online access the client authorizes the representative in their CRA account, or confirms a request made through Represent a Client.

### How long does a client have to confirm a Represent a Client request?
CRA's help for representatives says the client may need to sign in and confirm within 10 business days. If you submit an individual's request using tax information from their notice of assessment, CRA says there's no waiting period for confirmation.

### What's the difference between a RepID, GroupID and BN?
A RepID identifies one representative and comes with registering for Represent a Client. A GroupID authorizes a group of representatives. A business number registered with Represent a Client authorizes all the employees of that business.

## Form 11 Pay and File: a records timeline for agents (2027 season)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/form-11-pay-and-file-records-timeline-ireland/ (2026-11-10)

Form 11 Pay and File is the 31 October deadline in Ireland when a self-assessed taxpayer files the previous year's return, pays any balance of tax for that year and pays preliminary tax for the current year. Revenue extends the date for people who both pay and file through ROS: in 2026 the extended date was 18 November 2026 (Revenue eBrief 034/26). For the 2027 season, agents should request 2026 records from January, once employment details are available in myAccount, and set a records cut-off in early September.

Form 11 Pay and File puts three things on one date: the return for last year, the balance of last year's tax and preliminary tax for this year. For an agent, the hard part isn't the filing. It's [getting complete records from every client](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-documents-on-time/) early enough to prepare, review and agree the figures before the deadline, while every other practice in the country is doing the same.
This post sets out what Revenue says is due, how the ROS extension works and where it catches people out, what preliminary tax means for your records request, and a month-by-month timeline for the 2027 season (2026 returns). The Revenue facts were checked on revenue.ie in November 2026. Dates for 2027 are not confirmed yet, so treat them as the standard rule until Revenue publishes the year's eBrief.

### What's due on Pay and File
Revenue's guide to self-assessment says that by 31 October you must do three things. For the 2026 season it gives the example below; the 2027 season follows the same pattern one year on.
What | 2026 season (Revenue) | 2027 season (standard rule)
--- | --- | ---
File the Form 11 for the previous year | 2025 return by 31 October 2026 | 2026 return by 31 October 2027
Pay any balance of tax for the previous year | 2025 balance | 2026 balance
Pay preliminary tax for the current year | 2026 preliminary tax | 2027 preliminary tax
ROS extension (pay and file through ROS) | 18 November 2026 (eBrief 034/26) | Not announced yet

### The ROS extension, and the catch
Revenue extends Pay and File for people who use ROS, and announces it in an eBrief. For 2026 it was eBrief 034/26, published on 16 February 2026, which moved the date to Wednesday 18 November 2026 for customers who file a 2025 Form 11 and pay, through ROS, both the 2025 balance and 2026 preliminary tax.
The catch is in one line of the eBrief: to qualify, customers must both pay and file through ROS. If only one of the two is done through ROS, the extension does not apply, and the deadline for both the return and the payment is 31 October. A client who pays outside ROS, or who sends a paper return, is back on 31 October.
Two planning points follow. First, don't build your 2027 plan around an extension Revenue hasn't announced: plan to 31 October 2027 and treat any extension as breathing space for review, not as extra time for clients to send records. Second, 31 October 2027 falls on a Sunday, so check the exact dates in Revenue's 2027 eBrief before you put them in client letters.

### Preliminary tax: what your records request needs to cover
Revenue's preliminary tax page says it must be paid by 31 October of the tax year in question, and that the amount must be at least the lowest of: 90% of the tax due for that year, 100% of the tax due for the previous year, or 105% of the tax due for the year before that. The 105% option only applies where the client pays by direct debit, and not where that earlier year's tax was nil. In the first year in self-assessment, the client can choose 100% of the previous year (usually nothing) or 90% of the current year. Revenue charges interest for each day, or part of a day, that a payment is late.
For your records timeline, this means the request has two halves. The 2026 records let you finish the return and the balance. But if a client's income has dropped and they want to pay on the 90% basis, you also need year-to-date 2027 figures in the autumn. Ask for them separately, in September, so they're current.

### A records timeline for the 2027 season
This is a suggested plan for 2026 returns, not a Revenue rule. Move the dates to suit your practice, but keep the order: request early, [remind on a rhythm](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/), set a cut-off, and keep October for review, agreement and payment.
When | What to send or do | Who it's for
--- | --- | ---
January 2027 | Short heads-up: 2026 has closed, here's your list and upload link. Revenue says the Employment Detail Summary for 2026 is available in January | All Form 11 clients
February to March | Full records request with each client's own list: trading records, rental income and expenses, pension contributions, medical expenses, capital gains | All clients
When Revenue's eBrief is out | Check the 2027 dates and conditions, and update your letters | Your team
April to May | Reminder listing only what's still missing | Partial and silent clients
June | Second reminder with your records cut-off date in the first line | Partial and silent clients
Early September (your cut-off) | Final reminder; ask for year-to-date 2027 figures from anyone using the 90% preliminary tax basis | Everyone not yet complete
September to mid-October | Draft returns and the tax figure out for approval, with the amount to pay and how | Complete clients
Mid to late October | Phone calls, not emails, to anyone not yet approved; confirm who pays through ROS | The last stragglers
By 31 October (or the ROS date) | File and pay. Clients who won't pay through ROS go on the 31 October list | Everyone

### A records request email you can copy
Form 11 records request (January to March):
```
Subject: Your 2026 tax return: what we need from you

Hi [first name],

It's time to start your 2026 Form 11. To have it ready well before Pay and File on 31 October 2027, we need your records by [cut-off date].

Here's what we need from you:
[client's own list, for example: sales and expenses for 2026, bank statements for the business account, rental income and expenses, pension contribution certificates, receipts for medical expenses]

Upload everything here: [upload link]

If something won't be ready by [cut-off date], reply and tell us which item and when you expect it. We'll plan around it.

Thanks,
[name]
```

### What a late Form 11 costs your client
Use the real cost in your later reminders. Revenue's guide to self-assessment says a return filed less than two months after the filing date gets a surcharge of 5% of the tax due, up to €12,695. A return filed more than two months late gets 10%, up to €63,485. Revenue also notes that a 10% surcharge can apply if Local Property Tax obligations aren't met, even when the income tax return was on time, so it's worth a line in your checklist. Late payment adds daily interest on top.

### For illustration: one practice's cut-off
For illustration: a two-person practice files 120 Form 11 returns. Together they can prepare and review about 15 a week alongside their other work. If every record arrived on the same day, they'd need eight weeks, so the last records must arrive by early September to leave October for client approvals and payment.
They publish a cut-off of 5 September, knowing a handful of clients will still be late. Anyone who sends records after that goes into a later slot, with a late-records fee only if their engagement letter sets one out. They don't count on the ROS extension: if it comes, it's used for review.

### How Mike Automations would build this
A timeline only works if every request and reminder goes out on the right date to the right clients, and stops when they're complete. Doing that by hand for 120 clients is what eats the autumn. A workflow can send each message on your dates, list only what each client still owes, file what arrives into the right folder, and give you a morning list of who's complete, [partial](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/clients-who-send-some-documents-but-not-all/) or silent, plus who has said they'll pay outside ROS.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about your season. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your email, your shared drive or practice software where it allows a connection, and your client list), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. Every message uses wording you approved, and nothing is filed with Revenue by the automation: that stays with you.

### What is due on Form 11 Pay and File?
By 31 October, a self-assessed taxpayer must file the previous year's return, pay any balance of tax for that year and pay preliminary tax for the current year, according to Revenue's guide to self-assessment.

### Who gets the ROS extension?
Only people who both pay and file through ROS. Revenue eBrief 034/26 says that if only one is done through ROS, the extension does not apply and the deadline is 31 October. In 2026 the extended date was 18 November 2026.

### When should an agent request Form 11 records?
Start in January, when Revenue says the Employment Detail Summary is available, send the full request by March, and set a records cut-off in early September so October is free for review, approval and payment.

## An agency client approval workflow that gets sign-off on time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/agency-client-approvals/ (2026-11-10)

An agency client approval workflow is a fixed path every piece of work follows from internal review to written client sign-off: one named approver per client, one place to review, a set number of revision rounds and a deadline for each response. Reminders go out on fixed days, late approvals are escalated to an agreed contact, and every approval is logged with who approved which version and when.

An agency client approval workflow decides whether your timeline holds. The work is often done on time; it's the sign-off that slips. A draft sits in a client's inbox for a week, three people reply with different notes, and the launch date moves while your team waits.
This guide sets out a workflow you can run for marketing, design, content or video work, a reminder sequence, a sign-off message to copy, and an approvals log that settles "who said yes to this?" for good. It works for [UK and US agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agencies/), and with the tools you already use. If monthly reporting is the bigger time sink, see [client reporting automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-reporting-automation/).

### Why client approvals stall
- Nobody on the client side owns the decision, so everyone comments and no one approves.
- Feedback arrives by email, Slack, a call and comments in the file, and some of it conflicts.
- The request doesn't say what kind of answer you need or by when.
- Revision rounds were never agreed, so "one more small change" never ends.
- There's no record of which version was approved, so a later complaint is hard to answer.

### Agree the rules at onboarding
Most approval problems are fixed before the first draft. Put these in the proposal or statement of work, and repeat them in the kick-off email, so the client has agreed to them before anything is late.
- One named approver per client, plus one backup for holidays. Others may comment; only the approver signs off.
- One place to review: a shared folder, a proofing tool or your project tool. Feedback sent elsewhere gets copied there before work starts.
- Response time: for example, two working days for a social post, five for a website page.
- Revision rounds included (two is common), and what happens after that: a change request with its own price or time.
- What happens when an approval is late: the delivery date moves by the same number of days. If you want silence to count as approval, that must be written into the contract and agreed in advance; check the wording with your own lawyer.

### The approval workflow, step by step
1. Internal review: a second person checks the work against the brief before the client sees it.
2. Send for approval: upload the version to the review place, with a version number in the file name (v1, v2).
3. Send the approval request to the named approver: what to review, the type of answer needed, and the due date.
4. Collect feedback in one place. If notes conflict, ask the approver to decide; don't pick for them.
5. Revise once per round, using a consolidated list of changes, and send the next version.
6. Get a written sign-off that names the version: "Approved v2".
7. Log it: who approved, which version, the date and where the approval is saved.
8. Lock or archive the approved file so later edits can't be mistaken for the approved version.

### The reminder sequence
Send reminders on fixed days so nobody has to remember. Each one gets shorter and more specific. The working days below are an example for work with a two-day response time; stretch them for bigger pieces.
When | Who gets it | Message
--- | --- | ---
Day 0 | Approver | The approval request: what, where, answer needed, due date.
Due date morning | Approver | A short reminder that the review is due today, with the link.
1 working day late | Approver | "Still waiting on your sign-off. The [launch] date depends on it."
2 working days late | Approver and backup | A note that the date will move if there's no answer by [day], and the new date.
3 working days late | Account lead | A phone call or meeting request. A person handles it from here.
After approval | Approver and team | Confirmation of what was approved, the version and the next step.

### Sign-off request template
Make it easy to answer in one line. The client should know exactly what "approved" means and what happens next.
Approval request (email or project-tool message):
```
Subject: Approval needed by [day, date]: [deliverable] v[number]

Hi [first name],

[Deliverable] v[number] is ready for your review: [link]

Please reply with one of these by [day, date]:
1. Approved: we'll go ahead with [next step].
2. Approved with the small changes listed: we'll make them and go ahead.
3. Changes needed: please add your notes in [review place]. This is revision round [x] of [y].

To keep [launch date], we need your answer by [day, date]. If it comes later, the launch moves by the same number of days.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### The confirmation message
When the approval comes in, reply the same day with a short confirmation. It turns a casual "looks good" into a clear record.
"Thanks [first name]. Confirming you've approved [deliverable] v[number] on [date]. We'll now [next step] and [deliver / publish] on [date]. Any changes from here are a new request."

### The approvals log
Keep one log per client, in a spreadsheet or your project tool. It answers disputes in seconds and shows which clients are slowing projects down. The rows below are for illustration.
Deliverable | Version | Sent | Due | Approver | Status | Approved on | Where saved
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
Homepage copy | v2 | 3 Nov | 5 Nov | J. Smith | Approved | 5 Nov | Email, filed to project
November social posts | v1 | 4 Nov | 6 Nov | J. Smith | Changes requested (round 1 of 2) |  | Review folder comments
Launch video edit | v3 | 6 Nov | 11 Nov | A. Patel (backup) | Waiting, reminder sent |  | 

### Tools that can do part of this
You don't need a special system to start. A shared folder, a version number in each file name, a project tool and a spreadsheet log will run this workflow. Proofing tools add comments on the file and an approve button, which helps for design and video.
Google Drive has a built-in approvals feature, but Google's help centre says it's only available on Enterprise and Education Plus plans, so many small agencies won't have it. Check your own plan before building around it.

### Where automation helps
The parts that eat time are sending each reminder on the right day, noticing which approvals are late, and keeping the log current. A workflow can send the approval request when a file is marked ready, follow the reminder sequence, stop the moment the client approves, flag late approvals to the account lead, and write each sign-off into the log with the version and date. The account lead still handles the conversations, and a person always decides when a date moves.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how approvals work in your agency today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### What is a client approval workflow for an agency?
A fixed path from internal review to written client sign-off: one named approver, one review place, agreed revision rounds, response deadlines, reminders and a log of who approved which version and when.

### How do I get clients to approve work faster?
Agree one approver and response times [at onboarding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-onboarding-automation/), send a request that says exactly what answer you need and by when, and remind on fixed days with the effect on the launch date.

### Does silence count as client approval?
Only if your contract says so and the client agreed in advance. Otherwise, treat no answer as no approval and move the delivery date. Check contract wording with your own lawyer.

### How many revision rounds should an agency include?
Two is common, but the number matters less than agreeing it in writing before work starts, along with what happens after the included rounds.

## A process map template for a small business (free, with an example)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/ (2026-11-10)

A process map template for a small business is a one-page table that lists every step of one process in order, with who does it, which tool they use, how long the work waits before the next step, and what goes wrong. Fill it in from a real recent case, not from how the process should work. The waits and the exceptions show you what is worth automating and what should stay with a person.

A process map template for a small business doesn't need boxes, arrows or special software. It needs one honest table: what happens, in what order, who does it, in which tool, how long things sit, and where it goes wrong. You can fill it in with a pen in half an hour, and it's the most useful thing you can do before you automate anything.
Below: why mapping comes first, the template to copy, how to fill it in, a filled-in example, and how to read the finished map to decide what to automate first.

### Why map a process before you automate it
Automating a process you haven't mapped usually means automating the tidy version in your head. The real version has a step where someone copies a phone number from an email into a spreadsheet, a client who always replies on WhatsApp instead, and a job that sits for three days because the person who approves it is on site. Those are the places an automation breaks, and also the places it saves the most time.
A map also stops you automating the wrong thing. Often the biggest delay isn't a task at all. It's a wait: a quote sitting in a draft folder, or an invoice nobody sends until Friday. You only see that when you write the waits down.

### Pick one process and fix its start and end
Map one process at a time. Choose something that happens at least weekly and that someone complains about. Then write two lines before anything else:
- Starts when: the event that kicks it off ("a new enquiry arrives by phone, email or web form")
- Ends when: the point where it's finished ("the job is booked in the calendar and the client has a confirmation")
- If you can't say both in one sentence each, the process is too big. Split it

### The process map template
Copy this into a document or spreadsheet. One row per step. Keep each step to a single action by a single person or system.
Process map template (copy and fill in):
```
Process name: [for example: new enquiry to booked job]
Starts when: [the trigger]
Ends when: [what finished looks like]
How often: [times per week or month]
Mapped from: [a real recent case, with the date]

Step | What happens | Who | Tool | Wait before next step | What goes wrong (exceptions)
1 | | | | |
2 | | | | |
3 | | | | |
4 | | | | |
5 | | | | |
6 | | | | |

Decisions a person must make: [list them]
Information that gets typed twice: [list it]
What "done well" means: [one sentence you could check]
```
Column | What to write | Why it matters
--- | --- | ---
What happens | One action, starting with a verb: "send quote", "check calendar" | Vague steps hide the real work
Who | A name or role, or "the system" | Shows hand-offs, where things get dropped
Tool | Where it happens: email, WhatsApp, spreadsheet, accounting software, paper | Shows what can connect and what's copied by hand
Wait before next step | Typical time the work sits before anyone touches it | Waits are usually where the days go
What goes wrong | The common exceptions: missing details, no reply, wrong format | Exceptions break automations if nobody plans for them

### How to fill it in
1. Pick a real case from last week, not an average one. Open the actual emails, messages and files.
2. Write each step as it happened, in order, including the awkward bits ("Sam forwards the photo to the office WhatsApp").
3. For each step, write who did it and which tool they used. If two tools were involved, it's probably two steps.
4. Add the wait: how long between this step finishing and the next one starting. Guess if you must, then check against timestamps.
5. Ask the person who does the work to read it. They will add the steps you didn't know about.
6. Fill in the exceptions column from memory of the last month: what made this case go wrong, or nearly go wrong?
7. List the decisions only a person should make, and the information that gets typed in more than once.

### For illustration: a filled-in map
For illustration only, not a real client: a small cleaning company maps "new enquiry to booked first clean". It happens about 15 times a week. Starts when an enquiry arrives; ends when the first clean is in the calendar and the client has a confirmation.
Step | What happens | Who | Tool | Wait before next | What goes wrong
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
1 | Enquiry arrives | Client | Web form, email or phone | Up to a day (inbox checked at night) | Phone enquiries written on paper and lost
2 | Ask for address, size and preferred days | Owner | Email or WhatsApp | 1 to 2 days for the reply | Client never replies
3 | Work out the price | Owner | Price sheet in a spreadsheet | Same day | Unusual jobs need a visit
4 | Send quote | Owner | Email | 2 to 5 days for a decision | No follow-up, quote forgotten
5 | Client accepts; agree a date | Owner | Phone and calendar | Same day | Back-and-forth over dates
6 | Add client to the client list and calendar | Owner | Spreadsheet and calendar | Same day | Details typed twice, sometimes wrongly
7 | Send confirmation and what to expect | Owner | Email | None | Often skipped when busy

### How to read the finished map
Once the map is filled in, go through it with four questions. Each answer points to a different kind of fix.
- Where are the longest waits? Waits for the client (steps 2 and 4 above) are fixed with a reminder that goes out on a set day. Waits for you (step 1) are fixed with an instant reply and a daily list.
- What gets typed twice? Copying the same details between a form, a spreadsheet and a calendar (step 6) is the most reliable thing to automate.
- Which steps need judgement? Pricing an unusual job (step 3) stays with a person. An automation can collect the details and prepare a draft, and you approve it.
- Which steps get skipped when you're busy? Confirmations and follow-ups (steps 4 and 7) are exactly what an automation does every time.

### Common mistakes when mapping
- Mapping how it should work instead of how it did work last week
- Mapping the whole business at once instead of one process with a clear start and end
- Leaving out the waits, which hides the biggest delays
- Leaving out the people who actually do the work
- [Jumping to tools](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) before the map is finished: the map tells you what you need, then you choose how

### From map to brief
A finished map is most of an [automation brief](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-brief-an-automation-project/). Add what "working" means, what must stay manual, and who approves anything sent to clients, and you can hand it to whoever builds it. Our guide on how to brief an automation project has a one-page template for that. If you have several maps and can't decide which to start with, [what to automate first in a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) walks through how to choose.

### How Mike Automations would build this
Mapping how your business works is the first thing Michael does, before anything is built. It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/): bring a filled-in map if you have one, or just describe the process and he'll ask the questions that fill the gaps. Within 48 hours you get a [written plan with a fixed price](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/how-it-works/), showing which steps get automated, which stay with you, and what "working" means.
It's built on the tools you already use, so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days, $2,000 one-off, and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. A person always approves anything AI prepares, and every message to clients uses wording you approved.

### What should a process map include for a small business?
The trigger that starts the process, the point where it ends, and every step in between with who does it, which tool they use, how long the work waits before the next step, and what usually goes wrong.

### Do I need special software to map a process?
No. A table in a document or spreadsheet is enough for a small business. Boxes and arrows help with large processes, but the useful information is the steps, the people, the tools, the waits and the exceptions.

### How long does it take to map a process?
For one process with a clear start and end, about half an hour with a real recent case open in front of you, plus a few minutes for the person who does the work to check it.

## A GDPR checklist before you automate anything with client data
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/ (2026-11-10)

Before you automate anything with client data in the UK, check seven things under the UK GDPR: your lawful basis for each use, a processor contract (Article 28) with every tool that touches the data, that you only move the fields you need, how long each copy is kept, how it is secured, whether it leaves the UK, and whether the work is high risk enough to need a DPIA. If the automation sends emails or texts, the PECR marketing rules apply too.

This GDPR checklist for automating client data is for UK small businesses about to connect a form, a CRM, an email tool or an [AI assistant](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/) to the details clients give them. Automation doesn't change the rules. It changes how many places the data ends up, and how fast a mistake spreads.
Each point below goes back to the UK GDPR text on legislation.gov.uk or to the regulator's guidance, checked in November 2026. This is a practical checklist, not legal advice. If your data is sensitive (health, criminal records, children) or the stakes are high, get advice from a data protection specialist or solicitor before you build.

### First, a change of name: the ICO is now the Information Commission
On 30 September 2026 the office of the Information Commissioner was abolished and its job passed to a new body, the Information Commission, under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 9) Regulations 2026. The guidance is still published at ico.org.uk, and the regulator expects the same things from you. When this article says "the ICO", it means the guidance on that site.
The same Act changed parts of the UK GDPR during 2025 and 2026. Some ICO pages carry a note that they are under review because of it, so check the date at the top of any page you rely on.

### The checklist
Work through this for each automation, not once for the whole business. A tick means you can show it in writing.
# | Check | What "done" looks like | Where the rule is
--- | --- | --- | ---
1 | Lawful basis for each use | A written note: what the automation does with the data, which basis applies, and why | UK GDPR art 6; ICO guide to lawful basis
2 | Privacy notice covers it | Your notice names the purpose and the lawful basis | UK GDPR arts 13 and 14
3 | Processor contract with every tool | Signed or accepted data processing terms for each app in the chain | UK GDPR art 28
4 | Only the fields you need | A list of the fields each step moves, with anything unused removed | UK GDPR art 5(1)(c)
5 | A retention rule for every copy | How long each tool keeps the data, and who deletes it | UK GDPR art 5(1)(e)
6 | Security | Two-factor sign-in, named users only, a tested way to restore | UK GDPR art 32
7 | Where the data goes | Each tool's storage country and the transfer mechanism, if outside the UK | UK GDPR Chapter V; ICO international transfers guide
8 | DPIA if high risk | A screening note, and a full DPIA where the ICO list applies | UK GDPR art 35; ICO DPIA guidance
9 | Automated decisions | A person reviews any significant decision, and clients can contest it | UK GDPR art 22C
10 | Emails and texts | Marketing only with consent or the soft opt-in; service messages kept free of promotion | PECR reg 22; ICO "Identify direct marketing"
11 | Breach plan | Who decides, and how you would report within 72 hours | UK GDPR art 33
12 | Data protection fee | Paid, unless you have checked that you are exempt | Data Protection (Charges and Information) Regulations 2018

### 1. Pick and record a lawful basis
The ICO's guide to lawful basis (updated 2 April 2026) now lists seven lawful bases, not six. The Data (Use and Access) Act added "recognised legitimate interest", which covers a short list of pre-approved purposes such as safeguarding and preventing crime. For most small-business automations the basis will be contract (you need the data to do the work the client asked for), legal obligation (for example, records you must keep) or legitimate interests.
The ICO says you must decide the basis before you start, write it down, and put it in your privacy information. It also warns that you can't usually swap bases later. So decide now: sending a client their appointment details is likely contract; adding them to a newsletter is a different purpose that needs its own basis.

### 2. Get a processor contract for every tool
When an app (or the person who [builds your automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/)) handles client data on your behalf, it is your processor. Article 28 says you may only use processors that give "sufficient guarantees", under a binding contract. Most software companies publish this as a data processing agreement or addendum. Find it for every app in the chain: the form, the automation platform, the CRM, the email or [text sender](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/text-or-whatsapp-clients-for-documents/), and any AI tool.
Article 28(3) lists what the contract must cover. The points worth checking yourself:
- The provider only processes the data on your documented instructions.
- Its staff are bound by confidentiality.
- It has the security measures Article 32 requires.
- It doesn't bring in another processor (a sub-processor) without your authorisation.
- It helps you answer clients' requests, such as access or deletion.
- At the end, it deletes or returns the data, at your choice.
- It gives you the information you need to show compliance, including audits.

### 3. Move only the fields you need
The data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c)) says personal data must be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary". Automation tools make it easy to pass the whole record from one app to the next. Don't. If a reminder text needs a first name, a date and a time, map those three fields and nothing else.
The same goes for AI tools. If you want a draft reply to an enquiry, the AI usually needs the question, not the client's date of birth, address and payment history.

### 4. Set a retention rule for every copy
Article 5(1)(e) says data must be kept in a form that identifies people for no longer than necessary. Every automation makes copies: run logs in the automation platform, rows in a spreadsheet, attachments in an inbox. Check how long each tool keeps its logs, shorten it where you can, and write down who deletes what and when. A rule nobody owns is not a rule.

### 5. Secure the accounts the automation uses
Article 32 asks for security appropriate to the risk, and names measures such as encryption, the ability to restore data after an incident, and regularly testing your measures. For a small business that mostly means: two-factor sign-in on every app, named accounts instead of a shared login, connections made with the least access the tool allows, and a person who is told when something fails.

### 6. Check where the data is stored
Sending personal data to, or making it accessible from, a separate organisation outside the UK is a "restricted transfer". The ICO's brief guide to international transfers (15 January 2026) says it must be covered by UK adequacy regulations, appropriate safeguards (such as the International Data Transfer Agreement or the UK Addendum, plus a transfer risk assessment), or an exception. It also says the rules apply to sole traders, and to small, infrequent transfers.
Many automation and AI tools are run by US companies. The UK-US "data bridge" covers transfers only to US organisations certified to the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, according to the government's factsheet. So check whether the provider is certified, or which safeguard its processing terms rely on. The answer is usually in its data processing agreement.

### 7. Decide whether you need a DPIA
Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. The ICO's list of cases that need one includes "innovative technology", which it says covers the novel use of existing technology, including AI; "data matching", meaning combining personal data from several sources; and decisions about someone's access to a service based to any extent on automated decision-making. The ICO notes that this guidance is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act.
A simple reminder or invoice workflow rarely needs a full DPIA. An AI tool that reads client documents, or a system that combines data from several apps to score clients, may well do. If in doubt, write a short screening note saying why you did or didn't do one.

### 8. Keep a person on significant decisions
Since February 2026 the UK GDPR has Articles 22A to 22D on automated decision-making. Article 22C says that where a significant decision is based solely on automated processing, you must have safeguards that tell the person about the decision, let them make representations, let them get human intervention, and let them contest it. The simplest way to stay on the right side of this: a person approves anything that refuses, charges or cuts off a client.

### 9. Emails and texts: PECR, not only GDPR
Marketing by email or text to individuals falls under the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR). Regulation 22 allows it with consent, or under the "soft opt-in": you got the contact details while selling, or negotiating to sell, something to that person; the marketing is about your own similar products or services; and they were given a simple way to refuse at the time and in every message since.
Many automated messages aren't marketing. The ICO's "Identify direct marketing" guidance treats purely administrative messages, such as confirming or reminding someone about an appointment, as service messages. That only holds while they contain no promotion. Add "book your next service and get 10% off" and the whole message counts as marketing.

### 10. Plan for a breach before it happens
Article 33 says a personal data breach must be reported to the regulator, now the Information Commission, without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. An automation that emails one client's documents to another client is a breach. Decide now who looks at it, who decides whether to report, and where you record it.
Finally, the ICO's data protection fee page says organisations, including sole traders, that use personal information must pay a fee under the Data Protection (Charges and Information) Regulations 2018, unless they are exempt. Check this once and keep a note.

### A note to keep for each automation
Automation data record (one per workflow):
```
Automation: [name, for example "new enquiry to CRM and reply draft"]
Purpose: [what it does for the client or the business]
Lawful basis: [contract / legal obligation / legitimate interests / consent], because [reason]
Data moved: [fields, for example first name, email, enquiry text]
Tools in the chain: [form] > [automation platform] > [CRM] > [email]
Processor terms in place: [yes, link to each DPA]
Stored in: [country per tool]. Transfer mechanism: [adequacy / data bridge / IDTA / Addendum]
Kept for: [period per tool]. Deleted by: [person]
Person who approves: [name, for anything sent to a client or any significant decision]
DPIA: [not needed because... / done on date]
Messages sent: [service only / marketing, with consent or soft opt-in]
Last checked: [date]
```

### How Mike Automations handles this

Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, and the plan lists the fields each step moves, the tools involved and where a person approves. We're not lawyers, and the plan isn't legal advice. You stay the controller of your clients' data, and you decide on the lawful basis and any DPIA.

### Is it GDPR-compliant to automate client emails and reminders?
It can be. The UK GDPR doesn't ban automation. You need a lawful basis, processor terms with each tool, only the data you need, a retention rule and good security. Reminders that only confirm an appointment are service messages; anything promotional must follow the PECR marketing rules.

### Do I need a DPIA to use an AI tool with client data?
Possibly. Article 35 requires one for processing likely to be high risk, and the ICO's list includes innovative technology, including AI. A short screening note helps you decide and shows you considered it.

### Is my automation platform a processor?
Usually yes, when it handles client data on your instructions. Article 28 then requires a contract with the terms it lists. Most providers publish a data processing agreement you can accept.

### Who regulates data protection in the UK now?
The Information Commission, which took over from the Information Commissioner on 30 September 2026 under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Its guidance is published at ico.org.uk.
